en: Vālmīki:
Having entered the great forest of Daṇḍaka, the self-possessed one—
The invincible Rāma beheld the circle of the ascetics' hermitage,
strewn with *kuśa* grass and bark garments, and enveloped in Brahmanic splendor;
it was like the blazing orb of the sun in the sky, difficult to gaze upon.
It was a refuge for all beings, with its courtyards always well-swept;
it was constantly honored and celebrated by throngs of Apsarases,
and provided with spacious fire-sanctuaries, sacrificial ladles, vessels, deerskins, and kusha grass.
It was adorned with sacrificial fuel, water-jars, and fruits and roots;
it was surrounded by great, holy forest trees bearing sweet fruit;
it was sanctified by offerings and oblations, and resounded with the chanting of the Vedas.

It was surrounded by wild flowers and a lotus pond filled with lotuses; it was filled with ancient sages who subsisted on fruits and roots, were self-controlled, wore garments of bark and black antelope skins, and possessed a radiance like that of the sun or fire.
Adorned by supreme sages who subsist on merit and have no fixed diet,
that place resembles the abode of Brahmā and resounds with the chanting of the Vedas;
it is graced by highly fortunate Brahmins who are knowers of Brahman.
Having seen that circle of ascetic hermitages, the glorious Rāghava,
possessed of great splendor, approached it after unstringing his mighty bow.
Upon seeing Rāma, those great seers, endowed with divine knowledge, [welcomed him].
Then, filled with joy, they approached the illustrious Vaidehī;
seeing him like the rising moon, those practitioners of dharma,
firm in their vows, welcomed him while reciting auspicious blessings.
Those dwelling in the forest gazed with expressions of wonder upon Rāma’s physical symmetry, his splendor, his delicacy, and his elegant attire;
they looked at Vaidehī, Lakṣmaṇa, and Rāma as if with unblinking eyes.
All those forest-dwellers beheld him as something truly marvelous. For there, those highly fortunate ones, devoted to the welfare of all beings,
settled the descendant of Raghu, their guest, within a leaf-hut.
Then those highly fortunate practitioners of dharma, resembling fire in their brilliance, having honored Rāma according to the prescribed rites, brought water,
roots, flowers, wild fruits, and the hermitage of that great-souled one.
Having made their report, those knowers of dharma then spoke with palms joined in reverence:
"The protector of this people, the refuge of all, and the one of great fame; the king who is to be worshipped and honored, the wielder of the rod of justice, and the teacher."

"O Raghava, a king protects his subjects as the fourth part of Indra himself; therefore, honored by the world, he enjoys the pleasures of the forest. We, who dwell within your domain, are to be protected by you."
Whether you dwell in the city or in the forest, you are our king, O lord of men.
We have laid aside the rod of punishment, O King, having conquered anger and mastered our senses; we, whose wealth is asceticism, must be constantly protected by you as if we were embryos.
Having spoken thus, they honored Rāghava, along with Lakṣmaṇa, with wild fruits, roots, flowers, and various other kinds of food. Likewise,
other perfected ascetics, who were like the god of fire, paid homage to Rāma.
3.001.022c Conducting themselves with righteousness, they gratified the Lord according to the prescribed rule.
3.002.001a Then Rāma, having performed the rites of hospitality until sunrise,
took leave of all the sages and entered deep into the forest.

It was crowded with various herds of wild animals and frequented by tigers and wolves; its trees, creepers, and shrubs were destroyed, and its pools of water were difficult to see; it was devoid of the cries of various birds and resounded only with the humming of swarms of crickets.

Followed by Lakṣmaṇa, Rāma beheld the middle of the forest. In the midst of that forest, which was teeming with fierce wild beasts, the descendant of Kakutstha saw a man-eater of great roar, resembling a mountain peak.
With deep-set eyes, a large mouth, and a hideous, uneven belly; loathsome, asymmetrical, tall, deformed, and terrible to behold;
he was wearing a tiger skin, moist with fat and smeared with blood.
It struck terror into all beings, like Death himself with his mouth wide open.
[He saw] three lions, four tigers, two wolves, ten spotted deer,
and the great head of an elephant, complete with tusks and smeared with fat.
Seeing him impaled upon an iron stake, screaming with a great roar,
and beholding Lakṣmaṇa and Sītā, the princess of Mithilā,
Rāma rushed forward in a towering rage like Death himself at the end of an eon.
3.002.009c Emitting a terrifying roar as if making the earth tremble,
3.002.010a he took Vaidehī in his arms, stepped aside, and then said:
3.002.010c "You two, wearing matted hair and bark garments, along with your wife, have reached the end of your lives."

"Having entered the Daṇḍaka forest bearing arrows, bows, and swords, how can you two dwell there with a young woman? You are practitioners of unrighteousness and sinners; who are you two who defile the sages?"
"I am a Rākṣasa named Virādha, who roams this impenetrable forest,
always armed and devouring the flesh of sages. This woman of beautiful limbs shall become my wife."
"O you two wicked ones, I shall drink your blood in battle!
Hearing these arrogant words spoken by that insolent and evil-minded Virādha, Janaka’s daughter was filled with agitation.
3.002.014e Sītā trembled with agitation like a plantain tree in a gale.
3.002.015a Seeing the auspicious Sītā held in Virādha’s embrace, Rāghava,
his mouth parched, spoke these words to Lakṣmaṇa.
"Behold, gentle one, the daughter of King Janaka,
my wife of auspicious conduct, who has been cast into the lap of Virādha—
this illustrious princess, raised in extreme luxury."
"O Lakṣmaṇa, that which was intended for us, that dear boon which was chosen, has now been fully accomplished for Kaikeyī this very day;
she who, though far-sighted, found no satisfaction in the kingdom for the sake of her son."
"By her I was sent to the forest for the welfare of all beings;
today at last that middle mother of mine has had her desire fulfilled. Yet, nothing is more painful to me than the touch of Vaidehī by another."
"O Saumitri, because of the destruction of my father and likewise the seizure of my own kingdom"—
when the descendant of Kakutstha had spoken thus, overwhelmed by tears and grief,
Lakṣmaṇa, enraged and hissing like a confined serpent, replied.
"O descendant of Kakutstha, you are the protector of all beings like Vasava himself, yet you are like one who is helpless. Why do you grieve when I, your servant,
have today struck down this Rākṣasa with my arrow in my wrath?"

3.002.022c For the earth shall drink the blood of the lifeless Virādha. 3.002.023a That anger of mine which was directed toward Bharata because of his desire for the kingdom— 3.002.023c I shall release it upon Virādha, as the wielder of the thunderbolt hurls the vajra at a mountain.
Let this great arrow, impelled by the force and speed of my arm-strength, fall upon his broad chest and take away the life from his body.
Then, reeling, he fell to the earth;
and thereafter Virādha, filling the forest with his voice, spoke these words again:
"Tell me who you are as I ask you: where are you two going?"
Then Rāma, possessed of great splendor, spoke to that rakṣasa of flaming countenance who was inquiring about his own Ikṣvāku lineage:
"Know us to be two kṣatriyas, endowed with virtuous conduct, now dwelling in the forest."
"But we wish to know you: who are you that wanders through the Daṇḍaka forest? Virādha spoke to Rāma, whose prowess is truth:
"Indeed, O King, I shall tell you; listen to me, O Raghava."
"I am indeed the son of Jaya, and my mother is Śatahradā;
all the rākṣasas on earth call me Virādha.
Furthermore, through my ascetic penance, I have obtained [these powers] born of the grace of Brahmā."
"Your invulnerability to weapons in this world, as well as your indestructibility and impenetrability—
casting aside this woman and disregarding her, depart quickly as you came; I shall not take your lives."
3.003.008 With eyes bloodshot with anger, Rāma replied thus to that evil-minded Rākṣasa Virādha of deformed appearance:
3.003.009 "O base one, shame on you! You of inferior purpose are surely seeking your own death."
"Stay! You shall meet me in battle; you will not escape from me alive.
Then Rāma, having strung his bow and aimed very sharp arrows with great speed, struck down the rākṣasa.
With his bow strung with a cord, he released seven arrows— gold-feathered, of great velocity, and moving like Garuda or the wind— which,
adorned with peacock feathers, pierced the body of Virādha.
Smeared with blood and resembling fire, they fell upon the earth.
Having let out a great roar and seizing a spear that resembled the banner of Indra,
he then appeared resplendent like Death himself with his mouth wide open.
Rāma, the best among wielders of weapons, severed that spear— which resembled a thunderbolt and blazed like fire in the sky— with two arrows;
then the son of Sumitrā broke the left arm of that fierce one.

But Rāma, with his own strength, [seized] the right arm of that rākṣasa. With his arm broken and filled with agitation, the rākṣasa, resembling a cloud, quickly fell to the earth like a mountain shattered by a thunderbolt.
3.003.016e Virādha spoke thus to that descendant of Kakutstha, the bull among men:
3.003.017a "O dear one, you are known by me as Rāma, the noble son of Kausalyā;
and so too are the highly fortunate Vaidehī and the greatly illustrious Lakṣmaṇa."
"Due to a curse, I have entered this terrible rakshasa body;
for I am a gandharva named Tumburu who was cursed by Vaiśravaṇa. Though I sought his favor, that highly illustrious one spoke thus to me:"
"When Rāma, the son of Daśaratha, slays you in battle,
then, having returned to your natural state, you shall go to heaven.
Thus did King Vaiśravaṇa speak to him who was infatuated with Rambhā.
"Being neglected by me, he spoke to me in great anger:
'By your grace, I have been released from a most terrible curse;
I shall go to my own abode. May it be well with you, O scorcher of foes!'"
"Three yojanas from here, my dear, dwells the righteous and powerful great seer Śarabhaṅga, who resembles the sun.
Go to him quickly; he will provide for your welfare."
"O Rāma, having cast me even into a pit, depart in safety;
for this is the eternal law for Rākṣasas whose vitality has departed:
those who are placed in a pit attain eternal worlds."

Having spoken thus to the descendant of Kakutstha, the mighty Virādha, afflicted by the arrows, cast off his body and attained heaven. Lifting up that loud-voiced one, whose ears were like spikes, he held him by the neck.
He threw Virādha, who was crying out with a terrifying sound, into a pit.
Then, having slain the Rākṣasa, those two, whose variegated golden bows were still in their hands, took hold of the princess of Mithilā.
3.003.027c Those two roamed joyfully in the great forest,
like the moon and the sun stationed in the sky;
3.004.001a having slain that Rākṣasa Virādha of fearsome strength in the forest.
Then, having embraced Sītā and comforted her,
the valiant Rāma spoke to his brother Lakṣmaṇa, who was possessed of radiant splendor:
"This forest is difficult and perilous, and we are not accustomed to dwelling in the woods."
"Let us go quickly to Śarabhaṅga, whose wealth is his asceticism.
Rāghava then proceeded to the hermitage of Śarabhaṅga,
who possessed divine power and whose soul was purified by austerity.
Near Śarabhaṅga, he beheld a great marvel:
the Lord of the Gods, shining with a body like the sun or fire,
he saw him not touching the earth.
He saw the god adorned with radiant ornaments, wearing stainless garments,
being worshipped by many great-souled beings of his own kind,
seated upon a chariot drawn by tawny horses and traveling through the intermediate space.
Not far from him, he saw a spotless umbrella, resembling the young sun,
appearing like a mass of white clouds, and similar to the orb of the moon;
it was adorned with variegated garlands.
Two excellent yak-tail fans with golden handles, of great value,
were held by two forest goddesses and fanned over his head;
and many Gandharvas, gods, Siddhas, and supreme sages [were present].
They praised with supreme words the god who had come through the intermediate space.
Having seen Indra, the performer of a hundred sacrifices, there, Rāma said to Lakṣmaṇa:
"These are the horses of Puruhūta Śakra that we have heard of in the past."
"3.004.011 These celestial bay horses moving through the atmosphere are certainly divine.
3.004.012 And these tigers among men who stand around the chariot— by the hundreds, young men wearing earrings and holding swords in their hands."
3.004.013a On the chests of them all were necklaces resembling blazing fire;
3.004.013c they bore, O son of Sumitrā, the appearance of twenty-five-year-olds. 3.004.014a For this, it is said, is the constant age of the gods.
"Just as these tigers among men appear so pleasing to behold,
stay here for a moment with Vaidehī, Lakṣmaṇa,
while I ascertain clearly who this radiant man on the chariot is."
Having spoken thus to the son of Sumitrā, "Stay right here," the descendant of Kakutstha proceeded toward the hermitage of Śarabhaṅga. Then,
seeing Rāma approaching, the Lord of Śacī—
Having taken leave of Śarabhaṅga, he spoke thus to the gods:
"While this Rāma is approaching here and has not yet addressed me, lead me to my final end;
only then will he be worthy to see me."
"Before long, I shall behold him victorious and having accomplished his purpose;
for he must perform a great task that is exceedingly difficult for others. Having thus addressed and honored the ascetic, the wielder of the thunderbolt [departed].
3.004.020c The subduer of enemies departed for heaven in a chariot yoked with bay horses.
3.004.021a When the thousand-eyed Indra had departed, Rāghava, together with his retinue,
approached Śarabhaṅga as he sat performing the *agnihotra* sacrifice.
Having clasped his feet, Rāma, Sītā, and Lakṣmaṇa sat down,
permitted by him, having been invited and granted lodging.
Then that descendant of Raghu inquired about Śakra’s arrival.
And Śarabhaṅga reported all of that to Rāghava:
"O Rāma, this granter of boons wishes to lead me to the world of Brahmā;
it has been won by him through fierce austerity, a place difficult for those of undisciplined souls to attain."
"O tiger among men, knowing that you were nearby,
I did not go to the world of Brahmā without having seen you, my beloved guest. Having met with you, I shall go to the third heaven, which is frequented by the gods."
"O tiger among men, imperishable and auspicious worlds have been won by me;
accept from me those belonging to Brahmā and those situated upon the vault of heaven.
Thus addressed, that tiger among men, who was learned in all the scriptures, [replied].
The seer Śarabhaṅga spoke these words to Rāghava:
"O great sage, I myself shall bring all the worlds [to you];
however, I desire a dwelling place designated for me here in this forest."
Thus addressed by Rāghava, who was indeed equal in strength to Śakra,
the highly wise Śarabhaṅga spoke these words once more:
"Go to the ascetic Sutīkṣṇa in that pure region."
"In a delightful forest region, he will provide you with a dwelling.
This is the path, O tiger among men; wait for me for a moment, dear one, while I cast off my limbs like a serpent sheds its worn-out skin."

Then, having kindled the fire and offered oblations of clarified butter with mantras, the highly effulgent Śarabhaṅga, who was skilled in sacred lore, entered the flames. The fire consumed the body hair and the hair on the head of that great-souled one.
Having cast off his worn-out skin, as well as his bones, flesh, and blood,
that youth, resembling fire itself, came into being;
rising from that heap of fire, Śarabhaṅga shone with splendor.
3.004.035a Having transcended the worlds of those who maintain the sacred fires, of the high-souled rishis,
and of the gods, he ascended to the world of Brahmā.
3.004.036a That bull among the twice-born, a man of meritorious deeds, [ascended] to that realm.
He beheld the Grandfather together with his attendants; and the Grandfather, seeing that twice-born one,
rejoiced and said, "A most welcome greeting to you!"
When Śarabhaṅga had ascended to heaven, hosts of sages gathered together and approached Rāma, the descendant of Kakutstha, who was blazing with splendor—
namely the Vaikhānasas, the Vālakhilyas, the Saṃprakṣālas, and the Marīcipās.
There were many ascetics who ground their food with stones, those who subsisted on leaves,
those who used their teeth as a mortar, and likewise others who remained submerged in water; there were sages who lived on water and others who subsisted on air alone.
Some dwell in the open air, while others sleep upon the bare ground; likewise, some live with their heads uplifted, self-restrained, and clad in wet garments;
they are constant in their recitations and penances, and some practice the austerity of the five fires.
3.005.005 All those ascetics, endowed with the splendor of Brahman and firmly established in yoga,
approached Rāma at the hermitage of Śarabhaṅga. 3.005.006 And having approached Rāma, the knower of dharma and the best among the upholders of dharma, they [spoke].
3.005.006c The assembled hosts of sages, composed in mind, spoke to him who knows the supreme dharma:
3.005.007a "You are the great chariot-warrior of this Ikṣvāku lineage and of the earth;
3.005.007c you are the foremost and the protector, just as Maghavan is for the gods."

Renowned throughout the three worlds for both your glory and your prowess, in you reside devotion to your father, truthfulness, and abundant righteousness. Having approached you, a high-souled one who knows the dharma and is devoted to dharma—
"O Lord, out of necessity we shall speak; you ought to forgive us for that.
For great unrighteousness, O dear one, would accrue to that lord of the earth who takes a sixth part as tribute yet does not protect his subjects like his own children."
3.005.011 Like one harnessing his own vital breaths with his breaths, or like one tending to beloved sons,

he who is ever-yoked and always protects all those dwelling within his realm, O Rāma, attains eternal fame that lasts for many years. 3.005.012 He attains eternal fame, O Rāma, that endures for many years.
Having attained the station of Brahman, he is glorified there as well. Whatever supreme dharma a sage who subsists on roots and fruits performs,
a fourth part of that belongs to the king who protects his subjects with righteousness.

"O Rāma, this great multitude of forest-dwellers, consisting mostly of brahmins, has you as its protector; yet, being like those without a protector, it is being slaughtered mercilessly by the rākṣasas. Come and behold the bodies of these sages of purified souls."

A great slaughter is being carried out in the forest against many who dwell by the Pampā river, along the Mandākinī, and in Citrakūṭa— many of whom have been slain in various ways by the terrible Rākṣasas.
"Thus, we cannot endure this terrible mistreatment being inflicted upon an ascetic in the forest by Rākṣasas of fearsome deeds; therefore,
we have come to you for refuge, O worthy protector."
"O Rāma, protect us who are being slaughtered by the night-stalkers!
Having heard this from the ascetic practitioners of penance, the righteous-souled descendant of Kakutstha spoke these words to all those ascetics:
"You should not speak to me in this way; I am one who must command the ascetic.
I have come here by chance for the sake of accomplishing your purpose, and my dwelling in this forest shall yield great fruit."
"O ascetics, I desire to slay the Rākṣasa enemies in battle. Having granted this boon to those whose wealth is their austerity, my soul is now fixed upon righteousness, together with Lakṣmaṇa."
Accompanied by those whose wealth was asceticism and following their prescribed conduct,
the hero went to Sutīkṣṇa.
Then Rāma, the scorcher of enemies, together with his brother and Sītā, [proceeded].
3.006.001 He went to the hermitage of Sutīkṣṇa together with those twice-born ones.
3.006.002 Having traveled a long distance and crossed many rivers of abundant water,
he beheld a vast mountain rising high like a great cloud.
Then those two descendants of Raghu, the best of the Ikṣvākus, entered that forest together with Sītā— a forest constantly filled with various kinds of trees.
Having entered the formidable forest, which was full of trees bearing many flowers and fruits, they proceeded.

In a secluded spot, he beheld an hermitage adorned with garlands of bark-cloth. There, Rāma addressed Sutīkṣṇa— who was seated, bearing matted locks and covered in the dust of dirt, and who had increased in ascetic merit— in accordance with the prescribed rites.
"I am Rāma, O Blessed One; I have come to see you.
Therefore, address me, O knower of dharma, O great seer of true valor.
Then, having gazed upon the hero Rāma, the best among the upholders of dharma, he [spoke].
Embracing him with both arms, he spoke these words:
"Welcome indeed to you, O hero, O Rāma, best among the upholders of dharma!
This hermitage, now that it has been entered by you, is as if it has found its protector."
"O illustrious hero, waiting for you alone,
I did not ascend to the world of the gods from this earth after casting off my body;
for I have heard that you were exiled from the kingdom and had gone to Citrakūṭa."
"Kakutstha, the king of the gods, Śatakratu, has arrived here and said that all the worlds have been conquered by my meritorious deeds—
those worlds frequented by celestial sages which were won by me through ascetic penance."
"By my grace, you may dwell together with your wife and Lakṣmaṇa.
To that great seer of fierce austerities, radiant and truthful in speech,
the self-possessed Rāma replied, as Vāsava might to Brahmā.
"O great sage, I myself shall create the worlds;
however, I desire a dwelling place designated for me here in this forest. You are skilled in all matters and devoted to the welfare of all beings."
3.006.014c He was thus described by the high-souled Śarabhaṅga Gautama.
3.006.015a Having been addressed in this way by Rāma, the great seer renowned throughout the world 3.006.015c spoke these sweet words, overflowing with great joy.
"O Rāma, this very hermitage is virtuous; let us take our pleasure here. It is frequented by throngs of sages and is always provided with roots and fruits.
O highly illustrious one, having come to this hermitage, the herds of deer [dwell here]."
Having wandered about and enticed them, those who have nothing to fear depart.
Having heard those words of the great seer, the steadfast elder brother of Lakṣmaṇa drew his bow with an arrow and spoke these words.
"O highly fortunate one, if I were to strike those gathered herds of deer with a sharp-edged arrow possessing the brilliance of a thunderbolt,
you would be grieved by that; what could be more distressing than that?"
"I do not intend to dwell in this hermitage for long.
Having spoken thus to the granter of boons, Rāma approached the evening twilight;
having performed the evening rites, he made his dwelling there for the night.
Then the high-souled Sutīkṣṇa himself, having honored them with great respect, gave those two bulls among men auspicious food fit for ascetics.
When the twilight had passed and seeing that night had arrived,
Rāma, together with the son of Sumitrā, having been honored by Sutīkṣṇa,
spent the night there and woke up at dawn.
Then, having risen at the proper time, Rāghava, together with Sītā,
performed his ablutions with very cool water scented with the fragrance of lotuses.
Then Vaidehī, Rāma, and Lakṣmaṇa [honored] the fire and the gods.
Having duly worshipped [the deity] at dawn in that forest, the refuge of ascetics,
and having seen the sun rising, they were cleansed of their sins;
approaching Sutīkṣṇa, they spoke these gentle words.
"O Blessed One, we have been well-rested and honored by you, who are yourself worthy of honor. We take our leave and shall depart, for the sages urge us on.
We are in haste to see the entire circle of hermitages."
"We wish to be permitted to depart together with these bulls among sages— the seers of virtuous character dwelling in the Daṇḍaka forest,
who are constant in dharma, self-controlled through austerity, and like fires without smoke."
"Until the sun, with its unbearable heat, shines no longer intensely—
like one devoid of lineage who has obtained fortune arrived by an improper path—
we wish to depart," having said this, [they touched] the feet of the sage.
Rāghava, together with Saumitri and Sītā, paid his respects.
Raising them up as they touched his feet, that bull among sages embraced them firmly and spoke these words with affection:
"Go safely on your path, Rāma, together with the son of Sumitrā and with this Sītā, who follows you like a shadow. Behold the lovely hermitage of those who dwell in the Daṇḍaka forest."
O hero, for these ascetics whose souls are purified by austerity,
there are forests abounding in excellent fruits and roots and in full bloom,
where herds of deer are peaceful and flocks of birds are tranquil.
You will see ponds and lakes filled with blooming lotuses and clear waters, strewn with *kāraṇḍava* ducks, as well as mountain cascades that are delightful to the sight.
"The forests are delightful and filled with the cries of peacocks. Go, my child Saumitri, and you too must go;
but after you have seen [all that], you must return once more to my hermitage."
Having been addressed thus, the descendant of Kakutstha, together with Lakṣmaṇa, replied, "So be it," and after circumambulating the sage, he prepared to depart.
Then the large-eyed lady [Sītā] took up her two most auspicious quivers and her two bows.
Then Sītā gave those two brothers two stainless swords;
having fastened on two auspicious quivers and taking up their sounding bows,
both Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa departed from the hermitage to go forth.
3.008.001 When the joy of the Raghus had been granted leave by Sutīkṣṇa and was about to depart,
Vaidehī addressed these words to her husband in an affectionate voice:
3.008.002 "This great dharma is attained through a most subtle method."
And by one who has desisted from this, it is possible to be freed from the calamity born of desire;
for here there are indeed three calamities born of desire:
false speech is the foremost, while the other two are even more serious than that.

3.008.003e Approaching another’s wife without enmity and cruelty; 3.008.004a False speech—such has not occurred for you, O Rāghava, nor will it ever happen. 3.008.004c How could there be a longing for the wives of others, which destroys righteousness?

"O mighty-armed one, all of that can be borne by those who have conquered their senses. O you of auspicious appearance, I know your mastery over the senses; yet there remains this third, terrible thing: the harming of the lives of others."

Out of delusion, you have committed an act of enmity, and now that very consequence has arrived for you. O hero, you promised for the sake of protecting the sages dwelling in the Daṇḍaka forest the slaughter of the rākṣasas in battle.
And for this reason, this forest is renowned as Daṇḍaka.
You have set out with your brother, bearing your bow and arrows;
seeing you thus departed, my mind is overwhelmed with anxiety.
3.008.009c While reflecting upon your conduct, there will surely arise what is most beneficial and salutary.
3.008.010a O hero, my departure toward the Daṇḍaka forest does not please me.
3.008.010c I shall state the reason for this; listen to me as I speak.
"For you, with bow and arrows in hand, having gone to the forest with your brother,
might you not discharge your shafts upon seeing all those who dwell in the woods? For in this world, the bow is the weapon of Kṣatriyas, and firewood is for the sacrificial fire."
3.008.012c Standing nearby, his splendor and strength increased greatly.
3.008.013a O mighty-armed one, it is said that in former times there was a certain ascetic, truthful in speech and pure, who took delight in a sacred forest filled with deer and birds.
Then Indra, the lord of Śacī, in order to create an obstacle to that very asceticism,
arrived at the hermitage bearing a sword in his hand and assuming the form of a soldier.
That excellent sword was deposited by him in that hermitage site.
3.008.015c Given according to the rite of deposit while he remained engaged in meritorious asceticism,
3.008.016a having received that weapon, he became intent on guarding the deposit;
3.008.016c wandering indeed through the forest, he protected his own reputation.
Wherever he went to gather roots and fruits,
he never left that sword behind, being intent on guarding his deposit;
constantly carrying that weapon, that ascetic gradually [advanced].
He made his own intellect fierce, abandoning his resolve for asceticism. Then, devoted to cruelty, intoxicated, and dragged down by unrighteousness,
that sage went to hell because of his association with that weapon.

Out of affection and great respect, I am merely reminding you; I am not instructing you. You must never, under any circumstances, entertain the thought of killing the Rākṣasas dwelling in Daṇḍaka with your bow drawn, unless it is for the sake of enmity.

"O hero, I do not desire to slay people without fault. For Kṣatriya heroes who have restrained their selves in the forests, the purpose of the bow is solely this: the protection of those who are distressed."
Where is the weapon, and where is the forest? Where is the duty of a Kshatriya, and where is asceticism? This [way of life] is contradictory for us; rather, let the laws of the country be honored.
Thus, from the practice of weapons, a mind clouded by ignoble thoughts arises.

"Having returned once more to Ayodhyā, you shall practice the duty of a kṣatriya. My mother-in-law and father-in-law would experience inexhaustible joy if, having renounced the kingdom, you were to become a devoted sage."
From dharma arises wealth; from dharma arises happiness.
Through dharma one obtains everything; this world has dharma as its essence. Having diligently disciplined the self through various restraints, [one attains this].

3.008.027c Dharma is attained by those who are skillful; happiness is not obtained through ease. 3.008.028a O gentle one, with a mind ever pure, practice dharma in this forest of asceticism. 3.008.028c For everything, even the three worlds, is known to you in its true essence.
"This was spoken by me out of a woman's fickleness;
for who is capable of teaching you the Dharma? Yet, having reflected with your intellect along with your younger brother,"
"Do whatever pleases you; do not delay.
Having heard these words spoken by Vaidehī out of devotion to her husband, Rāma, remaining firm in dharma, then replied to the princess of Mithilā.
"O Queen, you have spoken words that are beneficial and worthy of your affectionate nature, O knower of dharma, daughter of Janaka, as you proclaim your noble lineage.
However, O Queen, I shall say this: these very words were already spoken by you."
3.009.003c Kṣatriyas carry the bow so that the cry of the distressed may not arise.
3.009.004a Yet those sages of firm vows in the Daṇḍaka forest are themselves distressed; O Sītā, having come to me in person, they—worthy of providing refuge—have sought my protection.
3.009.005a Dwelling in the forest, devoted to dharma and subsisting on roots and fruits,
3.009.005c they find no happiness, being terrified by the Rākṣasas of cruel deeds. 3.009.006a And at the proper times, they remain engaged in various religious observances within the forest.

"They are being devoured by terrifying Rākṣasas who subsist on human flesh. While being devoured, those sages dwelling in the Daṇḍaka forest, the best of the twice-born, said to me, "Come to our aid!"
Having heard these words falling from their very mouths,
and having performed service at their feet, I spoke this speech:
"May you all be gracious toward me, for this shame of mine is indeed incomparable."
"Since I have been attended by such Brahmins worthy of being approached,
what shall I do?"— this was spoken by me in the presence of the twice-born. Then, having all come together, this speech was uttered by them all:

"O Rāma, we have been greatly oppressed by many Rākṣasas in the Daṇḍaka forest who can assume any form at will; you ought to protect us. O sinless one, when the time for the fire-oblation has arrived, as well as during the sacred festival days,"
The invincible, flesh-eating Rākṣasas have been attacking [us].
For us ascetics and practitioners of austerity who have been thus assailed by the Rākṣasas and are searching for a refuge, you are our supreme refuge.
"Granted, by the power of our asceticism we are capable of slaying the night-stalkers;
yet, we do not wish to diminish our ascetic merit accumulated over a long time.
For asceticism, O Raghava, is constantly beset by many obstacles and is indeed difficult to practice."
Therefore, even while being devoured by the *rākṣasas*, we did not release the curse.
Thus, as we are being tormented by the *rākṣasas* dwelling in the Daṇḍaka forest, you, together with your brother, must protect us; for in the forest, we have you as our protector.

"O daughter of Janaka, having heard these words of the sages in their entirety, I pledged to protect them in the Daṇḍaka forest. And having made that pledge, I shall not be able to remain alive if I fail to fulfill my promise."
For it is my constant desire that the truth of the sages should never be otherwise;
O Sītā, I would sooner abandon my own life, or even you along with Lakṣmaṇa,
than break a promise once made, especially one given to brahmins.

"Therefore, O Vaidehī, the protection of the sages must certainly be carried out by me, even if it were not spoken; how much more so now that I have given my promise? These words were spoken by you out of affection and friendship for me."
"I am well pleased with you, Sītā; for one who is not displeased does not offer instruction. O beautiful one, this is worthy of and befitting your lineage.
Having spoken these words, the high-souled one—
Accompanied by his beloved Sītā, the princess of Mithilā, and by Lakṣmaṇa, Rāma, bearing his bow,
proceeded to the delightful forest hermitages of ascetics.
Rāma went in front, Sītā of the slender waist in the middle,
and Lakṣmaṇa followed behind with bow in hand.
The two of them beheld various mountain ridges and forests.
Together with Sītā, they went to various delightful rivers;
[they saw] cranes and ruddy geese wandering on the riverbanks,
and lakes filled with lotuses and frequented by water-birds.
They saw spotted deer bound in herds, horned buffaloes intoxicated with rut,
wild boars, and elephants— the enemies of trees.
Having traveled a long distance while the sun was hanging low, they proceeded further.
Together they beheld a delightful lake, a yojana in length,
thick with lotuses and water-lilies, adorned by herds of elephants,
and teeming with cranes, swans, ducks, and other water-birds.
In that beautiful lake of clear waters,
the sound of singing and musical instruments was heard, yet no one at all could be seen.
Then, out of curiosity, Rāma and the great chariot-warrior Lakṣmaṇa [approached].
He began to question the sage named Dharmabhṛt:
"O great sage, having heard this most wonderful thing from all of us, a great curiosity has arisen; please tell us what this is."
Thus addressed by Rāghava, the righteous sage then began to recount the entire power of that lake:
"This reservoir is named Pañcāpsaras; it possesses water at all times."

O Rāma, this was created by the sage Māṇḍakarṇi through his ascetic power. For that great sage Māṇḍakarṇi performed intense penance for ten thousand years, subsisting on air alone and dwelling in the water.
Then all the gods, led by Agni, were deeply distressed;
having gathered together, they all spoke these words:
"This sage seeks the station of one of us."
Then, all the gods dispatched five principal Apsarases, whose splendor was like flashing lightning, to create an obstacle to his asceticism. Thereupon,
the sage— who had realized both the higher and the lower truths— was encountered by those Apsarases.
He was brought under the power of passion for the sake of accomplishing the purpose of the gods;
and those very Apsarases became the wives of the five sages. For them, a hidden dwelling was constructed within this lake.

Right there, five Apsarases dwell at their pleasure; through the power of his asceticism, they delight the sage who has been restored to youth. This sound of musical instruments belongs to them as they sport together.

"The enchanting sound of singing, mingled with the tinkling of ornaments, is heard. To these words of that noble-minded one, "How wonderful! the highly illustrious Rāghava, together with his brother, gave his assent.
While he was speaking thus, he beheld the precincts of the hermitage,
surrounded by mats of kusha grass and bark garments, and filled with various kinds of trees.
Having entered it together with Vaidehī and Lakṣmaṇa, Rāghava [proceeded further].
Then, having dwelt most happily in that glorious circle of hermitages while being honored there by the great seers, that descendant of Kakutstha proceeded in turn to the hermitages of those ascetics.
That master of great weapons formerly dwelt in the presence of some for ten months, in others for one year,
in some for four months, and in others for five or six.
In some places he dwelt for more than a month, and in others for a month and a half; Rāghava lived happily for three months and eight months in the hermitages of the sages as he resided there.

3.010.025e And as they took their pleasure together in harmony, ten years passed by. 3.010.026a Having wandered about, the illustrious Rāghava, who knows the dharma, returned once again with Sītā to the hermitage of Sutīkṣṇa.

Having arrived at that hermitage and being honored by the sages, Rāma, the subduer of enemies, dwelt there for some time as well. Then, while staying in the hermitage, he once approached that great sage with humility.
Seated there, that descendant of Kakutstha spoke thus to Sutīkṣṇa:
"O Blessed One, I have constantly heard from those telling stories that the most excellent of sages, Agastya, dwells in this forest."
But due to the vastness of this forest, I do not know that region;
where is the holy hermitage of that wise great seer?
Through your favor, may he [be found] there along with his younger brother and Sītā.
"I would go to Agastya to pay my respects to that sage;
this great desire revolves within my heart—
that I myself might serve that best of sages."
Having heard these words of the righteous Rāma,
the sage Sutīkṣṇa, being pleased, replied thus to the son of Daśaratha:
"I too was desirous of saying this very same thing to you, along with Lakṣmaṇa."
"O Rāghava, go to Agastya together with Sītā.
"By good fortune, you yourself now speak to me regarding this matter.
"My child, I shall tell you where the great sage Agastya dwells."
"O dear one, go four yojanas from this hermitage;
to the south there is the great and glorious hermitage of Agastya’s brother,
situated in a region of land mostly covered by forest and adorned with groves of long pepper trees."
Abounding in many flowers and fruits, delightful, and resounding with the songs of various birds;
there were various lotus ponds with clear, auspicious waters,
crowded with swans and kāraṇḍava ducks, and graced by ruddy geese.

Having stayed there for one night, O Rāma, you should set out at dawn toward the southern direction, along the edge of the forest tract. Having gone there, you will reach the site of Agastya’s hermitage after a distance of one *yojana*.
In that delightful forest region, thickly covered with many trees,
Vaidehī shall find delight there along with Lakṣmaṇa and you;
for that forest region is indeed charming and crowded with many trees.
"If you have made up your mind to see that great sage Agastya,
O highly illustrious one, resolve now to go this very day.
Having heard this from the sage, Rāma, together with his brother, offered his salutations.
Accompanied by his younger brother and Sītā, he set out toward Agastya,
beholding on the way various wonderful forests, mountains resembling clouds,
lakes, and rivers, following the course of the path.
Having traveled easily along that path as instructed by Sutīkṣṇa,
he, filled with supreme joy, spoke these words to Lakṣmaṇa:
"This must surely be the hermitage of that great-souled one."
The meritorious deeds of the sage Agastya, his brother, are visible here;
for just as these trees of this forest are known by the thousands along the path, they are all bent low by the weight of their fruit and the weight of their flowers.
"47. And this scent of ripe pippalī fruits, rising pungently and suddenly wafted by the wind, has come from this forest. 48.
And here and there, heaps of wood are seen gathered together."
3.010.048c And along the path, cut darbha grasses are seen, possessing the luster of lapis lazuli.
3.010.049a And this, situated in the middle of the forest, resembling the peak of a black cloud— 3.010.049c the crest of smoke from the fire dwelling in the hermitage, is clearly visible.
3.010.050a And in secluded sacred fords, the twice-born, having performed their ablutions,
3.010.050c offer oblations of flowers with blossoms gathered by themselves.
3.010.051a O gentle one, that speech of Sutīkṣṇa was heard by me exactly as it was spoken.
"This must surely be the hermitage of Agastya’s brother,
who, desiring the welfare of the worlds, forcibly subdued Death;
it is by his meritorious brother that this quarter has been made a place of refuge."
3.010.053a Once upon a time here, it is said, there were two cruel and great asuras, Vātāpi and Ilvala, who lived together as brothers and were slayers of brahmins.
3.010.054a Assuming the form of a brahmin, that Ilvala would speak in refined Sanskrit.

3.010.054c That pitiless man invited the brahmins with the intent of performing a *śrāddha*. 3.010.055a Then his brother fed those twice-born ones— his brother who had been consecrated in the form of a ram— with the rites prescribed for a *śrāddha*.
Then, when those brahmins had finished eating, Ilvala spoke with a loud voice, saying, "Vātāpi, come forth!
Hearing his brother's words, Vātāpi then roared like a ram.

Piercing through the bodies of the Brahmins again and again, they emerged; in this manner, thousands of Brahmins were constantly destroyed by those flesh-eaters who could assume any form at will, acting together in unison.
Then, at the request of the gods, that great asura was indeed consumed by the great seer Agastya after he had partaken of him at a *śrāddha* ceremony. Then,
saying "It is accomplished," and having offered water for washing the hands, [the rite continued].
"Come out, brother! Ilvala spoke thus to him.
To his brother, the slayer of Brahmins, who was speaking in that manner, the wise Agastya, the best of sages, replied with a smile:
"How could there be any power for me to escape from this aged Rākṣasa,
your brother who has taken the form of a ram and gone to the abode of Yama? Then,
having heard those words concerning the death of his brother, [he spoke].
Out of anger, the night-stalker began to assault the sage.
He rushed toward that best of the twice-born, but he was consumed by the sage’s blazing splendor—
resembling fire in his gaze— and met his death.
"This is the hermitage of that brother of yours, adorned with ponds and forests,
by whom this difficult deed was performed out of compassion for the brahmins.
While he was speaking thus with the son of Sumitrā,
The sun had set for Rāma, and the time of twilight arrived. Having performed the evening twilight devotions together with his brother according to the prescribed rites,
he entered the hermitage grounds and paid homage to that ṛṣi.
Having been properly welcomed by that sage, Rāghava dwelt there for that single night, subsisting on roots and fruits. When that night had passed and the solar orb was bright, [he departed].
Rāghava took leave of that brother of Agastya:
"I salute you, O Blessed One; I have spent the night happily. I take my leave of you, for I am going to see your elder brother, my own guru."
"Go," he said, and the joy of the Raghus departed by the path indicated, gazing upon that forest and beholding wild rice,
jackfruit trees, palmyra palms, *timiśa* trees, *vañjula* reeds, and *dhava* trees.
There Rāma beheld hundreds of forest trees— ciribilvas, madhūkas, bilvas, and tindukas— all in bloom and entwined by creepers with flowering tips.
3.010.074a Crushed by the trunks of elephants and adorned by monkeys, 3.010.074c And resounding with hundreds of flocks of intoxicated birds;
3.010.075a Then the lotus-eyed Rāma spoke to the one standing nearby.
Following behind the heroic Lakṣmaṇa, the enhancer of prosperity,
they saw the hermitage of the great seer of purified soul not far away— a place where the trees were covered in glossy leaves and the deer and birds were full of patience.

3.010.077a Renowned in the world by his own deeds as Agastya, 3.010.077c his hermitage is seen here, which removes the fatigue of the weary; 3.010.078a its forests are filled with abundant smoke, and it is adorned with garlands of bark garments.
Where the herds of deer are tranquil and the place resounds with the songs of various birds;
where, desiring the welfare of the worlds, he by his meritorious deeds swiftly subdued Death and made the southern quarter a sanctuary for all.

3.010.080 This is his hermitage, by whose power this southern quarter is seen by the *rākṣasas* with fear and is not occupied. 3.010.081 Ever since this quarter was entered by that one of meritorious deeds...

From that time forward, the night-rangers became free from enmity and were pacified. Furthermore, this southern direction of the Blessed One became celebrated throughout the three worlds by the name "Pradakṣiṇā" (the Auspicious), being unassailable by those of cruel deeds.
To block the path of the sun constantly, that best of mountains,
Vindhya, does not grow, as he observes his command.
This [story] belongs to him, who was long-lived and whose deeds were renowned in the world.
3.010.084c The glorious hermitage of Agastya is frequented by well-disciplined deer.
3.010.085a This virtuous man, honored by the world, is ever devoted to the welfare of the righteous;
3.010.085c He will unite us, who have come here, with the highest good.
"O gentle one, O Lord, I shall propitiate the great sage Agastya here and dwell for the remainder of my forest exile. Here,
the gods along with the Gandharvas, the Siddhas, and the supreme ṛṣis [dwell]."

They constantly attend upon Agastya, who is restrained in his diet. No liar, nor a cruel man, nor a rogue, nor a pitiless person, nor one whose conduct is driven by lust could live here; such is this sage.
3.010.089a Here dwell the gods, the yakṣas, and the nāgas, together with the birds, 3.010.089c living on restricted diets and desiring to propitiate Dharma.
3.010.090a Here the high-souled Siddhas reside in celestial chariots that resemble the sun.
3.010.090c Having cast off their bodies, the great seers have ascended to heaven with new bodies.
3.010.091a Yakṣahood, immortality, and various kingdoms—
here the gods bestow these upon beings who have propitiated them through auspicious means.

"O son of Sumitrā, we have arrived at the hermitage; enter first and announce to the sage that I have arrived here with Sītā. Having entered the hermitage, Lakṣmaṇa, the younger brother of Rāghava, [did as he was told].
Having approached the disciple of Agastya, he spoke these words:
"There is a king named Daśaratha; his eldest son, the powerful Rāma, has arrived with his wife Sītā to see the sage."
"I am his younger brother, named Lakṣmaṇa, who is devoted and well-disposed toward him— provided you have heard of me. We have entered this most formidable forest by the command of our father."
"We all wish to see the Blessed One; let it be announced.
Having heard those words of Lakṣmaṇa, the ascetic said, "So be it," and entered the fire-sanctuary to announce them.
Having entered, he addressed the best of sages, who was difficult to overcome due to his ascetic power,
with palms joined in reverence, straightforwardly reporting the arrival of Rāma:
"These two sons of Daśaratha are Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa."
"O subduer of enemies, we two have entered this hermitage together with our wife Sītā; we have come to see you for the purpose of serving you. You should now command us as to what must be done next."
Then, having heard from his disciple that Rāma had arrived along with Lakṣmaṇa and the highly fortunate Vaidehī, he spoke these words:
"By good fortune, after a long time, Rāma has come today to see me."
Indeed, his arrival was long desired by my mind;
let Rāma go, duly honored, together with his wife and Lakṣmaṇa. Let him be ushered into my presence—why has he not already been brought in?
Thus addressed by the high-souled sage who knows the dharma,
the disciple saluted him and, with palms joined in restraint, said, "So be it.
Then, emerging in haste, the disciple spoke to Lakṣmaṇa.
"Where is that Rāma? Let him come to see the sage; let him enter himself.
Then, having gone to the hermitage with his disciple Lakṣmaṇa, he showed the descendant of Kakutstha and Sītā, the daughter of Janaka.
3.011.015a Speaking those humble words, the disciple, conveying Agastya’s message, 3.011.015c ushered him in according to custom, having honored him with great hospitality.
3.011.016a Then Rāma entered together with Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa.
Beholding that hermitage, which was filled with peaceful deer,
he saw there the abode of Brahmā, as well as the abode of Agni,
the abode of Viṣṇu, the abode of Mahendra, and the abode of Vivasvat.
The abode of Soma, the abode of Bhaga, and the abode of Kubera;
the abode of Dhātṛ and Vidhātṛ, and likewise the abode of Vāyu.
Then the sage, surrounded by his disciples, also emerged.
Rāma saw him before him, the sage of blazing splendor;
the hero spoke these words to Lakṣmaṇa, the increaser of prosperity:
"Lakṣmaṇa, here comes the venerable ṛṣi Agastya."
"By his magnanimity, I recognize him as this treasury of ascetic powers.
Having spoken thus, the mighty-armed scorcher of foes, filled with supreme joy, grasped the feet of Agastya, who was radiant as the sun.
Having offered his salutations, the righteous Rāma stood with joined palms together with Sītā, the princess of Videha, and Lakṣmaṇa. Then,
having received the descendant of Kakutstha and honored him with a seat and water, [the sage addressed him].

Having asked after their welfare, he said, "Please be seated. Having offered oblations into the fire and presented the *arghya* water, he honored the guest and provided them with food according to the dharma of forest-dwellers (*vānaprastha*).
3.011.025a Then, having first sat down, that bull among sages, who knew the dharma,
spoke to Rāma, who was seated with joined palms and was himself an expert in dharma.
3.011.026a "O descendant of Kakutstha, a practitioner of austerities should indeed behave otherwise..."
Like a false witness in the next world, one might have to eat one's own flesh.
You are a king who practices righteousness for the whole world, a great chariot-warrior;
you are worthy of worship and honor, and you have arrived as a beloved guest.
Having spoken thus, and having honored Rāghava according to his desire with fruits, roots, flowers, and other offerings, he then spoke once more:
"This is a great divine bow, adorned with gold and diamonds."
O tiger among men, this Vaiṣṇava bow was fashioned by Viśvakarman;
it is unfailing, radiant as the sun, and the supreme arrow bestowed by Brahmā.
These two quivers with inexhaustible shafts were given to me by Mahendra.
Filled with sharpened arrows that were like blazing fires,
this sword— encased in a great silver sheath and adorned with gold— is here,
O Rāma; with this bow, having slain the great asuras in battle, [you shall prevail].
In ancient times, Viṣṇu brought forth the blazing splendor of the gods;
O giver of honor, take up that bow, those two quivers, the arrow, and the sword for the sake of victory, just as the wielder of the thunderbolt takes up the vajra.
Having spoken thus and having given all those excellent weapons to Rāma, the illustrious and highly resplendent Agastya spoke again:
"O Rāma, I am pleased; may prosperity be yours! O Lakṣmaṇa, I am well-satisfied."
"That you have come together with Sītā to pay me homage—
great fatigue from the journey surely oppresses you both. It is evident that Maithilī, the daughter of Janaka, is also filled with longing."

For she is indeed delicate and has never been humiliated by hardships; yet, impelled by her love for her husband, she has reached this forest abounding in faults. O Rāma, act in such a way that Sītā may find delight here.
"She has performed a difficult deed in following you into the forest.
For this, O delight of the Raghus, is the nature of women since the beginning of creation:
they are devoted to one when he is in prosperity, but they abandon him when he is in adversity."
Women emulate the fickleness of lightning-flashes, the sharpness of weapons,
and the swiftness of Garuḍa and the wind;
yet this wife of yours is free from these faults.
"Praiseworthy and worthy of renown, just like the lady Arundhatī;
this land is truly adorned where you, O Rāma, subduer of enemies, shall dwell together with the son of Sumitrā and this daughter of Videha."
Thus addressed by the sage, Rāghava, with palms joined in reverence, spoke these humble words to the seer who blazed like fire:
"I am blessed; I am favored, since the bull among sages [has come to me]."
The Giver of Boons is well-pleased with the virtues of you, along with your brother and wife. However, point out to me a region provided with water and abundant forests,
where I may establish a hermitage and dwell happily and devotedly.
3.012.012 Then, having heard Rāma’s speech, the best of sages, that righteous and steadfast soul, reflected for a moment and spoke these most prudent words:
3.012.013 “Two yojanas from here, my dear, there is a place abundant in roots, fruits, and water.”
3.012.013c There is a glorious region, rich in deer, renowned as Pañcavaṭī.
3.012.014a Having gone there and established a hermitage together with the son of Sumitrā, 3.012.014c take your delight while fulfilling your father’s command exactly as it was spoken.
"O sinless one, this entire account of yours is indeed known to me through the power of my asceticism and through my affection for Daśaratha; moreover,
the desire residing in your heart has been perceived by me through my ascetic power."
"Having promised me residence here in this ascetic grove, I therefore say to you: 'Go to Pañcavaṭī.
For that region of the forest is delightful, and there the daughter of Mithilā will find pleasure."
That region is praiseworthy and not too far away, O Rāghava;
it is near the Godāvarī, and there Maithilī will find delight.
It abounds in plentiful roots and fruits and is filled with various flocks of birds.
O mighty-armed one, it is secluded, sacred, and likewise delightful;
you, along with your wife, are capable of protecting it.
Moreover, while dwelling here, Rāma will protect the ascetics.
"O hero, this great forest of Madhuka trees is visible;
one must go north of it to reach the Nyagrodha tree.
Then, having ascended the plateau not far from the mountain,"
"It is known as Pañcavaṭī, its forests ever in bloom. Having been addressed thus by Agastya, Rāma, together with the son of Sumitrā,
paid his respects and took leave of that truth-speaking ṛṣi.
Having been granted permission by him and having performed obeisance at his feet,
those two sons of the lord of men, taking up their bows, then departed from that hermitage for Pañcavaṭī together with Sītā.
With their quivers fastened and undaunted in battles,
they both proceeded with concentrated minds toward Pañcavaṭī by the path as instructed by the great seer.

Then, while proceeding toward Pañcavaṭī, the joy of the Raghus encountered a vulture of massive body and terrifying prowess along the way. Seeing him stationed in the forest, those two illustrious ones, Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, [were struck with wonder].
Perceiving him to be a Rākṣasa bird, they both asked, "Who are you?
He, as if pleasing them with his sweet and gentle speech, said,
"Child, know me to be a friend of your father."
Recognizing him as a friend of his father, Rāghava honored him;
he then calmly inquired about his lineage and his name. Having heard Rāma’s words regarding his family and himself, [the other replied].
The twice-born one explained to him the origin of all beings:
"O mighty-armed Rāghava, listen from the beginning as I recount to you all those who were the lords of creatures (Prajāpatis) in former times."
3.013.007a Kardama was the first among them, and Vikṛta immediately after him;
3.013.007c Śeṣa, Saṃśraya, and the powerful Bahuputra; 3.013.008a Sthāṇu, Marīci, Atri, and the mighty Kratu.
Pulastya, Aṅgiras, Pracetas, and likewise Pulaha;
Dakṣa, Vivasvat, and another, Ariṣṭanemi, O Rāghava;
and Kaśyapa of great splendor was the last among them.
O highly illustrious Rāma, we have heard that Prajāpati Dakṣa had sixty daughters of great renown. Among them,
Kaśyapa accepted eight slender-waisted ones as his wives.
Aditi and Diti, Danu and Kālakā,
Tāmrā and Krodhavaśā, as well as Manu and Anālā—
Kaśyapa, being pleased with these daughters, spoke to them again:
"You shall indeed give birth to sons who will be the lords of the three worlds and equal to me. O Rāma, Aditi, Diti, Danu,
and Kālakā were thus minded, O mighty-armed one, while the others were not so disposed.
O subduer of enemies, thirty-three gods were born of Aditi;
O scorcher of foes, these were the Ādityas, the Vasus, the Rudras, and the two Aśvins.
But Diti, O dear one, gave birth to the illustrious sons known as the Daityas.
This earth, with its oceans and sacrificial grounds, once belonged to them.
Danu, O subduer of enemies, gave birth to a son named Aśvagrīva;
and Kālakā also gave birth to Naraka and Kālaka.
Tāmra also gave birth to these five daughters, world-renowned: Krauñcī, Bhāsī, Śyenī, Dhṛtarāṣṭrī, and Śukī. Krauñcī gave birth to owls, and Bhāsī gave birth to hawks.
Śyenī gave birth to hawks and vultures of great brilliance;
Dhṛtarāṣṭrī, may you be blessed, that beautiful woman also gave birth to swans, ruddy geese, and cakravāka birds in their entirety.
Śukī gave birth to Natā, and Vinatā was the daughter born of Natā.
O Rāma, Krodhavaśā also gave birth to ten daughters from her own body:
Mṛgī, Mṛgamandā, Harī, and Bhadramadā.
Then, O best of men, Mṛgī gave birth to offspring consisting of all kinds of deer— Mātaṅgī, Śārdūlī, Śvetā, Surabhī, as well as Surasā and Kadrukā, all endowed with every auspicious mark.
And from Mṛgamandā were born ṛkṣas, sṛmaras, and likewise camaras.
Then Bhadramadā gave birth to a daughter named Irāvatī;
her son was Airāvata, the great elephant and lord of the world.
Haryā gave birth to offspring who were both tawny monkeys and ascetic vanaras;
Śārdūlī gave birth to sons who were golāṅgūlas and tigers. Then, O bull among men, Mātaṅgī’s offspring were the mātaṅgas.
Śvetā gave birth to a son, Diśāgaja, who had white eyes. Then, O Rāma, the goddess Surabhī gave birth to two daughters:
Rohiṇī—may you be blessed—and the illustrious Gandharvī.
Rohiṇī gave birth to cows, and the Gandharvī bore sons who were steeds; Surasā gave birth to the Nāgas, O Rāma, and Kadrū to the Pannagas.
Manu begot human beings from the high-souled Kaśyapa.
3.013.029c O bull among men, [he created] Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras.
3.013.030a The Brāhmaṇas were born from his mouth, and likewise the Kṣatriyas from his chest;
3.013.030c the Vaiśyas were born from his thighs, and the Śūdras from his feet—so says the sacred revelation (śruti).
Anala also gave birth to all the trees that bear meritorious fruit;
Vinatā, Śukī, Kadrū—the granddaughter of Kaśyapa—and Surasā were her sisters.
Kadrū, however, gave birth to a thousand nāgas who support the earth.
Vinatā had two sons, Garuḍa and Aruṇa. I was born from that Aruṇa, and Saṃpāti is my elder brother. Know me, O subduer of enemies, as Jaṭāyu, the son of Śyenī.
"O father, if you so desire, I shall become your companion for your dwelling;
and when you have departed with Lakṣmaṇa, I will protect Sītā.
Then Rāghava, having honored Jaṭāyu...
Embracing him with joy, he bowed low;
for the self-possessed prince had heard Jaṭāyus speak again and again of his friendship with his father.
Having entrusted Sītā, the princess of Mithilā,
there to that exceedingly powerful bird, he went to Pañcavaṭī together with Lakṣmaṇa.
Desiring to consume his enemies like a fire consuming moths,
Rāma then went to Pañcavaṭī, which was filled with various beasts of prey and wild animals,
and spoke to his brother Lakṣmaṇa of radiant splendor.
"We have arrived at this place exactly as directed by the great seer.
O gentle one, this is the region of Pañcavaṭī with its flowering groves;
let your gaze be cast everywhere, for you are indeed skilled in observing the forest."
"In which region, O Lakṣmaṇa, would a hermitage be agreeable to us— a place where Vaidehī, you, and I might find delight? Let such a location be sought, one that has a nearby body of water."
3.014.005a Where there is the beauty of forests and likewise the beauty of waters, 3.014.005c and where sacrificial wood, flowers, *kuśa* grass, and water are nearby;
3.014.006a Having been thus addressed by Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa, with palms joined in reverence, [replied].
3.014.006c In the presence of Sītā, he spoke these words to the descendant of Kakutstha:
3.014.007a "O descendant of Kakutstha, I am dependent upon you for a hundred years;
3.014.007c but please tell me yourself to choose a beautiful location."
3.014.008a Greatly pleased by those words of Lakṣmaṇa, the immensely radiant one,
3.014.008c after reflecting, approved that region endowed with every excellence. 3.014.009a Having entered that delightful place for the purpose of establishing a hermitage,
Taking Saumitri by the hand with his own hand, Rāma said:
"This region is level and beautiful, covered with trees in full bloom;
here, O gentle one, you ought to establish a hermitage in the proper manner."
3.014.011 Not far away, this beautiful lotus pond, adorned with lotuses fragrant and radiant like the sun, is visible.
3.014.012 It was described thus by the sage Agastya, whose soul is purified through meditation.
This lovely Godāvarī river is surrounded by trees in full bloom;
it is filled with *haṃsa* and *kāraṇḍava* ducks and graced by *cakravāka* birds,
and it is frequented by herds of deer neither too far nor too near.
O gentle one, lofty mountains resounding with the cries of peacocks, delightful, and possessing many caves,
are seen covered with trees in full bloom;
they are adorned here and there with minerals of gold, silver, copper, and other ores.
Adorned with the highest devotion, the elephants appear as if latticed with windows;
they are further graced by *sāla*, *tāla*, and *tamāla* trees, by date palms, breadfruit, and mangoes,
as well as by wild rice, *timiśa*, and *puṃnāga* trees.
Covered with mango trees, *aśoka*, *tilaka*, *campaka*, and *ketaka* trees, as well as various other trees endowed with flowering shrubs and creepers;
and with sandalwood, *syandana*, *nīpa*, jackfruit, and breadfruit trees.
With *dhava*, *aśvakarṇa*, and *khadira* trees, and with *śamī*, *kiṃśuka*, and *pāṭala* trees—
this place is holy, this place is pure, and it abounds in many deer and birds. O son of Sumitrā, we shall dwell here together with this bird.
Thus addressed by Rāma, the mighty Lakṣmaṇa, slayer of enemy heroes,
soon constructed for his brother a spacious leaf-hut made of compacted clay at that hermitage.
3.014.021c With long bamboo poles as pillars, it was well-constructed and very beautiful.
3.014.022a Having gone then to the river Godāvarī, the glorious Lakṣmaṇa bathed, took lotuses, and returned again with fruit.
Then, having performed an offering of flowers and a ritual for peace according to the prescribed rites,
he showed that constructed hermitage to Rāma. Seeing that beautiful hermitage which had been prepared, he [Rāma], together with Sītā, gazed upon it.
3.014.024c Rāghava experienced supreme joy within the leaf-hut.
3.014.025a Then, greatly delighted, he embraced Lakṣmaṇa with both arms and spoke these words, which were exceedingly affectionate and firm:
"I am pleased with this great deed performed by you, O Lord;
for that reason, I have offered you this embrace,
Lakṣmaṇa— you who are discerning of intentions, grateful, and knower of dharma."
"Because of you as his son, my righteous father did not meet with his end.
Having spoken thus to Lakṣmaṇa, Rāghava, the enhancer of prosperity and master of himself,
dwelt happily in that region abounding in fruit.
For some time, that righteous-souled one dwelt there, attended by Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa, like an immortal in the heavenly realm. As that high-souled descendant of Raghu was dwelling there, his face—

At the departure of autumn, the beloved season of winter set in. Once, when the night had turned to dawn, that joy of the Raghus went to the beautiful Godāvarī River for the purpose of ritual ablution.

3.015.003a Bowing with a water-pot in his hand, the valiant brother, the son of Sumitrā, followed behind him together with Sītā and spoke these words: 3.015.004a "O you who speak kindly, that beloved time has now arrived which is dear to you."
By this, the auspicious year appears as if adorned; the world, though harsh with frost, is garlanded with crops upon the earth;
the waters are no longer fit for enjoyment, and the bearer of oblations (the fire) is beautiful.
Having worshipped the ancestral deities with offerings of the first-fruits (*āgrayaṇa*),

the virtuous people, having performed the *āgrayaṇa* rites at the proper time, were freed from sin; their desires were abundant, their lands were prosperous, and they possessed an abundance of cow's milk and dairy products.

3.015.007c The rulers of the earth wander about, desiring victory for the sake of military expeditions. 3.015.008a While the sun remains firmly in the quarter frequented by Death (the south), the northern direction does not shine, like a woman devoid of her forehead mark.

3.015.009 By nature rich in masses of snow and with the sun now far away, the mountain Himavat clearly lives up to its name as "the snowy one. 3.015.010 At midday, it is pleasant to the touch, making travel exceedingly comfortable.
The days now shine with a fortunate sun, yet their shadows and waters are wretched;
with mild suns, accompanied by mist, sharp cold, and winds,
these days appear empty, like desolate forests overwhelmed by frost.
3.015.012 Now the nights pass away, their beds of space withdrawn; led by the Puṣya constellation, they are reddened by frost, cold, and exceedingly long.
3.015.013 But the moon, its beauty transferred to the sun, has a disc reddened by the frost.
Like a mirror blinded by breath, the moon does not shine;
the moonlight, soiled by frost, does not gleam on the night of the full moon;
like Sītā darkened by the sun's heat, it is perceived but does not appear beautiful.
By its very nature cool to the touch, and now pierced by frost, the western wind blows at this time doubly cold. The forests, filled with barley and wheat, are shrouded in mist.
They shine as the sun rises, with the cries of cranes and saras cranes;
they shine like golden-hued rice stalks, slightly bending, their heads filled with grain and shaped like dates.
With its rays approaching, veiled by frost and mist,
the sun, though risen high, appears like the moon;
its power is ungraspable in the forenoon, yet it is pleasant to the touch at midday.
The sunlight, slightly reddened and somewhat pale, shines upon the earth;
the forest ground, its young grasses slightly moistened by the falling of dew, is beautiful as the fresh sunbeams settle upon it.
Enveloped in the darkness of dew and shrouded in the gloom of mist,
the rows of forest trees appear as if fast asleep, stripped of their flowers; their waters are veiled by vapor, and the cranes can only be discerned by their cries.
3.015.022c Now the rivers shine with banks whose sands are moistened by frost.
3.015.023a Due to the falling of snow and the mildness of the sun,
even the water situated on mountain peaks is generally flavorful because of its coolness.
3.015.024 With leaves withered by age, their filaments and pericarps decayed,
and reduced to mere stalks, the lotus ponds do not shine, destroyed by the frost. 3.015.025 But at this time, O tiger among men, [he] was filled with sorrow.
3.015.025c The righteous-souled Bharata practices austerities in the city out of devotion to you;
3.015.026a having renounced his kingdom, his pride, and many various enjoyments,
3.015.026c the ascetic, restricted in diet, lies upon the cold ground.
He too, surely, having prepared for his ablutions at this very hour,
goes regularly to the river Sarayū accompanied by his ministers;
he who was raised in extreme luxury, being delicate, is now afflicted by the cold.
How is it that during the latter parts of the night he bathes in the Sarayū—
this dark-complexioned, glorious, and great man with eyes like lotus petals,
who knows the dharma, speaks the truth, is restrained by modesty, and has conquered his senses?
3.015.030a Speaking kindly, sweet-tempered, long-armed, and a subduer of enemies,
3.015.030c having renounced various pleasures, he has with his whole being taken refuge in the Noble One.
3.015.031a Heaven has been won by your high-souled brother Bharata.
"Even though you are dwelling in the forest for the sake of asceticism, he who follows after you—
this well-known worldly proverb that 'bipeds follow the father's side or the mother's side' has been proven otherwise by Bharata."
"Her husband was Daśaratha, and her son was the virtuous Bharata;
how indeed could that mother Kaikeyī be so cruel in her vision?
While the righteous Lakṣmaṇa was speaking these words out of affection, [Rāma replied: 3.015.034a—b. [He spoke thus.]
Unable to endure that disparagement of his mother, Rāghava said:
"O father, your middle mother must not be censured in any way;
speak instead of Bharata, the lord of the Ikṣvākus."
"Though my mind is resolved and firm in its vow for forest-dwelling,
it is again made childish, tormented by affection for Bharata.
Lamenting thus, he reached the Godāvarī river there.
Kakutstha, together with his younger brother and Sītā, performed the consecration ceremony.
Then, having gratified the ancestors and the deities with libations of water,
they, being composed in mind, praised the risen sun and the gods.
Having performed his ablutions, Rāma shone resplendent,
accompanied by Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa; indeed,
having performed his ablutions with the daughter of the King of Mountains, he was radiant.
Like the blessed Lord Rudra accompanied by Nandin, Rāma— having performed his ablutions— along with Sītā and the son of Sumitrā,
departed from that bank of the Godāvarī and proceeded to their own hermitage.
3.016.002 Having approached that hermitage with Lakṣmaṇa, Rāghava,
having performed his morning rites, entered the leaf-hut.
3.016.003 There Rāma sat within the leaf-hut together with Sītā.
The mighty-armed one shone like the moon with its variegated [mark],
and together with his brother Lakṣmaṇa, he engaged in various conversations. At that time, Rāma sat with his mind deeply absorbed in these stories.
A certain ogress came to that place by chance;
she was named Śūrpaṇakhā, the sister of the ten-necked Rākṣasa, and having approached Rāma, she beheld him who resembled a god.
With lion-like shoulders and mighty arms, his eyes resembling lotus petals; delicate yet possessed of great strength, endowed with the marks of royalty;
Rāma, dark as a blue lotus, with a splendor like that of Kandarpa.

Seeing Rāma, who resembled Indra, the rākṣasī became infatuated with desire. Though she was ill-favored, she gazed upon him whose face was beautiful; though she had a large belly, she looked at him whose waist was well-proportioned; though her eyes were deformed, she beheld his wide eyes; and though her hair was copper-colored, she gazed upon his lovely locks.
She who was ugly toward one of pleasing form, she of terrible cries toward one of sweet voice;

the cruel old woman toward the young man, and the speaker of left-handed words toward the righteous; she of wicked conduct toward him of virtuous behavior, and the one of unpleasant appearance toward the beloved.

3.016.010c Possessed by Śarīraja, the Rākṣasī spoke to Rāma: 3.016.011a "How have you come to this region frequented by Rākṣasas, wearing matted hair in the guise of an ascetic, accompanied by your wife, and bearing a bow and arrows?"

Thus addressed by the Rākṣasī Śūrpaṇakhā, that scorcher of foes, out of his straightforward nature, began to relate everything. "There was a king named Daśaratha, whose prowess was equal to that of the gods."
I am his eldest son, known among people by the name Rāma;
this is my younger brother named Lakṣmaṇa, who is devoted to me;
and this is my wife, the princess of Videha, renowned as Sītā.
"Constrained by the command of my father, the lord of men, and my mother, and desiring righteousness for the sake of dharma, I have come here to dwell in the forest.
But I wish to know you; let it be told—who are you, and to whom do you belong?"
"For what purpose have you come here? Tell me the truth.
Hearing these words, the Rākṣasī, tormented by passion, spoke this speech:
"Listen, O Rāma; I shall tell you my words according to the true meaning."
"I am a rākṣasī named Śūrpaṇakhā, capable of assuming any form at will. I wander this forest alone, terrifying all beings.
My brother is the rākṣasa named Rāvaṇa, the lord of the rākṣasas."
The immensely powerful Kumbhakarṇa was always characterized by excessive sleep,
whereas the righteous Vibhīṣaṇa did not behave like a rākṣasa;
and the two brothers Khara and Dūṣaṇa were renowned for their prowess in battle.

"O Rāma, having transcended those [other men] because I have never seen one like you before, I have approached you with my whole being as my husband, the Supreme Person. For a long time, be my husband; what will you do with Sītā?"
"Deformed and misshapen, she is not a match for you;
see me, for I alone am a wife worthy of you in beauty. Look upon this ugly, unchaste woman, who is hideous and has a sunken belly."
"Together with this brother of yours, I shall devour a human woman.
Then, O beloved, wandering through the Daṇḍaka forest with me, you shall behold mountain peaks and various kinds of groves."

3.016.025a Having been addressed in this way, the descendant of Kakutstha, skilled in speech, smiled at the woman with intoxicating eyes and began to speak these words. 3.017.001a But Rāma [addressed] that Śūrpaṇakhā, who was bound by the noose of desire.
Then, with gentle words and a smile, he spoke according to his own will:
"O lady, I am already married; this wife of mine is my beloved. For women such as you, however, co-wifery is a source of great suffering."
"But this younger brother of mine,
named Lakṣmaṇa, is virtuous, handsome, illustrious, and heroic; he is unmarried,
seeks a wife, is young, and of pleasing appearance."
"And there shall be a husband for you who is worthy of this beauty of yours.
O large-eyed one, accept him as your husband and my brother;
O lady of noble form, be without a rival, just as the radiance of the sun is without a rival upon Mount Meru."
Thus addressed by Rāma, that rākṣasī, deluded by passion,
suddenly released Rāma and spoke to Lakṣmaṇa:
"O lady of excellent complexion, I am a fitting wife for this form of yours."

"You shall wander happily through all the Daṇḍaka forests together with me. Thus addressed by the Rākṣasī, Lakṣmaṇa, the son of Sumitrā who was skilled in speech, smiled at Śūrpaṇakhā and spoke these fitting words.

"How can you wish to become the wife of a slave like me? Noble lady, I am dependent upon my brother, the noble Siddhārtha, who has accomplished his purpose; therefore, O woman of pure and lotus-like complexion, may you too be joyful and pure."
"O large-eyed one, become the younger wife of this noble man. Abandoning this ugly, unfaithful, hideous, emaciated, and aged wife, he will surely devote himself only to you."
"O woman of excellent complexion, what wise man, having abandoned this most excellent form, would set his heart upon mortals, O lady of beautiful hips?
Thus was Karālā, with her sunken belly, addressed by Lakṣmaṇa.

3.017.013c She, unskilled in discerning jesting, considered those words to be true. 3.017.014a Deluded by passion, she spoke to Rāma— the scorcher of foes, difficult to overcome— who was seated with Sītā in the leaf-hut.
"Clasping this ugly, unchaste, hideous woman— this aged wife with a sunken belly— you do not hold me in high regard.
Today, while you look on, I shall devour this human woman."
"I shall wander with you, free from rivals, according to my pleasure.
Having spoken thus to the fawn-eyed woman, she whose eyes resembled glowing embers,
filled with great rage, rushed at her like a great meteor toward Rohiṇī.
Seeing that [noose] approaching like the noose of Death, the mighty Rāma seized it and, filled with anger, then said to Lakṣmaṇa:
"O Saumitri, jesting in any way with cruel and ignoble people is never appropriate."
"O gentle one, you must not act so as to harm Vaidehī while she still lives; look at her!
O tiger among men, it is fitting that you deform this Rākṣasī, who is misshapen, unchaste, excessively intoxicated, and pot-bellied."
Thus addressed, the mighty Lakṣmaṇa, filled with rage while Rāma looked on, drew his sword and cut off her ears and nose. With her ears and nose severed, she let out a discordant cry.
3.017.022c The terrible Śūrpaṇakhā fled back through the forest as she had come.
3.017.023a That deformed and most dreadful Rākṣasī, drenched in blood,
3.017.023c let out various cries like a rain-cloud in the monsoon season.
Flowing with blood in many ways, her appearance terrifying,
she raised her arms and, roaring, entered the great forest.
Then she [saw] the place crowded with throngs of Rākṣasas.
Having approached her brother Khara of fierce splendor, who had gone to Janasthāna and disfigured her,
she fell upon the ground like a thunderbolt from the sky.
Then, drenched in blood, she— overwhelmed by fear, delusion, and fainting— beheld Rāghava arrived in the forest with his wife and Lakṣmaṇa, and saw her own disfigurement.
The sister related everything to Khara. Seeing his sister fallen there, disfigured and drenched in blood, the Rākṣasa Khara, consumed by rage, questioned her.
Endowed with strength and prowess, able to go wherever you wish and assume any form at will, by whom have you been brought to this state, reduced to one who resembles Death itself?
[You who were once the object of] gods, gandharvas, spirits, and great-souled sages— by whom have you been brought to this?
"Who is this person of such great prowess who has thus disfigured you?
Indeed, I see no one in the world who could do me such an injury,
except for the thousand-eyed Mahendra, the subduer of Pāka."
