"Today I shall take my life with arrows that end all existence,
like a crane drinking up milk mixed in water.
When I have slain him in battle, his vital organs severed by my shafts— "
Whose blood, red and frothy, will the earth drink?
Whose bodies will the birds of prey,
gathering together, joyfully devour after tearing away the flesh of one slain by me in battle?

Neither the gods, nor the gandharvas, nor the piśācas, nor the rākṣasas are able to protect that wretched man once he has been dragged away by me in this great battle. Having slowly regained consciousness, you ought to tell me about him.
"By that ill-behaved one, you were overcome through prowess in the forest.
Hearing these words of her brother, who was especially enraged,
Śūrpaṇakhā then spoke these words through her tears:
Young, endowed with beauty, very delicate yet possessed of great strength,
with eyes as broad as lotus petals, dressed in bark and black antelope skins,
resembling two kings of the Gandharvas and marked with the characteristics of royalty.
Whether they be gods or humans, I am not able to discern who they are.
There, a young woman endowed with beauty, adorned with every ornament,
was seen by me between those two, she of the slender waist.
3.018.014a Because of those two acting together on account of that woman,
I have been brought to this state, as if I were truly helpless. 3.018.015a And I am now left with her, who is of crooked conduct, and those two who have been slain.
"I wish to drink blood with its foam at the forefront of the battle.
O father, let this first desire of mine be fulfilled by you;
I would drink the blood of her and those two in the fray."
While she was speaking thus, the enraged Khara commanded fourteen immensely powerful Rākṣasas who resembled the God of Death—
two human beings, equipped with weapons and clad in bark garments and black antelope skins.
"Having entered the terrible Daṇḍaka forest together with that young woman, you two must slay them and that wicked woman, and then return. And this sister of mine shall drink their blood."
"O Rākṣasas, go quickly and, having crushed those two by your own prowess, fulfill this cherished desire of my sister. Thus were those fourteen Rākṣasas commanded.
3.018.021c There they went along with her, like clouds driven by the wind.
3.019.001a Then the terrible Śūrpaṇakhā, having arrived at the hermitage of the Raghavas,
informed the Rākṣasas of those two brothers together with Sītā.
3.019.002 They saw the mighty Rāma seated in the leaf-hut together with Sītā, the princess of Videha, and Lakṣmaṇa.
3.019.003 Seeing them and that approaching Rākṣasī, the illustrious descendant of Raghu—
Rāma spoke to his brother Lakṣmaṇa, who was of radiant splendor:
"O son of Sumitrā, remain for a moment close behind Sītā;
I shall slay those who have come here along her path."
Having heard these words of Rāma, who was self-realized,
Lakṣmaṇa honored Rāma’s speech by saying, "So be it.
Then Rāghava [took] a great bow adorned with gold.
The righteous-souled one strung his bow and spoke to those rākṣasas:
"We two are the sons of Daśaratha, brothers Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa;
we have entered the difficult Daṇḍaka forest together with Sītā."
"Subsisting on fruits and roots, self-controlled, ascetics practicing righteousness,
why do you harm those dwelling in the Daṇḍaka forest?
We have come to slay you, sinful-souled evildoers in this great forest."

"By the command of the sages, I have arrived here equipped with my bow. Stay right where you are; you should not approach me, for I am well-pleased. O night-stalkers, if you have any regard for your lives, turn back!"
Having heard those words of his, those fourteen Rākṣasas—
slayers of Brahmins, bearing spears in their hands, with eyes bloodshot and terrible— spoke these words to Rāma, whose own eyes were red at the corners.
"O you who speak so sweetly while being harsh, you who have witnessed our great prowess— having provoked the wrath of our high-souled lord Khara,
you yourself shall lose your life today, slain by us in battle."
3.019.014a For what power do you have, being alone, to stand before us many at the head of the battle, let alone to fight in combat?
3.019.015a [You will not escape] these iron clubs, spears, and sharp-edged missiles hurled by our arms.
"You shall lose your life, your prowess, and the bow held in your hand. Having spoken thus, those fourteen enraged Rākṣasas,
with weapons and swords raised, rushed toward Rāma.
They hurled those spears at the invincible descendant of Raghu;
Kākutstha, with exactly as many gold-adorned arrows, severed all fourteen of those spears.
Then, thereafter, the one of great splendor, exceedingly enraged, took up fourteen iron arrows whetted on stone that were as radiant as the sun;
having grasped his bow and drawn it back, he aimed at the Rākṣasa targets.
Rāghava released arrows like Śatakratu discharging thunderbolts;
those shafts, with golden feathers, blazing, and adorned with gold,
became equal in luster to great meteors in the sky.
3.019.021a Having pierced the chests of the *rākṣasas* with force, drenched in blood, they then flew out, sounding like thunderbolts, and sank into the earth.
3.019.022a With their hearts shattered, they fell upon the ground like trees cut at their roots.

They fell down, their limbs drenched in blood, disfigured and deprived of life. Seeing them fallen upon the ground, the Rākṣasī, overwhelmed with rage and terrified, again let out a terrible cry there.
3.019.024a Letting out a great roar, Śūrpaṇakhā, with her blood somewhat dried, approached Khara again with speed; 3.019.024c she fell down once more in distress, like a creeper exuding its sap.
Seeing the Rākṣasas struck down in battle,
Śūrpaṇakhā then ran back again,
[describing] the slaughter of all those demons in its entirety.
The sister related everything to Khara;
seeing Śūrpaṇakhā fallen again, Khara, out of anger,
spoke with clear words to her who had come for a harmful purpose.
"But now, those heroic Rākṣasas who feed on blood have been dispatched by me for your sake;
why then do you weep again?
They are devoted, affectionate, and always intent on my welfare."
"Even though they strike you, you must not be killed; do not fail to follow my word.
I wish to hear the reason why, for what cause you now cry out 'O protector! and writh upon the ground like a serpent."
"Why do you lament like one who is helpless while I, your protector, am present? Arise, arise! Do not fear; let this distress be cast aside here.
Thus addressed and consoled by Khara, she of invincible resolve—
Wiping his tearful eyes, he spoke to his brother Khara:
"Fourteen brave and formidable Rākṣasas were sent by you to slay Rāghava along with Lakṣmaṇa for my sake."

But they, filled with indignation and bearing spears and sharp-edged axes in their hands, were all slain in battle by Rāma with arrows that pierce the vital organs. Seeing those mighty warriors fallen upon the ground in an instant, [he was struck with wonder].
And at the great deeds of Rāma, a great terror has come upon me.
O night-stalker, I am thus afraid, agitated, and despondent;
seeing danger on all sides, I have once again sought refuge in you.
"In this vast ocean of grief, inhabited by the crocodiles of despair and garlanded with the waves of terror, why do you not rescue me as I sink?
And here on the ground lie these who have been slain by Rāma with his sharpened arrows."
"And those flesh-eating Rākṣasas who have reached my path— if you have compassion for me, and if you have compassion for those Rākṣasas as well,
and if you possess power or energy against Rāma, O night-stalker."
"Destroy that thorn of a Rākṣasa who dwells in the Daṇḍaka forest!
If you do not slay my enemy Rāma this very day,
I shall cast off my life-breaths right before your eyes, shameless as I am."

3.020.015a By my intellect, I perceive that you are not capable of standing before Rāma in combat; 3.020.015c you have no power to face him with his bow in the great battle. 3.020.016a Thinking yourself a hero, you are not a hero; you have falsely assumed prowess.
"Since you are unable to slay those two humans, Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa,
depart quickly from Janasthāna along with your kinsmen. What kind of dwelling can there be for one such as you here, who is devoid of courage and possessed of little valor?"
Overpowered by Rāma’s splendor, you shall indeed perish quickly; for that Rāma, the son of Daśaratha, is endowed with great majesty,
as is his brother of mighty prowess, by whom I have been disfigured.
3.021.001 Thus insulted by Śūrpaṇakhā,
the heroic Khara then spoke these exceedingly harsh words in the midst of the rākṣasas:
3.021.002 "This incomparable anger of mine arises from the insult you have suffered."
3.021.002c It cannot be restrained, like salt water that has surged up.
3.021.003a I do not reckon Rāma as a mere mortal whose life is spent, nor do I consider him by virtue of his prowess;
3.021.003c it is my own self, through its evil deeds, that will today release its life-breaths.
3.021.004a Let these tears be restrained and this agitation be abandoned;
3.021.004c I, Rāma, together with my brother, shall lead you to the abode of Yama. 3.021.005a Today, as you lie on the ground, your life-breath exhausted, struck by my battle-axe—
"O Rākṣasī, you shall drink the warm, red blood of Rāma. Hearing these words falling from the mouth of Khara, she was delighted;
out of sheer foolishness, she praised her brother, the foremost of the Rākṣasas.
Having first been reviled by her and then praised once more,
Khara then spoke to his commander-in-chief named Dūṣaṇa:
"I have fourteen thousand followers who act in accordance with my will."
[He saw] those Rākṣasīs of terrifying speed, who never retreat in battles—
dark as blue clouds, fierce, performers of cruel deeds, sporting like lions among men, powerful, and of formidable splendor.

"O gentle one, command all the efforts of those Rākṣasas— who possess the pride of tigers, great faces, and immense power— and who are now exerting themselves with full vigor. O gentle one, quickly bring my chariot and my bows before me."
3.021.011c I desire to go forth at the head of the high-souled descendants of Pulastya, bearing variegated arrows, swords, and various sharp spears,
3.021.012a for the sake of slaying the ill-behaved Rāma, I who am skilled in battle.
3.021.013 As he was speaking thus, Dūṣaṇa then pointed out a great chariot, sun-bright in color, yoked with excellent, dappled horses.
3.021.014 It was shaped like the peak of Mount Meru and adorned with refined gold.
It had a golden wheel that was unobstructed and a pole made of beryl; it was covered with images of fish,
flowers, trees, mountains, and golden suns and moons,
as well as auspicious flocks of birds and stars.
3.021.016a Equipped with a banner and a sword, adorned with tinkling bells,
and yoked to excellent horses, Khara ascended the chariot out of indignation.
3.021.017a Beholding him mounted upon that chariot, the rākṣasas of terrifying prowess [prepared for battle].

They stood surrounding him, as did the mighty Dūṣaṇa. But Khara, standing upon his chariot and seeing all those Rākṣasas with their great bows, terrible shields, weapons, and banners, said to them, "March forth!"
Then that Rākṣasa army, with its terrible shields, weapons, and banners,
marched out from Janasthāna with a great roar and great speed,
equipped with mallets, spears, pikes, and very sharp battle-axes.
With swords and discuses held in their hands, with glittering javelins, with terrible and oversized spears and bows, and with maces, scimitars, clubs,
and thunderbolts of fearsome appearance grasped in their hands.
Fourteen thousand of the most terrible Rākṣasas, who followed the will of Khara, set out from Janasthāna. Seeing those Rākṣasas of fearsome prowess rushing toward him, [he spoke].
Immediately after that, even Khara’s chariot moved forward somewhat.
Then, having understood Khara’s intention, the charioteer urged on those dappled horses adorned with refined gold.
3.021.025a Urged on, that chariot of Khara, the slayer of enemies,
quickly filled the quarters and the intermediate directions with its sound. 3.021.026a But Khara, of harsh voice, his fury having increased;
Hurrying like Antaka for the sake of slaying his enemy,
the one of great strength, roaring like a cloud raining down stones, again urged on his charioteer.
As that formidable and inauspicious army marched forth, a tumultuous great cloud, the color of a donkey and ashen-grey, rained down blood-water. The swift horses yoked to his chariot fell down.
In a level place covered with flowers along the royal highway, by chance,
there appeared a dark halo with blood-red edges,
resembling a circle of fire as it received the sun.
Then, having approached the raised banner with its golden staff,
a massive and most dreadful vulture alighted upon it.
And near Janasthāna, harsh-voiced [demons] likewise alighted.
The flesh-eating beasts and birds made various discordant sounds;
and in the blazing quarter of the sky, they uttered terrifying cries. Inauspicious jackals howled with fierce and loud voices, emitting flames from their mouths.
Resembling mountains split asunder and having drained the waters from their bearers,
those formidable clouds made that sky appear as if it were no longer sky.
A terrible darkness arose, intense and hair-raising.
Neither the cardinal directions nor the intermediate quarters shone clearly;
even without it being the hour of twilight, the sky blazed with the hue of wet blood.
Then, facing toward Khara, beasts and birds let out terrible cries.
Always bringing ill fortune in battle, the jackals of terrifying appearance howled toward the army with mouths vomiting flames;
a headless torso, resembling a massive iron club, was seen near the sun.
The great planet Svarbhānu seized the sun out of season;
the wind blew fiercely, the maker of day lost its luster,
and stars with the brilliance of fireflies appeared even without night.
At that moment, the lotus ponds had their fish and birds huddled together; the trees were stripped of their flowers and fruits;
and a dust, red as a rain-cloud, was stirred up even without a wind.
There, the sarika birds began to shriek, "vīcī kūcī," while meteors of terrifying appearance fell with a thunderous roar;
even the earth, with its mountains, forests, and groves, trembled.
As the wise Khara stood upon his chariot and roared,
his left arm trembled and his bowstring slipped from his hand;
his vision became filled with tears as he looked in every direction.
A pain arose on his forehead, yet he did not turn back from his delusion. Beholding those great portents that had arisen, causing the hair to stand on end,
Khara then spoke to all the rākṣasas with a laugh:
I do not take any account of all these great portents that have arisen, so terrible to behold; for by my prowess, I am as strong as one who treats the weak as mere straw.
Even the stars I could strike down from the vault of heaven with my sharp arrows.
Enraged, I shall join Death himself with the law of mortality—
both that Raghava who is arrogant in his strength and his brother Lakshmana;
until I have slain them with my sharp arrows, I cannot turn back.

"Let my sister have her desire fulfilled after she has drunk their blood— the very cause for which this reversal of fortune has befallen Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa. Never before in any battle have I suffered defeat."
This is before your very eyes; I do not speak untruth to you.
Even the King of the Gods himself, though enraged and mounted upon Airāvata the intoxicated, with the thunderbolt in his hand—I could slay him in battle, let alone those two humans.
3.022.025a Hearing that roar of the rākṣasa, his great army,
though already bound by the noose of death, attained incomparable joy. 3.022.026a And high-souled beings gathered together, desiring to witness the battle.
The ṛṣis, gods, gandharvas, and siddhas, together with the cāraṇas,
having assembled and joined together, addressed that wrongdoer: "May there be well-being for cows and brahmins, and for those who are esteemed by the worlds."
"May Rāghava be victorious in battle over the night-stalkers, the descendants of Pulastya,
just as Cakrāhasta was victorious in battle over all the foremost of the Asuras.
Speaking these words and many others in great numbers, the supreme ṛṣis [spoke].
They beheld the army of those Rākṣasas whose lives were spent. Then Khara, by means of his chariot, rushed forth with speed from the front of the host;
seeing that Rākṣasa, the other Rākṣasas also sallied out.
Śyenagāmī, Pṛthugrīva, Yajñaśatru, Vihangama; Durjaya, Karavīrākṣa, Paruṣa, Kālakārmuka;
Meghamālī, Mahāmālī, Sarpāsya, and Rudhirāśana.
These twelve of great prowess set out toward Khara;
Mahākapāla, Sthūlākṣa, Pramāthī, and likewise Triśiras—
these four leaders of the army followed behind Dūṣaṇa.
That army of Rākṣasa heroes, possessing terrible speed and eager for battle, most dreadful,
suddenly fell upon those two princes.
When Khara, of terrible prowess, had departed for the hermitage like the sun and moon eclipsed by the grahas of the head of a garland,
Rāma, together with his brother, beheld those very portents.

Seeing those most terrible portents that had arisen, which caused the hair to stand on end and were harmful to all creatures, he spoke these words to Lakṣmaṇa: "Behold these, O mighty-armed one, which carry away all living beings."
To suppress these great portents that have arisen and to destroy all the rākṣasas—
these harsh-sounding clouds, dark as donkeys and reddish-brown, are revolving in the sky while discharging streams of blood.
"O Lakṣmaṇa, all my arrows are smoking as they rejoice in battle, and my gold-backed bows are twitching. Such is the way these forest-dwelling birds are warbling here."
3.023.006c Fear has come upon us from the front, and there is doubt regarding our very lives.
3.023.007a A truly great battle will surely take place; of this there is no doubt.
3.023.007c This arm of mine, throbbing again and again, tells me so.
"O hero, when we are in close proximity to the enemy, victory for us and defeat for the foe will surely follow;
for your face appears radiant and serene. Indeed, O Lakṣmaṇa, such is the sign of those who are about to rise up for battle."
Their faces become lusterless as their life-span comes to an end. A wise man who desires his own welfare and anticipates misfortune should take measures in advance to ensure his well-being.
Therefore, taking Vaidehī with you, bow in hand and armed with arrows,
take refuge in a mountain cave that is difficult of access and thick with trees;
for I do not wish for this command of mine to be disregarded by you.
"Bound by an oath upon my feet, go, my child, without delay.
Thus addressed by Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa,
taking up his arrows and bow, took refuge in a secure cave along with Sītā.
When Lakṣmaṇa had entered the cave together with Sītā, Rāma, saying "Well done, you are now appointed," donned his armor. Adorned with that armor which resembled fire, he shone brightly.
Rāma appeared like a smokeless fire rising in the darkness;
lifting his great bow and taking up his arrows, the heroic one stood there,
filling the quarters with the sounds of his bowstring.
Then the gods, along with the Gandharvas, Siddhas, and Cāraṇas,
as well as the Guhyakas, spoke to one another in great terror:
"There are fourteen thousand Rākṣasas of fearsome deeds."
"And how will the battle proceed when Rāma alone is the righteous one?
Then, an army of Yātudhānas was seen on all sides, with a deep resonance and formidable armor, weapons, and banners.
They let out lion-like roars, bellowing at one another,
repeatedly twanging their bows and yawning;
they raised a tumultuous clamor and beat upon the kettledrums.
3.023.021c Their tumultuous noise filled that forest.
3.023.022a Terrified by that sound, the wild beasts roaming the woods 3.023.022c fled silently to where they could not look back.
That army, possessing great speed, bearing various weapons, and deep like the ocean, approached Rāma. Rāma, too, skilled in battle, cast his eye in every direction.
He beheld that army of Khara, raised up and ready for battle.
Drawing his formidable bow and drawing arrows from his quivers,
he summoned a fierce rage for the sake of slaying all the rākṣasas.
Enraged and blazing like the fire at the end of an eon, he became difficult to behold.
Seeing him possessed by such splendor, the forest deities trembled with fear.
Then, they beheld the form of Rāma in his wrath.

Having arrived at the hermitage with his attendants, Khara beheld Rāma— the slayer of enemies— standing with his bow gripped, enraged and intent on destroying the sacrifice of Dakṣa, like the wielder of the Pināka bow when he has raised it to strike.
Seeing him, he raised his bow, which was endowed with excellent qualities and produced a harsh sound,
and urged the charioteer toward Rāma, saying,
"Drive forward! At Khara's command, the charioteer drove the horses.
3.024.003c Where the mighty-armed Rāma stood alone, shaking his bow,
3.024.004a seeing him rush forth, all those night-rangers,
3.024.004c his ministers, surrounded him while uttering a great roar.
3.024.005a Khara, delighting in the midst of those Yātudhānas, went forth;
3.024.005c he appeared in their midst like the red-limbed planet Mars risen among the stars.
3.024.006a Then all those night-rangers, enraged, [assailed] him who possessed the formidable bow.
3.024.006c They rained down various kinds of weapons upon the invincible Rāma.
3.024.007a With iron mallets, spears, javelins, swords, and axes,
the rākṣasas, intent on rage, struck Rāma in the battle.

Resembling clouds, possessing great roars and immense strength, they rushed toward Rāma, the descendant of Kakutstha, desiring to slay him in battle. Those hosts of Rākṣasas discharged showers of arrows upon Rāma.
Like a great mountain being showered with torrents of rain by those wealthy ones,
Rāghava was surrounded by those terrible hosts of Rākṣasas,
just as Mahādeva is surrounded by his throngs of attendants on sacred lunar days.

3.024.011a Those weapons released by the Yātudhānas, Rāghava received with his own arrows, as the ocean receives the torrents of rivers. 3.024.012a Though his body was pierced by those terrible missiles, he did not waver.
3.024.012c Like a great mountain struck by many blazing thunderbolts, 3.024.013a that Rāghava, pierced and smeared with blood across all his limbs,
3.024.013c became like the sun enveloped by the clouds of twilight.
The gods, Gandharvas, Siddhas, and supreme ṛṣis were filled with grief,
seeing that single being then surrounded by many thousands.
Then Rāma, highly incensed, drew his bow into a circle.
Then Rāma effortlessly released hundreds and thousands of sharp arrows in battle— straight-flying shafts fletched with heron feathers, irresistible and unbearable, resembling the nooses of Death.
Those arrows, released by Rāma with ease into the enemy armies,
took away the lives of the Rākṣasas like nooses fashioned by Time.
Having pierced those bodies of the Rākṣasas, those arrows were drenched in blood.
Moving through the atmosphere, they trembled, possessing a splendor equal to blazing fire.
From the circle of Rāma’s bow, however, there issued forth innumerable arrows—
exceedingly fierce and capable of snatching away the life-breaths of the rākṣasas.
With those [arrows], they struck bows, the tops of banners, armor, and heads;
many thighs, resembling the trunks of elephants, along with their hand-ornaments.
Then, with *nālīka*, *nārāca*, and sharp-pointed *vikarṇi* shafts, [they struck].

Being pierced, the night-stalkers let out a terrifying cry of distress. Afflicted by Rāma with sharp arrows that pierce the vital organs, that army found no comfort, like a dry forest consumed by fire.

3.024.023 Some heroic night-rangers of terrifying strength, filled with supreme rage, hurled pikes, swords, and battle-axes at Rāma. 3.024.024 The mighty-armed Rāghava, having warded off those weapons with his arrows—
In that battle, he took away their lives and severed their necks.
Those night-stalkers who remained there were despondent;
tormented by his arrows, they fled toward Khara himself for refuge.
Having gathered them all back together and comforted them, Dūṣaṇa,
enraged like Rudra at the end of time, rushed toward the descendant of Kakutstha. But they all turned back once more, rendered fearless by their reliance on Dūṣaṇa.
Armed with *sāla* trees, *tāla* palms, and rocks, they rushed toward Rāma.
That battle between Rāma and those rākṣasas was wonderful, tumultuous, hair-raising, and most terrible.
3.025.001a That great, life-destroying rain of trees and rocks,
3.025.001c the righteous-souled Rāghava received with his sharp arrows.
3.025.002a Having received that shower, he stood like a bull with its eyes closed.
3.025.002c Rāma gave way to supreme rage for the sake of slaying all the rākṣasas.
3.025.003a Then, possessed by anger and as if blazing with splendor,
he overwhelmed the army, along with Dūṣaṇa, on all sides with his arrows.
Then the enraged army commander Dūṣaṇa, the harasser of his enemies,
seized a hair-raising iron club that resembled a mountain peak,
was encircled with golden bands, and was capable of crushing the armies of the gods.

Seizing in battle that iron club, which resembled a great serpent, was strewn with sharp iron spikes, was smeared with the fat of enemies, possessed a touch like a thunderbolt, and could shatter the gate-towers of the foe; ||| 3.025.005c–3.025.006c ||| he [advanced].
3.025.006 Then the night-stalker Dūṣaṇa, a doer of cruel deeds, rushed toward Rāma.
3.025.007 As Dūṣaṇa was charging at him, that descendant of Raghu severed his two arms, along with their ornaments, using two arrows.
3.025.008a His massive body fell at the front of the battle, deprived [of its arm]. 3.025.008c The iron club of the one whose hand was severed lay before him like the banner of Śakra.
3.025.009a With his two hands scattered, Dūṣaṇa fell to the earth.
Like a wise great elephant with its two shattered tusks, [he lay there].
Seeing Dūṣaṇa fallen upon the ground, slain in battle, all living beings honored the descendant of Kakutstha, crying out, "Excellent! Excellent!"
In the meantime, three enraged leaders of the army,
bound by the noose of death, united and rushed toward Rāma—
Mahākapāla, Sthūlākṣa, and the exceedingly powerful Pramāthin.
3.025.012a The Rākṣasa Mahākapāla raised a massive spear,
3.025.012c Sthūlākṣa seized a *paṭṭiśa* weapon, and Pramāthin a battle-axe; 3.025.013a but as soon as Rāghava saw them rushing toward him, he [struck them] with sharp arrows.
With sharp-pointed arrows, he received those who arrived like guests;
the joy of the Raghus severed the head of Mahākapāla and crushed Pramāthin with countless floods of shafts.
He filled the eyes of Sthūlākṣa with sharp arrows;
struck down, he fell to the earth like a great tree with spreading branches.
Then, [he struck him] with arrows resembling fire, adorned with gold and diamonds.
With his arrows, the radiant one left only the rear of that army remaining.
Those gold-feathered shafts, like fires accompanied by smoke,
struck down those rākṣasas as thunderbolts fell upon great trees.
With a hundred barbed arrows, Rāma struck down a hundred Rākṣasas,
and with a thousand, he slew a thousand at the forefront of the battle. By those arrows, their armor and ornaments were shattered, and their bows were cut to pieces.
Smeared with blood, the night-stalkers fell upon the earth. With those fallen in battle— hair disheveled and drenched in gore—
the entire ground was strewn as if with sacrificial *kuśa* grass upon a great altar.
In an instant, however, that most terrible forest, its rākṣasas slain,
became like a hellish pit, mired in flesh and blood;
fourteen thousand rākṣasas of fearsome deeds lay there.
All were slain by the single Rāma, a human on foot;
of that entire army, only the great chariot-warrior Khara remained,
along with the Rākṣasa Triśiras and Rāma, the slayer of enemies.
Then, having observed that army of terrible strength slain in the great battle by the more powerful Rāma,
Khara [approached] Rāma with a great chariot.
Like Indra with his uplifted thunderbolt,
he approached; but as Khara was advancing toward Rāma,
the Rākṣasa general named Triśiras intercepted him and spoke these words.
"O valiant one, do not employ me; turn back from this rashness!
Behold the mighty-armed Rāma struck down in battle.
I swear this truth to you, and I touch my weapon as an oath."
3.026.003c Just as I shall slay Rāma, who is worthy of being slain by all the Rākṣasas;
3.026.004a either I shall be his death in battle, or he shall be mine in the encounter. Having restrained your enthusiasm for battle, be a witness for a moment.
"Either, with Rāma slain, you shall go to Janasthāna rejoicing;
or, with me slain, you shall approach Rāma for battle.
Thus was Khara entreated by Triśiras out of a desire for death.
Permitted with the words, "Go, fight!", he advanced toward Rāghava.
And Triśiras, on a radiant chariot yoked with horses,
rushed at Rāma in battle like a three-peaked mountain.
Releasing a multitude of arrow-showers like a great cloud pouring rain,
he let out a roar resembling that of a drum soaked in water.
Seeing the three-headed Rākṣasa approaching, Rāghava—
With his bow, he received [the attack] while brandishing sharp arrows.
That tumultuous and great encounter between Rāma and Triśiras was like that between two exceedingly powerful lions and elephants.
Then, struck on the forehead with three arrows by Triśiras, the indignant and enraged Rāma spoke these words in agitation:
"Ah! Such is the strength of this Rākṣasa, who is a hero in prowess!"
"I, who have been wounded here on my forehead by his arrows as if by flowers—
accept from me too these arrows released from the bowstring.
Having spoken thus, he, filled with fury, [discharged] arrows resembling venomous serpents.
Enraged, he struck the three heads upon the chest; with fourteen straight-knotted arrows,
the radiant hero brought down his four horses.
With eight arrows, Rāma struck down the charioteer from the seat of the chariot; with another shaft, he cut down his lofty standard. Then, the night-stalker leaped up from that destroyed chariot.
Rāma pierced him in the heart with arrows, and he became paralyzed;
then that one of immeasurable soul, filled with indignation,
struck off the three heads of that Rākṣasa with three hundred swift shafts.
Afflicted by Rāma’s arrow, that night-stalker fell upon the ground vomiting blood,
amidst his own heads that had previously fallen. Then the remaining Rākṣasas who had fled to Khara were broken and routed.
They fled and did not stand their ground, like deer terrified by a tiger. Seeing them fleeing, Khara turned back in a rage and himself rushed toward Rāma, just as Rāhu rushes toward the moon.
Having seen Dūṣaṇa slain in battle along with Triśiras,
and having witnessed the prowess of Rāma, even Khara was struck with terror.
Beholding that vast and exceedingly powerful army of Rākṣasas, he [was filled with fear].
Dūṣaṇa and Triśiras too were slain by Rāma alone. Seeing that army mostly destroyed, the dejected Rākṣasa Khara approached Rāma, just as Namuci once approached Vāsava.
Drawing his powerful bow, Khara discharged iron arrows that feed on blood,
like enraged venomous serpents, at Rāma;
repeatedly twanging his bowstring, he displayed his mastery of weapons through his training.
Mounted upon his chariot, Khara moved through the battlefields along various paths with his arrows.
That great car-warrior filled all the cardinal and intermediate directions with his shafts;
seeing this, Rāma also took up his exceedingly great bow.
With his unbearable arrows, which were like sparks of fire,
he left no space in the sky, just as Parjanya does with his showers of rain.
That [sky] became filled with the sharp arrows discharged by Khara and Rāma.

The sky all around was devoid of space, crowded on every side by arrows; shrouded by that web of shafts, the sun did not shine at that time as the two warriors fought each other with a fury intent on mutual slaughter.
Then, with barbed arrows, iron shafts, and sharp-pointed *vikarṇis*,
he struck Rāma in battle like a great elephant with goads.
He stood there upon his chariot, bow in hand, confronting the Rākṣasa.

All living beings beheld him as if he were Death himself with noose in hand. Seeing him, who was as valiant as a lion and possessed a gait like that of a lion, Rāma was not agitated, just as a lion is not disturbed by a small animal.
Then, in that battle, Khara approached Rāma on a great chariot resplendent like the sun, like a moth approaching a fire. Then,
[Khara struck] the bow with its arrow at the grip of that high-souled one.
Khara, displaying his lightness of hand, cut down Rāma’s [arrow];
then, taking up seven other arrows in the battle— each possessing a brilliance equal to Indra’s thunderbolt— he, filled with rage, struck them into Rāma’s armor.

Then that armor of Rāma, who possesses the splendor of the sun, fell to the ground, struck by those well-jointed arrows released by Khara. Pierced in all his limbs by those shafts, Rāghava became enraged.
Rāma shone in battle like a blazing, smokeless fire. Then Rāma, the destroyer of enemies, for the sake of the enemy's end, strung another great bow that emitted a deep resonance.
That truly great Vaiṣṇava bow, which had been bestowed by the great seer,
was raised as an excellent weapon, and he rushed toward Khara.
Then, with gold-feathered arrows of smooth joints, he struck him.
Enraged in the battle, Rāma cut down Khara’s banner. That beautiful golden banner, severed into many pieces,
fell to the earth like the sun descending at the command of the gods.
Then Khara, enraged and knowing the vital points, pierced Rāma in his limbs and heart with four arrows, as one strikes an elephant with iron pikes.
Rāma was struck by those many arrows released from Khara’s bow.
Pierced and with his limbs drenched in blood, he became exceedingly enraged.
Grasping his bow in that supreme battle, that best of archers and wielder of the greatest weapons released six well-aimed arrows.
With one arrow he struck his head, then with two he struck his arms,
and with three crescent-headed arrows he struck him in the chest.
Thereafter, the one of great splendor [shot] iron shafts resembling the sun.
Desiring to slay the Rākṣasa, the enraged [Arjuna] took thirteen arrows sharpened on stone; then, with one he cut off his yoke, with four the four horses,
and with the sixth he severed the head of Khara’s charioteer in that battle.

With three arrows, the powerful one [cut] the triple-bamboo pole; with two, the mighty one [cut] the axle. Then, with a twelfth arrow resembling a thunderbolt, Rāghava, as if laughing, severed Khara’s bow along with the arrow fixed to it.
Equal to Indra with his thirteenth arrow, he pierced Khara in battle.
With his bow shattered, his chariot destroyed, his horses slain, and his charioteer killed,
Khara then leaped down and stood upon the ground with a mace in hand.
The gods and the great seers, having assembled, joyfully praised with joined palms that deed of the great chariot-warrior Rāma.
Then, as they gathered together atop their foremost celestial chariots,
the immensely radiant Rāma spoke these harsh words, preceded by gentleness, to Khara, who stood there deprived of his chariot with a mace in hand.
While standing within a vast army crowded with elephants, horses, and chariots,
you have committed a most cruel deed, loathed by all the world. You are a source of terror to all beings— a pitiless doer of evil deeds.

Even the Lord of the three worlds cannot remain [in his position] if he performs an action contrary to the world, O night-stalker; for all people slay such a one instantly, like a fierce, venomous snake that has appeared.
3.028.005a He who, out of greed or desire, commits sins without realizing it,
3.028.005c falls and sees his end, just as a Brahmin woman [sees her own ruin] because of a water-pot.
3.028.006a While the ascetics practicing dharma were dwelling in the Daṇḍaka forest,
"O Rākṣasa, what fruit will you obtain by killing these illustrious ones?
Those who commit evil deeds, being cruel and despised by the world, do not remain long in power once they have attained it; they fall like trees whose roots are decayed."
The doer of an evil deed necessarily reaps its fruit when the time arrives, just as a tree bears seasonal blossoms;
in this world, the fruit of sinful actions is obtained before long.
O night-stalker, just as one who has eaten food mixed with poison [is destroyed], so have I,
the king, been encountered by you, O ranger of the night, who commit terrible evil and desire the misfortune of the world, in order to take my life.

3.028.011a For today, the gold-adorned arrows released by me upon you shall pierce through you and fall, like serpents into an anthill. 3.028.012a Those practitioners of dharma who were devoured by you in the Daṇḍaka forest—

Today, slain in battle along with your army, you shall follow after them. Today, let the supreme ṛṣis, who were stationed in their celestial chariots and whom you previously harmed, behold you struck down by my arrows as you dwell in hell.
"Strike as you please, O lowest of your lineage; exert yourself!
Today I shall strike down your head like a palm fruit.
Thus addressed by Rāma, he became enraged, his eyes bloodshot with anger.
Then, overcome with rage yet laughing, he replied to Rāma:
"O son of Daśaratha, having slain common rākṣasas in battle,
why do you praise yourself when you are not worthy of praise?"
Those bulls among men who are valiant or powerful do not say anything at all, being proud of their own splendor;
whereas those who are vulgar, of undisciplined soul, and the dregs of the kṣatriya caste in this world—
3.028.018c They boast pointlessly, just as you, Rāma,
are boasting. 3.028.019a O hero, when the time of death has arrived, what man would proclaim his own lineage in praise of himself when there is no occasion for it?

In every way, however, your own insignificance has been revealed by this boasting, like a heated piece of counterfeit gold tested in a fire of kusha grass. Yet you do not see me standing here, wielder of the mace.
Like an immovable mountain, a range of peaks variegated with minerals,
I am capable— mace in hand— of taking your life in battle,
even against all the three worlds, like Death himself with noose in hand.
3.028.023a Although much more could be said, I shall not speak it to you;
3.028.023c for if the sun were to set, there would then be an obstacle to the battle.
3.028.024a Fourteen thousand Rākṣasas have been slain by you.
"By your destruction, I shall today wipe away their tears. Having spoken thus, Kharas, filled with supreme rage, hurled that mace adorned with excellent armlets at Rāma, like a blazing thunderbolt.
That great, blazing mace, released by Kharabāhu,
having reduced the trees and shrubs to ashes, approached his side.
As that flaming mace, resembling the noose of Death, came rushing toward him—

Rāma cut that [mace] into many pieces with his arrows as it was coursing through the air; shattered and pierced by those shafts, it fell to the surface of the earth like a female serpent brought down by the power of spells, mantras, and medicinal herbs.
Having shattered that mace with his arrows, Rāghava, who is devoted to righteousness,
smilingly addressed these words to Khara in a state of agitation:
"O lowest of Rākṣasas, you have displayed all the extent of your strength."

"You are far weaker than I; you have roared in vain. Here is my mace, pierced by my arrows, fallen to the surface of the earth—it shall destroy the confidence of you who are so bold in your boasting."
"That which you said— 'I shall perform this wiping away of tears for the perished Rākṣasas'— that word of yours is also false, for you are a base Rākṣasa of vile character and deceitful conduct."
"Today, like Garuḍa seizing the nectar, I shall take away your life-breaths.
Today the earth shall drink the blood from your severed throat, adorned with bubbles of foam as you are torn apart by my arrows."
With all your limbs covered in dust and your two arms cast down and drooping,
you shall sleep embracing the earth as if it were a woman difficult to attain. When you, you foul-smelling Rākṣasa, have fallen asleep with deep slumber, [the world will be yours].
These Daṇḍakas shall become a refuge for those who have no refuge;
in Janasthāna, which shall now be a place of slaughter for you by my arrows,
the sages will roam fearlessly in every direction within the forest.

3.029.010a Today the rākṣasīs, whose kinsmen have been slain, will flee in all directions; 3.029.010c their faces wet with tears, wretched and terrified, they who once inspired fear in others shall now be struck with fear themselves.
3.029.011a O night-stalker, today they shall come to know the taste of sorrow.
3.029.011c Wives of corresponding lineage [are yours], you whose husband is such as this; 3.029.012a O you of cruel character, base-souled one, constant thorn in the side of the brahmins!
3.029.012c Because of you, the sages, filled with apprehension, cast their oblations into the fire.
3.029.013 To Rāghava, who was thus speaking with such vehemence in battle, Khara, his voice harsher than ever from rage, uttered this reproach:
3.029.014 "Truly, you are excessively arrogant, remaining fearless even in the face of terrors."
Therefore, you do not realize that you are subject to death, nor what should and should not be said.
For those men who are ensnared by the noose of Time do not distinguish between what ought to be done and what ought not to be done, as their six senses have been cast aside.
Having spoken thus to Rāma, the night-stalker knit his brows and,
looking all around for a weapon for the battle, beheld a great sāl tree not far away.
Seeing his lip, he tore it away;
lifting it with both arms and letting out a great roar, the one of immense strength hurled it toward Rāma and cried, "You are slain!"

3.029.019a Having cut down that [rākṣasa] as he was charging with a flood of arrows, the powerful Rāma 3.029.019c summoned a fierce rage in order to slay Khara in battle. 3.029.020a Then Rāma, covered in sweat, his eyes red at the corners from anger, [prepared for combat].
In that battle, he pierced Khara with a thousand arrows;
from the openings between those arrows, much frothy blood flowed forth,
like the discharge of waterfalls from a mountain.
Made frantic by Rāma’s arrows in the encounter, Khara,
intoxicated by the scent of blood, rushed swiftly toward him.
As he charged forward, agitated and drenched in blood, Rāma, skilled in weapons, [prepared for him].
3.029.023c Stepping back a little with swift strides,
3.029.024a Rāma then seized an arrow, glowing like fire, for the purpose of slaying Khara in battle— an arrow like a second staff of Brahmā.
3.029.025a That [arrow], given by Maghavan, the wise king of the gods,
3.029.025c that righteous-souled one fixed upon [his bow] and released it toward Khara. 3.029.026a Released, that great arrow had a sound like a thunderclap.
Raising his bow, Rāma let it fall upon Khara’s chest;
scorched by the fire of that arrow, Khara fell to the ground,
just as Andhaka was utterly consumed by Rudra in the Śveta forest.
Like Vṛtra by the thunderbolt, or Namuci by the foam, or Bala struck down by Indra’s lightning bolt, the slain Khara fell. Then all the royal sages and supreme ṛṣis gathered together.
Having honored Rāma with joy, they spoke these words:
"For this very purpose, the highly effulgent Mahendra, the subduer of Pāka and destroyer of cities,
came to the holy hermitage of Śarabhaṅga."
"O son of Daśaratha, you have been brought to this place by the great seers through their skillful means for the purpose of slaying these cruel Rākṣasas of evil deeds;
thus has this task of ours been accomplished by you."
3.029.032c The great seers will practice the Dharma in happiness among the Daṇḍakas.
3.029.033a In the meantime, the heroic Lakṣmaṇa, together with Sītā,
3.029.033c having emerged from the mountain fastness, entered his hermitage in comfort.

Then the victorious hero Rāma, being honored by the great seers and saluted by Lakṣmaṇa, entered the hermitage. Seeing him, the slayer of enemies who brought happiness to the great seers, [the seers rejoiced].
Vaidehī became overjoyed and embraced her husband.
Then Śūrpaṇakhā saw that fourteen thousand Rākṣasas of fearsome deeds had been slain by Rāma alone.
Having seen Dūṣaṇa, Khara, and Triśiras slain in battle, she,
who resembled a rain-cloud, let out a great roar once more.
Having witnessed that deed performed by Rāma, which would have been exceedingly difficult for others to achieve, she [rejoiced].
Extremely agitated, she went to Laṅkā, which was ruled by Rāvaṇa. There,
at the front of the palace, she beheld Rāvaṇa, blazing with splendor,
seated together with his ministers like Vāsava among the Maruts.
He was seated upon a supreme golden throne that resembled the sun,
like a blazing fire placed upon a golden altar,
for the gods, Gandharvas, spirits, and high-souled sages.
Invincible in battle, a hero like Death with its mouth wide open,
his chest marked by the scars of wounds inflicted by the thunderbolt and lightning during the conflicts between the gods and the asuras,
and bearing the calluses from being gored by the tips of Airāvata’s tusks.

He had twenty arms and ten necks, was adorned with beautiful regalia, possessed a broad chest, and was a hero marked by the signs of royalty; he resembled smooth lapis lazuli and wore earrings of refined gold.
With strong arms, white teeth, and a massive face like a mountain,
his body had been struck hundreds of times by the falling discus of Viṣṇu in battle with the gods, as well as by all the weapons of the deities.
He who swiftly agitates the unshakeable oceans,
who hurls down the peaks of mountains and crushes the gods,
and who destroys righteousness while violating the wives of others.
He who was always the employer of all divine weapons and the constant creator of obstacles for sacrifices;
who, having gone to the city of Bhogavatī and defeated Vāsuki,
took away Takṣaka’s beloved wife after vanquishing her.
Having gone to Mount Kailāsa and defeated Naravāhana, he seized his celestial chariot Puṣpaka, which travels at will;
as well as the divine Caitraratha forest, the Nalinī lake, and the Nandana grove.
That powerful one, who out of anger destroys the celestial gardens,
and who, resembling a mountain peak, restrains with his two arms the illustrious moon and sun as they rise, O scorcher of foes.
Having performed austerities for ten thousand years in the great forest,
that wise one who in former times offered his own heads to the Self-Existent One (Svayambhū) [is he whom] the gods,
dānavas, gandharvas, piśācas, birds, and serpents [could not withstand].
He who possesses fearlessness in battle, save for death at the hands of men;
he who is praised with sacred mantras by the twice-born during sacrifices; and that one of great strength who draws the Soma juice in the sacrificial sheds.

Rāvaṇa, who robbed sacrifices of their rightful recipients, was cruel, a slayer of Brahmins, and of wicked conduct; he was harsh, merciless, and devoted to the harm of all creatures, bringing fear to the entire world.
The Rākṣasī beheld her cruel, immensely powerful brother—
the illustrious lord of Rākṣasas, the delight of the Paulastya lineage— adorned with celestial garments and ornaments, and graced by divine garlands.
Having displayed him who possessed blazing, wide eyes,
she— faint with fear and delusion— spoke these most dreadful words to that one who moves fearlessly:
Then Śūrpaṇakhā, having been disfigured by the high-souled one, distressed and enraged, spoke these harsh words to Rāvaṇa, the one who makes the world cry out, in the midst of his ministers.
"Negligent in the enjoyment of sensual pleasures, acting according to your own whims and unrestrained,
you do not perceive the terrible danger that has arisen, even though it must be recognized. You are attached to vulgar enjoyments, O lord of the earth, and your conduct is driven by desire."
People do not hold a greedy man in high regard, just as living beings avoid the fire of a cremation ground.
That king who does not personally attend to his duties at the proper time surely perishes along with his kingdom and those very duties.

Men avoid from afar a king who does not employ spies, who is difficult to behold, and who lacks self-control, just as elephants avoid the mud of a river. Those kings who lack self-control do not protect their realm.

They do not shine with prosperity, just as mountains do not shine when submerged in the ocean. Having entered into conflict with self-possessed gods, gandharvas, and dānavas, how can you, being fickle and lacking secret spies, remain a king?
O best among victors, those kings whose spies, treasury, and policy are not under their own control are equal to common people;
for it is because of these that rulers perceive all matters, even those situated at a distance.
"Therefore, kings are said to be 'long-sighted' because of their spies. I consider you to be one who has failed to employ spies and is surrounded by common ministers,
since you do not even realize that your own people at Janasthāna have been slaughtered."

3.031.011a Fourteen thousand Rākṣasas of fearsome deeds, 3.031.011c and Khara along with Dūṣaṇa, were slain by Rāma alone. 3.031.012a Safety was granted to the sages, and the Daṇḍaka forest was rendered secure.
Janasthāna has been laid waste by Rāma of unwearied deeds;
yet you, O Rāvaṇa, are greedy, negligent, and subject to others,
for you do not perceive the danger that has arisen within your own domain.
All beings flee from a king who is harsh, a giver of little, negligent, arrogant, and deceitful during times of calamity; likewise,
they abandon a man who is excessively proud, ungraspable, and self-conceited.
Even his own kinsmen will slay a wrathful king when he is in distress.
He will not attend to his duties, nor will he fear danger;
soon cast out from his kingdom and wretched, he will become equal to a blade of grass.
A task may be accomplished with dry wood, or even with clods of earth and dust;
but no purpose can be served by kings who have fallen from their station.
Just as a garment that has been worn out, or as a garland that has been crushed—

Thus, even one who is capable becomes useless when fallen from his kingdom. But that king who is vigilant, all-knowing, has conquered his senses, is grateful, and is virtuous by nature— he remains for a long time.

Even when asleep, he remains awake through his eye of political wisdom; that king, whose anger and favor are manifest, is honored by the people. But you, O evil-minded Rāvaṇa, are devoid of these very qualities.
Since this great slaughter of the Rākṣasas was unknown to you through your spies,
you have become one who disregards his own domain;
you do not know the true nature of the distinctions between place and time.
"His intellect is unapplied to the discernment of virtues and faults;
having lost his kingdom, he will soon perish.
Thus were her own faults proclaimed by her.
Having reflected with his intellect, Rāvaṇa, the lord of the night-stalkers, endowed as he was with wealth, pride, and power, pondered for a long time.
Then Rāvaṇa, enraged in the midst of his ministers, questioned Śūrpaṇakhā as she was speaking harsh words:
"Who is Rāma? What is his prowess like? What is his appearance? And what is his valor?"
3.032.002c For what purpose did he enter the Daṇḍaka forest, so difficult to traverse? 3.032.003a What was Rāma’s weapon, by which the Rākṣasas were slain,
and by which Khara was killed in battle, as well as Dūṣaṇa and Triśiras?
Thus addressed by the lord of the rākṣasas, the rākṣasī, overcome with rage,
then proceeded to describe Rāma according to the facts:
"He has long arms and large eyes, and he is clothed in bark and black antelope skin."
Rāma, the son of Daśaratha, equal in beauty to Kandarpa,
drew his bow— which resembled the rainbow of Śakra— and, adorned with golden armlets,
discharged blazing iron arrows like highly venomous serpents.
I do not see the mighty Rāma taking up his terrible arrows, nor releasing them,
nor drawing his bow in battle;
yet I see that army being slaughtered by showers of arrows.
By Indra alone was the finest grain struck down by showers of stones;
yet fourteen thousand Rākṣasas of terrifying prowess were slain by his sharp arrows with that single man on foot.
In a little more than half a muhūrta, Khara along with Dūṣaṇa have been dealt with;
safety has been granted to the sages, and the Daṇḍaka forest has been made secure. Having disregarded me, I alone was somehow released by that high-souled one.
Fearing the murder of a woman, Rāma, who knows his own self,
[exiled him]; and his brother, the highly energetic Lakṣmaṇa— equal to him in virtue and prowess, devoted, loyal, and heroic— [remained].
3.032.013a Impatient, invincible, victorious, valiant, wise, and strong,
[he was] Rāma’s right arm, his very life-breath moving outward.
3.032.014a But Rāma’s illustrious and lawful wife was the large-eyed lady.
She named Sītā, the daughter of Videha, of excellent form and slender waist—
neither a goddess, nor a Gandharva woman, nor a Yakṣī, nor a Kinnarī—
such a woman has never been seen by me before on this earth.
He whose wife Sītā might become, and whom she might joyfully embrace,
would surpass even Purandara in all the worlds.
She is of virtuous character, her form is praiseworthy, and her beauty is peerless on earth.
"She is a wife suited to you, and you likewise are a husband for her.
I am prepared to bring that lovely-faced woman, with her broad hips and full, high breasts, to be your wife."
But having seen that Vaidehī today, whose face resembles the full moon,
you will become subject to the arrows of the God of Love,
if the desire for her as a wife arises within you.
"Quickly lift up your right foot here for the sake of victory! O Lord of Rākṣasas, do what is pleasing to those demons by slaying that cruel Rāma who dwells in the hermitage."
"Having slain him with sharpened arrows, as well as the great car-warrior Lakṣmaṇa,
you shall enjoy Sītā at your ease once she is left without a protector— provided, O Lord of Rākṣasas, that these words of mine are pleasing to you."
"O Raghava, let my word be carried out without hesitation.
Having heard this, Rama [saw] the night-stalkers who had gone to Janasthāna slain by his straight-flying arrows.
"Having learned that Khara has been killed and Dūṣaṇa as well,
you ought now to undertake what must be done.
Then Śūrpaṇakhā, having heard those hair-raising words, [spoke].
Having dismissed his ministers and understood the matter at hand, he departed.
Then, having investigated that matter thoroughly and ascertained it correctly, he deliberated upon the relative strength and weakness of the faults and virtues involved.
Having thus made a firm resolve within himself that "this is what must be done," he,
steady-minded, then went to the beautiful carriage shed.
Having gone to the carriage shed, the lord of the Rākṣasas remained there in concealment.
He urged the charioteer, saying, "Let the chariot be yoked.
Thus addressed, the charioteer, swift in his movements, yoked within a mere moment that excellent chariot which was his master's desire.
Mounting a golden chariot that moved at will, adorned with jewels,
and yoked to mules with faces like Piśācas and decorated with gold ornaments,
that younger brother of the Giver of Wealth [Yama] set out with a roar resembling the thunder of clouds.
The glorious lord of the Rākṣasas went toward the lord of rivers and streams;
that ten-faced one, with white hair-tassels and a white parasol,
resembled smooth lapis lazuli and was adorned with ornaments of refined gold.
Ten-faced and twenty-armed, with a magnificent retinue,
the enemy of the gods and slayer of the lord of sages shone like the ten-peaked king of mountains;
mounting his chariot that moves at will, the lord of the Rākṣasas was resplendent.
Like a cloud in the sky accompanied by lightning and cranes,
the valiant one gazed upon the ocean shore together with its mountains,
strewn with thousands of trees laden with various flowers and fruits.
It was surrounded on all sides by lotus ponds containing cool, auspicious waters,
and by spacious hermitage sites provided with sacrificial altars;
it was crowded with plantain and *āḍhaki* trees and adorned with coconut palms.
It was adorned with *sāla*, *tāla*, and *tamāla* trees in full bloom,
and graced by supreme ṛṣis who were extremely restricted in their diet,
as well as by thousands of *nāgas*, *suparṇas*, *gandharvas*, and *kiṃnaras*.
It was graced by those who have conquered their desires, by the Siddhas, and by the Cāraṇas; it was filled with Ājas, Vaikhānasas, Māṣas, Vālakhilyas, and Marīcipas,
and was surrounded by women of divine form adorned with celestial ornaments and garlands.
It was frequented by thousands of Apsarases who knew the arts of play and pleasure,
served by the illustrious wives of the gods,
and inhabited by hosts of gods and Dānavas who subsist on nectar.
It was crowded with swans, cranes, and water-fowl, and made resonant by the cries of cranes; it had delightful floors of cat’s-eye gem, glossy from the splendor of the ocean,
and featured vast, white pavilions adorned with celestial garlands.

The younger brother of the Giver of Wealth beheld celestial chariots on all sides, graced with the sounds of musical instruments and song; these vehicles, which travel at will, belonged to those who had conquered the worlds through their ascetic penance, and he saw Gandharvas and Apsarases as well.
Beholding thousands of sandalwood forests, pleasant to the sight and satisfying to the sense of smell, consisting of the finest resinous exudations and roots;
as well as groves and parks of the most excellent aloe-woods.
There were also *takkola* fruits of excellent quality and fragrant fruits;
there were blossoms of the *tamāla* tree and thickets of black pepper,
as well as heaps of pearls drying upon the shore.
He saw heaps of conch shells as well as clusters of coral,
and mountains of gold and silver on all sides; he also saw delightful springs and clear lakes.

Beholding cities abounding in wealth and grain, filled with jewels of women, and crowded with elephants, horses, and chariots; [beholding] that land which was level on all sides, pleasant, and where the breeze was soft to the touch.
He beheld the coastal region of the King of Rivers, which resembled the third heaven.
There he saw a banyan tree, dark as a cloud, surrounded by sages;
its branches extended for a hundred *yojanas* in every direction.
3.033.028c Having seized an elephant and a giant tortoise for the sake of food, the mighty Garuḍa came to a branch.
3.033.029a By the weight of those two, that best of birds suddenly [broke] the branch.
Then the mighty Suparṇa shattered that tree with its abundant foliage.
Therein were gathered the supreme ṛṣis— the Vaikhānasas, the Māṣas, the Vālakhilyas, the Marīcipas, the Ajas, and the Dhūmras.
Out of compassion for them, Garuḍa took that branch, which was a hundred yojanas long,
and departed with speed, carrying both the elephant and the tortoise; meanwhile,
the righteous-souled one, having devoured that meat, stood on one foot.
Having destroyed the Niṣāda territory with his talon, that best of birds attained incomparable joy after having liberated the great sages. With that very joy, his prowess was doubled.
Having formed this resolve for the sake of bringing back the nectar of immortality, the wise one then crushed the iron nets, broke through the excellent jewel-house,
and carried away the nectar from the protected abode of Mahendra.
The younger brother of the Giver of Wealth (Kubera) beheld that banyan tree named Subhadra, frequented by hosts of great seers and marked with the sign of Garuḍa;
having gone to the further shore of the ocean, the lord of rivers.
In a secluded, holy, and beautiful forest interior, he saw an hermitage.
There, he beheld a Rākṣasa named Mārīca, who wore a black antelope skin and matted hair and bark garments, and who was restricted in his diet.
3.033.038a Having met with that Rākṣasa according to custom, Rāvaṇa,
who was skilled in speech, then spoke these words thereafter:
3.034.001a "O Mārīca, my dear, listen to the words I am speaking."
"I am distressed, and for me in my distress, you are indeed the supreme refuge.
You know Janasthāna, where my brother Khara dwells,
as well as the mighty-armed Dūṣaṇa and my sister Śūrpaṇakhā."
The immensely powerful, flesh-eating Rākṣasa Triśiras,
and many other heroic night-stalkers who have attained their marks,
dwell here by my command and inhabit this residence.
In the great forest, they harassed the sages who practice dharma—
fourteen thousand Rākṣasas of terrifying deeds, heroes who have attained their mark and follow the will of Khara.
But now, those mighty ones dwelling in Janasthāna have come together and are utterly dependent upon Rāma for their safety in battle;
by that Rāma, whose wrath has been aroused at the forefront of the fray—
Without uttering even a single harsh word, he discharged his bow with arrows;
fourteen thousand rākṣasas of fearsome deeds were slain by those sharp shafts, by a mere human fighting on foot.
Khara was slain in battle and Dūṣaṇa was struck down;
having also killed Triśiras, the Daṇḍaka forest has been rendered free from fear.
Yet, together with his wife, he has been cast out by his enraged father, his life now at its end.
That Rāma, a disgrace to the Kṣatriyas, shall be the slayer of that army;
he is ill-behaved, harsh, cruel, foolish, greedy, and has no control over his senses.
Having abandoned dharma, he is unrighteous in soul and delights in the harm of living beings.
By him who, out of enmity, relying solely on his own strength in the forest,
disfigured my sister by cutting off her ears and nose—
his wife Sītā, who resembles the daughter of a god, [must be seized] from Janasthāna.
"I shall go forth with valor; be my companion in this task.
For with you as my ally standing by my side, O mighty one, and with my brothers, I do not stand in fear of all the gods in battle."
"O Rākṣasa, be my ally, for you are indeed capable;
in heroism, in battle, and in pride, there is no one equal to you.
It is for this purpose, O night-stalker, that I have come into your presence."
3.034.016c Hear that task which must be performed as assistance at my command: 3.034.017a Becoming a golden deer, variegated with silver spots,
3.034.017c roam in the hermitage of that Rāma, right before Sītā.
But undoubtedly, upon seeing you in the form of a deer, Sītā will say to her husband and Lakṣmaṇa, "Let him be captured! Then,
when those two have departed and it is empty, [you may take] Sītā as you please.
"Unimpeded, I shall carry him off, as Rāhu seizes the light of the moon. After that, when Rāma is emaciated by the abduction of his wife,
I shall strike him confidently with a heart that has already achieved its purpose."
Having heard that account of Rāma from the high-souled Mārīca,
his mouth became parched and he was struck with terror. With a mind trembling and dejected, he [addressed] Rāvaṇa.
In the great forest, he who knew Rāma’s prowess joined his palms in reverence and spoke these words,
which were true and beneficial both to him and to himself.
Having heard those words of the lord of the rākṣasas, the highly wise Mārīca, who was skilled in speech, replied to the sovereign of the rākṣasas:
"O King, men who always speak pleasant words are easy to find."
One who speaks what is unpleasant yet beneficial, and one who listens to it, are both rare to find.
Surely you do not realize that Rāma is of great heroism and exalted in virtue—
like Mahendra and Varuṇa— yet you are fickle and lack proper spies.
"O father, may it be well with all the *rākṣasas* on earth;
might Rāma, though enraged, not rid the world of *rākṣasas*; and might the daughter of Janaka not have been born for the end of your life?"
"May this great calamity not be caused by Sītā;
and may the city of Laṅkā, together with its rākṣasas, not perish along with you, even though you have obtained sovereignty and act according to your own desires without restraint."
For a king like you, who acts according to his lusts, is ill-behaved, and follows evil counsel— that evil-minded ruler destroys himself, his kinsmen, and his kingdom.
Yet he has not been abandoned by his father, nor has he ever transgressed the bounds of propriety in any way.
He was neither greedy nor ill-behaved, nor was he a disgrace to the kṣatriyas;
he was not devoid of the virtues of dharma, for he increased the joy of Kausalyā.
Indeed, he was not harsh toward any living beings, but was devoted to the welfare of all.
Seeing his father, who was truthful in speech, deceived by Kaikeyī,
the righteous-souled one then departed for the forest,
thinking, "I shall do so," for the sake of pleasing Kaikeyī and his father Daśaratha.
Having abandoned both his kingdom and its enjoyments, he has entered the Daṇḍaka forest.
My dear, Rāma is neither harsh, nor unlearned, nor one who has failed to conquer his senses;
you ought not to speak such falsehoods, for they are contrary to what has been heard.
Rāma is Dharma incarnate, virtuous, and one whose prowess is truth;
he is the king of the entire world, just as Vāsava is of the gods.
How could you [seize] his Vaidehī, who was protected by his own splendor?

3.035.014c You wish to seize [him] by force, as if seizing the radiance of the sun. 3.035.015a You ought not to rashly enter the blazing fire of Rāma in battle, which has arrows for its flames, is unassailable, and has bows and swords for its fuel.
With his mouth wide open like a bow, with rays of arrows for its flames, and full of indignation—
that hero bearing bow and arrow who destroys the enemy host—
[he has come] having renounced kingdom, happiness, and even his own dear life.
"O dear one, you ought not to provoke Rāma, the bringer of death, here. For immeasurable is that splendor of his, for whom that daughter of Janaka exists;
you are not capable of abducting her while she is protected by Rāma’s bow in the forest."

"O Lord of the Rākṣasas, what is the use of making this futile effort? Sītā, of slender waist, is dearer to him than his own life-breaths; she is ever devoted to him, like the blazing crest of a sacrificial fire."

"If you are seen by him in battle, that will be the end of your life, as well as your happiness and your kingdom, which are so difficult to attain. Together with all his ministers, led by Vibhīṣaṇa, [he spoke thus].
Having consulted with those most righteous in dharma and having reached his own decision,
he weighed the relative strength of faults and virtues,
and understood the true extent of his own power as well as that of Rāghava.
Having determined what is indeed for your benefit, you ought to do what is appropriate.
But I consider that an encounter in battle with the son of the King of Kosala is not suitable for you.
"O Lord of the Night-rangers, listen once more to these supreme words, which are both appropriate and fitting:
'Once, while wandering this earth by my own prowess,' "
Possessing the strength of a thousand elephants, resembling a mountain,
like a dark blue cloud, with earrings of refined gold,
wearing a diadem and armed with a mace, he struck fear into the world.
I roamed the Daṇḍaka forest, devouring the flesh of sages. Then the great sage Viśvāmitra, whose soul was righteous, being terrified of me,
went in person to King Daśaratha and spoke these words.
"May this Rāma, composed in mind, protect me during the time of the festival. O Lord of Men, a terrible fear of Mārīca has arisen within me.
When he had spoken thus, the righteous King Daśaratha then [replied].
He replied to the highly fortunate great sage Viśvāmitra:
"This descendant of Raghu is less than sixteen years of age and has not yet mastered the use of weapons;
however, my entire army shall go along with me as I please."
"O best of sages, I shall slay your enemy as you desire.
When he had spoken thus, the sage replied again to the king:
"In this world, there is no strength other than Rāma’s that is sufficient for that rākṣasa."
"Though he is but a child, this one possesses great splendor and is capable of subduing him.
I shall go taking Rāma with me; may you be well, O scorcher of foes!
Having spoken thus, the sage took that prince with him.

3.036.009c Viśvāmitra, supremely delighted, departed for his own hermitage. 3.036.010a At that time, Rāma remained stationed in the Daṇḍaka forest, having been initiated for the sake of the sacrifice, stretching his wonderful bow.
3.036.011a The glorious youth, whose secondary sexual characteristics were not yet developed, was dark-complexioned with beautiful eyes;
3.036.011c wearing a single garment, carrying a bow, and adorned with a topknot and a golden garland,
he graced the Daṇḍaka forest with his own radiant splendor.
At that time, Rāma appeared like the rising crescent moon.
Then I, resembling a cloud, wearing earrings of refined gold,
powerful and having received boons, approached that hermitage out of pride.
3.036.014a By him I was seen as I entered, suddenly with my weapon raised.
3.036.014c But upon seeing me, he calmly strung his bow. 3.036.015a Out of delusion, I disregarded that descendant of Raghu, thinking, "This one is but a child."
3.036.015c In great haste, I ran toward Viśvāmitra’s sacrificial altar.
3.036.016a Then that sharp arrow, the destroyer of enemies, was released by him.
3.036.016c Struck by it, I was cast into the ocean a hundred yojanas away.

"O dear one, struck by the force of Rāma’s arrow, my consciousness reeled; I was then cast down by him into the deep waters of the ocean. Only after regaining my senses after a long time did I return to the city of Laṅkā."

In this way, I was then liberated while your companions were struck down by the youthful Rāma, whose deeds are effortless, even though he was unskilled in weapons. Therefore, if you persist in conflict with Rāma despite being restrained by me, [you will suffer the same fate].
Having encountered a terrible calamity, you will soon perish;
you shall bring about distress and misfortune for the Rākṣasas, who are skilled in the arts of play and pleasure and devoted to social gatherings and festivals.

"You shall see the city of Laṅkā— crowded with mansions and palaces, adorned with various jewels— ruined for the sake of Maithilī. Even those who are pure and do not commit sins [suffer] because of their association with the wicked."
They will perish through their own sins, like fish in a dragon’s lake.
You shall see the Rākṣasas— whose limbs are smeared with divine sandalwood paste and adorned with celestial ornaments— struck down upon the ground because of your transgression.
You shall see those night-rangers— the survivors of the slaughter, now without refuge— fleeing in the ten directions, some having had their wives taken and others fleeing with their wives,
while you remain encircled by a net of arrows and enveloped in flames of fire.
"You shall undoubtedly behold Laṅkā with its houses consumed by fire.
O King, you have thousands of women as your wives;
therefore, O Rākṣasa, be devoted to your own wife and protect your own lineage."
"O Rāma, if you wish to enjoy for a long time your honor, prosperity, kingdom, and your own dear life, do not do what is displeasing to me.
Though being earnestly restrained by me, your well-wisher..."
If you violate Sītā by force,
you shall go to the abode of Yama with your strength diminished and your kinsmen,
your life having been taken by the arrows of Rāma.
In this way, I was somehow liberated from him in that battle;
now listen to what happened next.
Though treated in such a manner by the two Rākṣasas, I remained undaunted.
Accompanied by two deer-shaped creatures, he entered the Daṇḍaka forest.
With a flaming tongue, a massive body, sharp horns, and great strength,
that great beast, a consumer of flesh, roamed through the Daṇḍaka wilderness.
O Rāvaṇa, wandering about in the most terrifying manner, he harassed those ascetics at the Agnihotra sacrifices, at sacred fords, and at sacred trees;
having slain the practitioners of dharma in the Daṇḍaka forest.
Drinking their blood and likewise devouring their flesh,
I— a cruel eater of the flesh of sages— terrifying those who dwell in the forest,
roamed the Daṇḍaka woods, intoxicated by blood.
Then, while wandering in the Daṇḍaka forest as a destroyer of dharma, I encountered Rāma, who was devoted to the ascetic life and righteousness,
as well as the highly fortunate Vaidehī and the great chariot-warrior Lakṣmaṇa.
3.037.008c An ascetic of restricted diet, devoted to the welfare of all beings;
3.037.009a I, remembering our former enmity and thinking "this is a mere ascetic," disregarded the mighty Rāma while he was in the forest.
3.037.010a Extremely enraged, I rushed forward in the form of a deer with sharp horns;
3.037.010c desiring to kill him and remembering that previous blow, I was devoid of wisdom.
3.037.011a By him, three sharp arrows, destroyers of enemies, were released.
Drawing his powerful bow, those three arrows— resembling thunderbolts, most terrible, blood-drinking, and swift as the wind or Garuḍa— all arrived together with their joints perfectly straightened.
Knowing Rāma’s prowess and having previously witnessed his power, that deceitful one escaped;
thus he was released, while those two Rākṣasas were slain. Having somehow been spared by Rāma’s arrow, he regained his life.
"Having renounced the world here, I am a disciplined ascetic, composed in mind.
Yet, in every tree I see Rāma, clad in bark and black antelope skin,
holding his bow like Death himself with a noose in hand."
"O Rāvaṇa, terrified, I see even thousands of Rāmas;
this entire forest appears to me as being composed entirely of Rāmas.
Indeed, O Lord of the Rākṣasas, I see only Rāma everywhere, even in solitude."
Having seen Rāma in my dream, I wander about, deprived of my senses. O Rāvaṇa, names beginning with the letter "R"— such as Rāma—
and even jewels and chariots, cause me to tremble with fear.
"I know his power; a battle with him is not suitable for you.
Fight with Rāma in battle, or else grant him your pardon, O Rākṣasa. You should have no further talk of Rāma, if you wish to see me."

3.037.020a These words have been spoken by me, seeking the welfare of my kinsmen; if you do not accept them as they are being uttered, 3.037.020c you, along with your relatives, shall lose your life in battle.

"Today he has been slain by Rāma with straight-flying arrows. But Rāvaṇa did not accept those words spoken by Mārīca— words that were both appropriate and fitting— just as one desiring death refuses medicine.

3.038.002 Driven by fate, the lord of the Rākṣasas spoke these harsh and improper words to Mārīca, who had been speaking what was beneficial and wholesome: 3.038.003 "O Mārīca, as for this which you say to me— that it is contrary to reason— "

3.038.003 Your words are utterly fruitless, like seed sown in barren soil. 3.038.004 But it is not possible for me to be turned away from Rāma in battle by your words— especially those of a wicked-natured, foolish mortal.
3.038.005a He who, having abandoned his friends, his kingdom, as well as his mother and father,
3.038.005c went to the forest all at once upon hearing the vulgar words of a woman— 3.038.006a I must certainly [confront] him in battle, he who is the slayer of Khara.
"Sītā, who is dearer to you than life itself, must be carried off in your presence. O Mārīca, such is the firm resolve that dwells within my heart;
it cannot be turned back even by the gods and asuras led by Indra."
"Whether it be a fault or a virtue, you ought to speak thus when questioned regarding the failure or the means for the certain accomplishment of this task; indeed,
a wise minister who is questioned must provide an answer."

One who desires his own prosperity should speak to the lord of the earth with palms joined in reverence; he should address the sovereign with words that are not contrary, but gentle, auspicious, beneficial, and full of courtesy.

3.038.011a But when beneficial speech is spoken with harshness, Mārīca, 3.038.011c the king does not welcome it, for he is worthy of honor yet devoid of respect. 3.038.012a Kings of immeasurable power assume five forms.
The heat of Agni, the valor of Indra, the gentleness of Soma, the rod of Yama, and the serenity of Varuṇa— therefore,
in all circumstances, kings are to be honored and revered.
"But you, not understanding dharma and relying solely on delusion,
speak such harsh words out of wickedness to me, a guest who has arrived.
O Rākṣasa, I do not inquire into merits or faults, nor what is appropriate for myself."
"In this matter, you, sir, ought to provide assistance.
Becoming a golden deer, variegated with silver spots,
you should entice Vaidehī and then depart as you please."
But seeing you as a golden illusory deer,
Maithilī will be filled with wonder and will quickly say to Rāma, "Bring him here!
And when the descendant of Kakutstha has departed, as well as Lakṣmaṇa, she will do as she pleases.
"I shall bring back Vaidehī, just as the thousand-eyed Indra brought Śacī.
Having accomplished this task, O Rākṣasa, go wherever you please.
O Mārīca of noble vows, I shall give half of my kingdom to you."
"Go, gentle one, along an auspicious path for the success of this undertaking.
Having reached Sītā and having deceived Rāghava without a fight,
I shall return to Laṅkā with you, my purpose accomplished."
"You must perform this task for me, even by force.
For one who stands in opposition to a king never prospers in happiness. Having encountered him, your life will be in peril."
Death is indeed certain;
therefore, having reflected upon this properly with your intellect,
do whatever is beneficial for you in this situation.
Commanded like a king, the night-stalker Mārīca spoke these harsh words to the lord of the Rākṣasas:
"By what evildoer has this destruction been advised to you?"

"O night-stalker, who among the evildoers does not rejoice at you, O King, while you are happy along with your sons, your kingdom, and your ministers? By whom was this taught to you as a means to the gateway of death?"
"O night-stalker, it is quite evident that your enemies, being of inferior strength,
desire your destruction while you are held in check by one more powerful than yourself. By what base person, speaking for your detriment, was this counsel given to you?"
"O night-stalker, he who desires you as you perish through your own deeds—
O Rāvaṇa, your ministers are indeed worthy of death yet they are not slain,
for they do not restrain you in every way as you have ascended onto the path of ruin."

3.039.007a For a king who acts according to his whims and has taken to a wrong path must be restrained in every way by his virtuous ministers; yet you, who ought not to be restrained, are being restrained.
3.039.008a O best among victors, [you should have pursued] dharma, artha, kāma, and fame.
"O night-stalker, ministers obtain [their rewards] through the favor of their master;
but in the opposite case, O Rāvaṇa, all that becomes fruitless.
Other people, however, suffer calamity due to the deficiency of their master."
"For righteousness and victory, O best among victors, have their root in the king;
