therefore, in all circumstances, the lord of men must be protected.
"O night-stalker, it is not possible to govern a kingdom through harshness."
"O Rākṣasa, ministers who offer harsh counsel do not prosper when they act contrary to one's interests or when they are undisciplined; indeed, they perish along with him,
just as chariots driven by a slow driver quickly come to ruin on uneven terrain."
3.039.013 Many virtuous men in this world, who were devoted to the practice of dharma,
have perished along with their retinues because of the offenses of others.
3.039.014 O Rāvaṇa, when a ruler is hostile and harsh toward his subjects, they are destroyed.
Protected as they are, they do not prosper, like sheep guarded by a jackal.
All the Rākṣasas under Rāvaṇa will surely perish,
for you are their harsh king— evil-minded and one whose senses are unsubdued.
3.039.016a This terrible event has befallen you by chance, like the falling of a palm fruit upon a crow.
3.039.016c What good can come of this, that you, along with your army, shall perish?
3.039.017a Having slain me, that Rāma will surely kill you before long.
"By this, I have accomplished my purpose, since I am slain by my enemy. Consider me as already dead from the mere sight of Rāma;
know that you yourself, along with your kinsmen, are as good as dead for having abducted Sītā."
If you bring Sītā from the hermitage together with me,
then neither you shall exist, nor I, nor Laṅkā, nor the Rākṣasas. Yet, though I am trying to restrain you for my own welfare...
O night-stalker, you do not tolerate these words;
for men whose life-span is spent and who are like the dead do not accept beneficial advice offered by friends.
Having spoken these harsh words, Mārīca then,
dejected from fear of the lord of the night-rangers, said, "Let us go.
And he was seen again by him, who bore a bow, arrows, and a sword.
My life has been destroyed by one like me with a raised weapon;
yet, what can I do against you, O evil-minded one?
I am going now, my dear, may it be well with you, O night-stalker.
At those words, that Rākṣasa became overjoyed;
embracing him very tightly, he spoke these words:
"This speech you have uttered is full of heroism, as if it had been spoken by my own voice."
"Now you are Mārīca; formerly you were another night-stalker.
Quickly mount this sky-faring chariot adorned with jewels, which is yoked by me to donkeys with the faces of Piśācas."
Then Rāvaṇa and Mārīca, having mounted that chariot which was like a celestial vehicle, departed swiftly from that circle of hermitages;
even as they went, they beheld there cities and forests.
Having traversed all the mountains, rivers, kingdoms, and cities,
Rāvaṇa, the lord of the rākṣasas, together with Marīca, then reached the Daṇḍaka forest and beheld the hermitage of Rāghava.
Having descended from that chariot adorned with gold,
Rāvaṇa took Mārīca by the hand and spoke these words:
"This hermitage of Rāma is visible here, surrounded by plantain trees."
"Friend, quickly do that for which we have come.
Hearing Rāvaṇa's words, the Rākṣasa Mārīca then assumed the form of a deer and wandered about at the entrance of Rāma’s hermitage.
With the tips of his horns adorned with the finest jewels, his face was white and black in appearance;
his mouth was like a red lotus and a blue water-lily, and his ears were like blue lotuses.
His neck was slightly uplifted, and his belly was the color of sapphire.
His flanks resemble the *madhūka* flower, and he is like the filaments of a lotus; his hooves have the luster of *vaidūrya* gemstone, his legs are slender and well-knit,
and he is graced by a tail, the color of a rainbow, which rises upward.
With a captivating and glossy complexion, adorned with various kinds of jewels,
the Rākṣasa in an instant became a most beautiful deer,
setting ablaze that lovely forest and the site of Rāma’s hermitage.
Having assumed a captivating and beautiful form,
variegated with various minerals, that Rākṣasa wandered about, moving gracefully through the grassy meadows on all sides in order to entice Vaidehī.
Variegated with hundreds of silver spots and beautiful to behold,
he wandered about, breaking off and eating the tender shoots of the trees.
Having gone to a grove of plantain trees, he moved here and there among the *karṇikāra* flowers.
Moving slowly, seeking then to catch sight of Sītā,
that great deer, with a back variegated like a lotus,
shone brightly as he roamed at his ease near the vicinity of Rāma’s hermitage.
Having gone forth and returned again, that best of deer roamed about;
having gone with haste for a moment, he would turn back once more;
and while sporting, he would now stand upon the ground and now sit down again.
Having reached the gate of the hermitage, he goes toward the herds of deer; followed by the herds of deer, he returns once more—
the Rākṣasa who had assumed the form of a deer, longing for the sight of Sītā.
Darting forth, he whirled in various circles;
and all the other forest-dwelling deer, having gazed upon him and sniffed him, fled in the ten directions.
That Rākṣasa, though devoted to the slaughter of wild animals, did not eat those forest deer even upon touching them, for the sake of concealing his true nature. Then,
at that very time, the fair-eyed Vaidehī—
Busily engaged in gathering flowers,
the intoxicating-eyed woman with her beautiful face passed by the *karṇikāra*, *aśoka*, and mango trees as she moved about plucking the blossoms.
3.040.029c That supreme woman, who was unaccustomed to dwelling in the forest, beheld that deer made of jewels, 3.040.029e its limbs variegated with pearls and gems.
3.040.030a It indeed had beautiful tusks and lips, and its fine hair was like silver ore.
With eyes wide open in wonder, she gazed at him with affection.
And that illusory deer, O Rāma, beholding his beloved,
wandered there as if illuminating the forest.
Having seen that deer, composed of various jewels, never seen before,
Sītā, the daughter of Janaka, was filled with the utmost wonder.
Beholding it while she was gathering flowers, the woman of beautiful hips gazed intently at it.
It was adorned on its two sides with surfaces of gold and silver. Delighted, she of faultless limbs and the luster of refined gold cried out for her husband and for Lakṣmaṇa, who was armed.
Summoned by her, those two tigers among men, Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa,
while surveying that region, then beheld a deer.
Seeing it, Lakṣmaṇa, filled with apprehension, spoke to Rāma.

3.041.004c I consider this very deer to be that Rākṣasa, the son of Mārīca. 3.041.005a While we were joyfully hunting in the forest, O Rāma, kings were slain by him through this sinful artifice, for he can assume any form at will.
"O tiger among men, this deer-form has been created by the illusory power of this master of magic;
it is radiant and resembles a city of the Gandharvas.
For there is no such deer, variegated with jewels, in reality, O Raghava."
"O Lord of the World, this is surely an illusion upon the earth; of this there is no doubt.
To the descendant of Kakutstha who was speaking thus, Sītā—her mind captivated by the deception—replied with a pure smile, restraining him and filled with joy.
"O noble son, this deer, so delightful, captivates my mind. Bring it here, O mighty-armed one; it will serve as our plaything.
In this hermitage of ours, there are many others of auspicious appearance."
3.041.010c Deer roam together, as do yaks and sṛmaras; 3.041.011a Bears, herds of spotted deer, monkeys, and kiṃnaras likewise,
3.041.011c Roam about, O mighty-armed one— beings of supreme beauty and great strength.
"O King, never before has a deer like this been seen; in its splendor, patience, and radiance, this best of deer is peerless.
Its limbs are variegated with many colors, and it is covered with spots like precious gems."
Illuminating the forest with undisturbed brilliance, he shines like the moon.
Oh, what beauty! Oh, what splendor and what a magnificent perfection of voice! This wondrous and extraordinary deer seems to steal my very heart.
If your deer should come within range while still alive,
it will be a marvel that will produce great wonder;
and for us, when our forest exile has ended and we are established once more in our kingdom—
"This deer shall serve as an ornament for the inner apartments,
O Lord— for the sake of Prince Bharata, my mothers-in-law,
and myself. This divine form of a deer will produce wonder."
"O tiger among men, if this best of deer does not come into my grasp while alive, its beautiful hide will be mine; for when this creature is slain upon its Jāmbūnada-golden skin,"
"I wish to attend upon him while he is seated on a cushion of young grass.
This fierce conduct, driven by passion, is considered unseemly for women; yet, at the sight of this being's physical form, wonder has been born within me."
By that [chariot] with golden hair, with horns made of the finest jewels,
possessing the hue of the rising sun and the splendor of the path of the stars,
even the mind of Rāghava was filled with wonder.
3.041.022 Having thus heard Sītā’s words and having seen that wonderful deer,
Rāghava, filled with joy, spoke these words to his brother Lakṣmaṇa:
3.041.023 "Behold, Lakṣmaṇa, this longing of Vaidehī directed toward the deer."
"Indeed, because of his supreme beauty, this deer shall not exist today—
not in the Nandana grove, nor in the Caitraratha forest;
how much less, O Saumitri, could there be any deer on earth equal to him?"
His beautiful streaks of hair, both growing in the opposite and natural directions,
shine like variegated patterns upon the deer, adorned with golden spots. Behold this [deer] as it yawns, its [tongue] blazing like a flame of fire.
With his tongue darting from his mouth like lightning from a cloud,
with a face like emerald and sapphire and a belly like a conch or a pearl—
whom indeed would this deer not entice with his mind? His form is truly beyond description.
3.041.028a Upon seeing whose form, radiant as refined gold (jāmbūnada),
divine and composed of various jewels, would the mind not be struck with wonder?
3.041.029a Even for the sake of meat, archers pursue deer for the purpose of sport.
"O Lakṣmaṇa, kings kill [beasts] during hunts in the great forest.
Wealth is gathered with diligence in the great forest,
as well as various minerals consisting of gems, jewels, and gold."
That is the entire essence for men, a wealth that increases one's store;
it is everything conceived by the mind, O Lakṣmaṇa, just as it was for Śukra. By means of this purposeful action, a seeker proceeds without hesitation.
"O Lakṣmaṇa, those who know the treatises on statecraft and those who seek worldly gain say that this matter is worthy of pursuit:
upon the priceless golden skin of this jewel among deer,
the slender-waisted Vaidehī shall sit together with me."

"In my opinion, neither the *kādalī*, nor the *priyakī*, nor the *praveṇī*, nor the wool of sheep could ever equal this one in touch. And this glorious deer is the same as that divine being who travels through the sky."

"Both these deer are divine: the celestial deer and the terrestrial deer. Or, if what you tell me regarding this one is true, O Lakṣmaṇa—that it is the illusory power of a Rākṣasa—then its slaughter must be carried out by me."
For by this cruel Mārīca, who was undisciplined in soul, many eminent sages were previously harmed while he was wandering in the forest; and by him,
many lords of men were slain when they had risen for the hunt.

"Those supreme archers have been slain; therefore, this deer must be killed. Previously here, Vātāpi, having humiliated the ascetics, would kill the twice-born while staying within their bellies, like a fetus in a mule."

Once, after a long time, he encountered the great sage Agastya, who was endowed with spiritual power; indeed, [the demon] became his food. And seeing him desiring to assume that form upon rising, he [the demon]—
Smiling, the Blessed One said this to Vātāpi:
"O Vātāpi, because you disregarded and insulted the best of the twice-born in the world of the living by means of your power, you have therefore reached old age."

"O Lakṣmaṇa, such a Rākṣasa as this would not exist, like Vātāpi, were anyone like me—who is constant in dharma and has conquered his senses—to treat him with contempt. He would have been slain by me, just as Vātāpi was by Agastya; let there be no doubt of this."
"Stay here, girded and alert, and protect Maithilī;
for our duty depends upon her, O descendant of Raghu.
As for this deer, I shall either slay it or capture it."
"O Saumitri, I shall go quickly to bring back the deer.
Look, Lakṣmaṇa, at Vaidehī, who has set her heart upon the deer-skin;
for today this deer shall no longer exist, as its preeminent skin will have been taken."
"You must remain vigilant while staying in the hermitage with Sītā,
until I have slain this spotted deer with a single arrow. Having killed it and taken its hide, I shall return quickly, Lakṣmaṇa."
O Lakṣmaṇa,
having received Maithilī with vigilance, you must remain alert alongside the exceedingly powerful bird Jaṭāyu, who is possessed of great intelligence.
Being suspicious of him at every moment and from every direction,
the highly resplendent descendant of Raghu, having thus instructed his brother, fastened his sword with its hilt of gold.
Then, taking up his bow Trivinata, which was his own ornament, and fastening on two quivers, he of fierce prowess set forth. Indeed,
observing that lord of kings approaching, he began to elude him.
Out of fear, he vanished and then appeared once more;
girding his sword and taking up his bow, he ran toward where the deer was.
He saw it before him, shining as if with its own radiance.
With bow in hand in the great forest, he watched again and again as [the deer] ran, never once luring him away from his aim beyond the range of his arrow;
yet it remained suspicious and bewildered, as if leaping into the sky.
In certain new regions, it was visible and yet invisible;
like the autumnal orb of the moon enveloped by scattered clouds,
it was seen for only a moment and then suddenly appeared from afar.
By appearing and then disappearing, he drew Rāghava toward him;
Kākutstha became enraged, yet he was rendered helpless and deluded by him. Then, being utterly exhausted, he stood resting in the shade upon a grassy plot.
Surrounded by wild beasts, he was seen nearby;
seeing him, the highly effulgent Rāma, having resolved to kill him,
drew his very firm bow with great force, being himself powerful.
Aiming at that very deer, he released a blazing, flaming weapon created by Brahmā, which was like a serpent on fire. That excellent arrow violently pierced through the form of the deer.
Resembling a thunderbolt, it pierced the very heart of Mārīca.
Then, leaping up to the height of a palm tree, he fell down, afflicted by the arrow;
with his life nearly spent, he let out a terrible cry upon the earth.

3.042.013e As he was dying, Mārīca abandoned that artificial body. 3.042.014a Knowing that the time had come, he then produced a voice 3.042.014c exactly like that of Rāghava, crying out, "Alas, Sītā! O Lakṣmaṇa!"
Pierced in his vital organ by that incomparable arrow,
Mārīca abandoned his deer form and assumed his own rakṣasa form; as he was giving up his life, his body became exceedingly large.

Then that Rākṣasa, adorned with variegated armlets and all ornaments, wearing a golden garland and possessing great tusks, fell, struck by the arrow. Seeing that Rākṣasa of terrible appearance fallen upon the ground, [he was filled with joy].
Remembering Lakṣmaṇa’s words, he went toward Sītā in his mind; crying out "O Sītā! O Lakṣmaṇa! in a loud voice, that Rākṣasa died. Hearing this, how might Sītā fare?
"What state will the mighty-armed Lakṣmaṇa fall into?"—
thinking thus, the righteous Rāma, his hair standing on end with joy,
was overcome by a sharp fear born of despondency regarding Rāma [the king].
Having killed that Rākṣasa in the form of a deer and heard its cry,
and having slain another spotted deer and taken its meat,
Rāghava then hurried toward Janasthāna.
Recognizing that cry of distress in the forest as being like her husband's, Sītā said to Lakṣmaṇa: "Go and find Rāghava;
for neither my life nor my heart remains steady."
"I heard the sound of one crying out in extreme distress;
you ought to rescue your brother who is lamenting in the forest. Run quickly toward that brother of yours who seeks your protection."
Having fallen under the power of the Rākṣasas like a bull among lions,
he did not go even though thus addressed, for he was mindful of his brother’s command.
Then, the daughter of Janaka spoke to him there in anger.
"O Saumitri, in the guise of a friend, you are like an enemy to your brother,
since in this state you do not go to your brother's side;
O Lakṣmaṇa, you desire that Rāma perish for my sake."
"I consider this calamity to be dear to you; you have no affection for your brother.
That is why you remain here so confident, not seeing that one of great splendor. For what could I possibly do here while he has fallen into such danger?"
"What must be done by me while staying here, since you, the foremost one, have come?"—
to Vaidehī, who was speaking thus, overwhelmed with tears and grief,
Lakṣmaṇa spoke to the terrified Sītā, who resembled a doe.
"O Goddess, among gods and humans, among Gandharvas and birds,
among Rākṣasas, Piśācas, Kiṃnaras, and animals,
and even among the terrible Dānavas— O beautiful one, such a person is not to be found."
3.043.011c He who would fight against Rāma, who is like Vāsava, in battle— 3.043.012a Rāma is invincible in combat; you ought not to speak thus.
3.043.012c I cannot bear to leave you in this forest without the descendant of Raghu.
His power is irresistible even by the forces of the strongest, even by the three worlds united together, including the lords and the gods. Let your heart be at peace; let this distress be abandoned.
"Your husband will return soon after having slain that best of deer.
That voice was clearly neither his nor any deity's;
it was an illusion of that Rākṣasa, resembling a city of the Gandharvas."
"O Vaidehī, you have become a trust; you were entrusted to me by the high-souled Rāma. O lady of beautiful hips, I do not venture to abandon you here.
O blessed one, we have incurred the enmity of these night-stalkers."
"O Queen, regarding the slaughter at Janasthāna and the death of Khara,
the Rākṣasas are uttering these words by way of destiny in the great forest. O Vaidehī, you should not worry about those who take pleasure in violence."
Thus addressed by Lakṣmaṇa, she, enraged and with bloodshot eyes,
spoke these harsh words to the truth-speaking Lakṣmaṇa: "O ignoble one, you who initiate acts of compassion, cruel wretch, defiler of your lineage!"
"I consider you dear to me; that is why you speak these words. It is no wonder, O Lakṣmaṇa, that such evil should exist among enemies—among cruel men like you who always move in disguise."
"You are most wicked, for you follow Rāma alone into the forest all by yourself. Are you acting on my behalf in disguise, or have you been employed by Bharata?
How is it that you follow Rāma, who is dark as a blue lotus and has eyes like lotuses?"
Having taken refuge in my husband, I would desire another man;
in your very presence, O son of Sumitrā, I shall give up my life without a doubt,
for I cannot live on this earth even for a moment without Rāma.
Having been addressed with these harsh words, which were as heart-rending as the moon's eclipse,
Lakṣmaṇa— whose senses were fully subdued— spoke to Sītā with palms joined in reverence:
"I do not venture to offer a reply, for you are my deity."
"O Maithilī, such improper speech is not surprising among women;
indeed, this is the nature of women seen throughout these worlds. Women are devoid of righteousness, fickle, sharp-tongued, and divisive."
"Let all these forest-dwellers, who have become my witnesses, hear me: I have spoken words of justice, yet you have addressed me with harsh speech.
Shame on you! May you perish today, for you suspect me in such a manner."
"Because of my womanhood and my wicked nature, I have failed to abide by the word of my elder. O fair-faced one, may it be well with you; I shall go where the descendant of Kakutstha is.
May all the forest deities protect you, O large-eyed one."
"For those terrible omens that appear before me—
if only I might see you returned again together with Rāma. Thus addressed by Lakṣmaṇa, the daughter of Janaka wept.
Then, overwhelmed with tears, she spoke these harsh words:
"O Lakṣmaṇa, without Rāma, I shall enter the Godāvarī;
or else, I shall hang myself or cast my body from a precipice."
"I would rather drink fierce poison or enter the blazing fire than ever touch a man other than Rāghava even with my foot. Having thus rebuked Lakṣmaṇa, Sītā was overwhelmed with grief.
Weeping from grief, she struck her belly with both hands.
Seeing her in such a state of distress, dejected, and weeping— that large-eyed lady— Saumitri [looked upon her].
She comforted him, yet Sītā said nothing at all to her husband’s brother.
Then Lakṣmaṇa, having paid his respects to Sītā—
With palms joined in reverence and bowing slightly,
the self-possessed one looked back many times at Maithilī as he went into the presence of Rāma.

But having been addressed harshly by her, the younger brother of Rāghava became enraged; longing intensely for Rāma, he set out as if not long at all. Then Daśagrīva, having reached him, quickly took his opportunity.
Assuming the form of a wandering mendicant, he approached Vaidehī;
wrapped in smooth saffron robes, wearing a topknot, a parasol, and sandals,
and having hung a beautiful staff and water-pot over his left shoulder.
In the guise of a wandering mendicant, he approached Vaidehī in the forest; the exceedingly powerful one found her there, deprived of her two brothers,
like the great darkness that falls upon twilight when it is bereft of both the sun and the moon.
Then, like a most cruel planet, he beheld that illustrious young princess, who was like the star Rohiṇī separated from the Moon. At that fierce evildoer, the trees growing in Janasthāna [shook].
Having observed him, they did not tremble, nor did the wind blow;
and seeing him with his blood-red eyes looking on,
the swift-flowing Godāvarī river began to flow sluggishly out of fear.
Seeking an opportunity against Rāma, the ten-necked Rāvaṇa took advantage of that interval and approached Vaidehī in the guise of a mendicant,
appearing as a worthy man though he was unworthy, while she was grieving for her husband.
He approached Vaidehī like Saturn approaching the star Citrā; that wicked man, disguised in a handsome form like a well concealed by grass,
stood gazing at Vaidehī, the illustrious wife of Rāma.
She was beautiful, with lovely teeth and lips, her face resembling the full moon;
she sat in the leaf-hut, oppressed by tears and grief. He [beheld] her, whose eyes were like lotus petals, wearing yellow silk garments.

3.044.012c The evil-minded night-stalker approached Vaidehī. 3.044.013a Overcome by the arrows of the god of love, the lord of the Rākṣasas uttered a Vedic chant and spoke these humble words in private:
Rāvaṇa praised her, who was the most excellent in the three worlds, shining with a form like the goddess Śrī without her lotus:
"Who are you, O lady with the luster of gold, dressed in yellow silk?"
Bearing a beautiful garland of lotuses like a female lotus-plant, O fair-faced one, are you Hrī, Śrī, Kīrti, or the auspicious Lakṣmī; or perhaps you are an Apsaras,
O lady of noble form, or Bhūti, or Rati wandering at will?
Your teeth are even, pointed, smooth, and white;
your eyes are large and clear, with red corners and black pupils.
Your hips are broad and full, and your thighs resemble the trunks of elephants.

These two breasts of yours are well-developed, rounded, and perfectly formed; with their full and elevated nipples, they are lovely and resemble smooth palm fruits. Adorned with the finest of jewels, they are truly beautiful.
"O lady of lovely smiles, lovely teeth, and lovely eyes, O playful one!
O Rāma, you steal my heart as a river's current erodes its bank.
You have a waist that can be spanned by the hand, beautiful hair, and firm breasts."
Neither a goddess, nor a Gandharva woman, nor a Yakṣī, nor a Kiṃnarī—
never before have I seen a woman of such form upon this earth. And her dwelling here in the wilderness agitates my heart.
"Go away, may you be blessed; you ought not to dwell here.
This is the abode of terrible Rākṣasas who can assume any form at will—[the dwellings of] magnificent palaces and delightful city groves."
"O beautiful one with dark eyes, these things are excellent, fragrant, and fit to be used by you: choice garlands, choice drinks, and choice garments;
yet I consider your husband alone to be the most excellent thing for you."
"Who are you among the Rudras or the Maruts, O lady of radiant smiles? Or are you one of the Vasus, O beautiful woman? You appear to me to be a goddess.
Neither Gandharvas, nor gods, nor Kinnaras come here."
"This is the dwelling of the *rākṣasas*; how indeed have you come here?
Here dwell monkeys, lions, leopards, tigers, and deer, as well as bears, hyenas, and *kaṅkas*—how is it that you do not fear them?"
"O lady with the face of a forest creature, how is it that you, alone in this great forest, do not fear these swift and terrible elephants filled with rut?
Who are you, to whom do you belong, from where have you come, and for what purpose are you in the Daṇḍaka forest?"
"O auspicious lady, you wander alone through these terrible regions inhabited by rākṣasas.
Thus was Vaidehī addressed by the evil-minded Rāvaṇa, who had approached her disguised in the form of a brahmin. Upon seeing that Rāvaṇa had arrived, she spoke.
3.044.031e With every hospitality due to a guest, Maithilī honored him;
3.044.032a having first brought forth a seat and invited him with water for his feet, she then said to that one of gentle appearance, "It is ready."
Seeing Maithilī in the guise of a twice-born,
carrying a bowl and a water-pot as he approached,
she could not be incited to anger because of the perceived means [of his arrival].
He invited him like a brahmin according to the traditional custom: "O brahmin, here is a grass mat; please sit as you wish. And please accept this water for washing the feet."
"And this excellent forest-grown produce, already prepared,
should be enjoyed here without distraction for your sake.
Being thus invited, [he spoke to] her who replied with full words:
Having gazed upon Maithilī, the wife of Nara’s Lord,
Rāvaṇa laughed and, having set his mind on her abduction, delivered her over for execution.
Then, while waiting for her husband— who was well-attired and had gone out hunting— along with Lakṣmaṇa,
she looked about and beheld that green grove.
But Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa were not in that great forest; however,
when Vaidehī was questioned by Rāvaṇa— who desired to carry her away while disguised as a wandering mendicant— she identified herself by her own account.
"He is both a Brahmin and a guest; if unaddressed, he might indeed curse me.
Having reflected thus for a moment, Sītā spoke these words:
"I am the daughter of the high-souled Janaka of Mithilā."
"O best of the twice-born, may you be blessed; I am Sītā by name, the wife of Rāma.
I have lived for one year in the residence of the descendant of Raghu, enjoying human pleasures and having all my desires fulfilled."

Then, after a year had passed, the king, having assembled with his royal ministers, resolved to consecrate my husband Rāma. While the preparations for Rāghava’s consecration were being made, [the following occurred].
The noble lady named Kaikeyī is asking my husband for a boon.
Having won over my father-in-law by her good deeds toward me,
she seeks my husband’s exile and the consecration of Bharata.
She made two requests of her husband, that best of kings who was true to his word:
"I shall not eat today, nor shall I sleep, nor shall I ever drink;
this will be the end of my life if Rāma is consecrated."

While Kaikeyī was speaking thus, my father-in-law, who bestows honor, entreated her with meaningful requests, yet she did not grant his plea. My husband, possessed of great splendor, was twenty-five years of age.
3.045.010c Known in the world as Rāma, he is virtuous, truthful, and pure;
3.045.010e large-eyed and mighty-armed, he is devoted to the welfare of all beings.
3.045.011a When Rāma approached his father for the sake of the consecration—
"Kaikeyī spoke these words quickly to my husband:
'O Rāghava, listen to this which has been commanded by your father:
this kingdom, free from all obstacles, must be given to Bharata.'"
"You must indeed dwell for fourteen years in the forest;
go forth as an ascetic, O descendant of Kakutstha, and deliver your father from falsehood.
"So be it," Rāma replied to Kaikeyī, free from all fear.
My husband, firm in his vows, carried out her word:
"One should give, but not accept; one should speak the truth, and never a falsehood.
O Brahmin, this is Rāma’s constant and unsurpassed vow.
His half-brother, however, was the valiant one named Lakṣmaṇa;
that tiger among men was Rāma’s companion in battle and a slayer of enemies.
That brother named Lakṣmaṇa was a practitioner of righteousness and firm in his vows.
3.045.017c With bow in hand, he followed me as I went forth into exile.
3.045.018a We three, deprived of our kingdom on account of Kailēyī,
3.045.018c wander by our own prowess through this deep forest, O best of the twice-born.
"Take heart for a moment; it is possible for you to remain here.
My husband will arrive bringing abundant forest produce.
Therefore, tell me truly your name, your lineage, and your family."
"And why do you wander alone in the Daṇḍaka forest, O twice-born one?
While Sītā, the wife of Rāma, was speaking thus, the mighty Rāvaṇa,
lord of the rākṣasas, gave this harsh reply.

"O Sītā, by whom the worlds— including the gods, asuras, and pannagas— were terrified, I am that one named Rāvaṇa, the lord of the hosts of rākṣasas. Having seen you, who possess the luster of gold and are clothed in silk,"
"O blameless one, I find no pleasure in my own wives. Among all these excellent women brought here from various places— blessings be upon you— become my chief queen."
3.045.025a My great city named Laṅkā is situated in the midst of the ocean; 3.045.025c it is surrounded by the sea and established upon the summit of a mountain.
3.045.026a There, O Sītā, you shall roam with me through the forests.
"And you will no longer long for this forest life, O beautiful lady,
if you become my wife; five thousand female slaves, adorned with every ornament, shall attend upon you, Sītā."
Thus addressed by Rāvaṇa, the daughter of Janaka, her limbs faultless, became enraged and replied to that rākṣasa with utter disregard,
[addressing] her husband who was like Mount Mahendra, as immovable as a great mountain.
I am devoted to Rāma, who is as unshakeable as the great ocean; I am devoted to Rāma, the long-armed and broad-chested one, who moves with the prowess of a lion,
a lion among men who resembles a lion.
I am devoted to Rāma, the hero with a face like the full moon, a prince who has conquered his senses, possessed of great fame and mighty arms; you,
however, are a jackal who desires me here, a lioness so difficult to attain.
"I cannot be touched by you, just as the radiance of the sun cannot. O unfortunate Rāvaṇa, you surely see many golden trees because you desire the beloved wife of Rāghava."
You wish to take a fang from the mouth of a hungry, swift lion, the enemy of deer, or from the mouth of a venomous serpent;
you wish to carry away Mandara, the best of mountains, with your bare hand.
Having drunk the Kālakūṭa poison, you wish to go away in safety;
with your tongue you wipe away an eye-needle and lick a razor—
yet you still desire to obtain the beloved wife of Rāghava.
3.045.037a Having hung a stone around your neck, you wish to cross the ocean;
3.045.037c you wish to seize both the sun and the moon with your bare hands;
3.045.037e you who wish to violate the beloved wife of Rāma.
Having seen a blazing fire, you wish to seize it with your garment;
O auspicious one, you who wish to abduct Rāma’s wife, whose conduct is virtuous,
you wish to walk upon the tips of iron-tipped spears.
"You who desire to obtain a wife equal to Rāma—
consider the difference between a lion and a jackal in the forest, or the difference between a small stream and the ocean."
The difference between the finest wine and sour gruel is the same as the difference between you and the son of Daśaratha; the difference between gold and lead or iron is likewise the same.
The difference between you and Daśaratha is exactly the same as that between sandalwood paste and mud, or between an elephant and a cat in the forest.
As is the difference between a crow and the son of Vinatā, as is the difference between a water-fowl and a peacock, and as is the difference between a crane and a vulture in the forest;
In that interval, while Rāma— the son of Daśaratha and yourself— remained with bow and arrow in hand, possessing a splendor equal to that of the thousand-eyed Indra.
"Even though I have been taken by you, I shall not undergo old age, just as a diamond swallowed by a fly [remains unchanged].
Thus spoke she of uncorrupted nature.
Having spoken thus to that night-stalker,
she became distressed by the trembling of her limbs;
like a slender plantain tree shaken by the wind.
Observing Sītā trembling,
Rāvaṇa, whose power was equal to that of Death himself,
[proclaimed] his own lineage, strength, name, and deeds.
She spoke thus for the purpose of causing fear.
While Sītā was speaking in this way,
Rāvaṇa, provoked and knitting his brows upon his forehead, replied with harsh words.
"O lady of excellent complexion, I am the half-brother of Vaiśravaṇa;
my name is Rāvaṇa, may you be blessed, the ten-necked one of great prowess,
before whom the gods, along with the gandharvas, piśācas, birds, and serpents [bow]."

3.046.003c Like subjects ever fleeing from death, they run away in fear of him. 3.046.004a By him, his half-brother Vaiśravaṇa was encountered in a duel for a certain reason and, through his prowess in battle, was conquered out of anger.
Afflicted by fear of me, he has abandoned his own prosperous capital and now dwells on Kailāsa, the best of mountains; he whose auspicious aerial chariot named Puṣpaka travels at will.
"O blessed lady, it is by virtue of my prowess that I travel through the sky.
O Maithilī, at the mere sight of my face when I am provoked to anger,
the gods, led by Śakra, flee in utter terror."
Wherever I stand, the wind blows there with apprehension; out of fear, the sun becomes both scorching and cool. The leaves of the trees are motionless, and the rivers have still waters.
Wherever I stay and wherever I move, there they appear. Beyond the ocean lies my auspicious city named Laṅkā,
filled with terrible rākṣasas like Indra’s Amarāvatī.
Encircled by a pale white wall, it shone resplendent;
the lovely city had golden courtyards and gateways made of lapis lazuli. It was crowded with elephants, horses, and chariots, and resounded with the sound of musical instruments.
Adorned with groves crowded with trees that bear the fruit of every desire,
O Sītā, princess, you shall dwell there with me;
O high-minded lady, you will never grow weary among women such as these, who are not of human origin.
"O woman of excellent complexion, enjoying human and divine pleasures,
you will no longer remember Rāma, that mortal whose life has passed away—
he who, having been installed by King Daśaratha as his beloved son,"

"O large-eyed lady, what will you do with that Rama, the eldest son who has become weak in vigor, who has been sent away to the forest, whose kingdom has been lost, and whose mind is gone— a mere ascetic practicing austerities?"

"You ought not to reject him who has come here of his own accord out of love, the lord of all rākṣasas, for he is pierced by the arrows of the God of Love. For if you reject me, O timid one, you will surely fall into deep remorse."
As if striking Purūravas with her foot, Urvaśī spoke thus;
and Vaidehī, addressed in this way, became enraged with blood-red eyes and spoke harsh words to the lord of the Rākṣasas in that secluded place.
"How can you wish to commit such an evil deed by claiming Vaiśravaṇa as your brother— he who is the god honored by all beings? O Rāvaṇa, all the Rākṣasas will surely perish."
"For those for whom you are a harsh king— evil-minded and of unsubdued senses—
it might be possible to live after abducting Śacī, the wife of Indra;
but there is no life for me once I, the wife of Rāma, have been taken away."
May he live long after having violated Śacī, whose beauty is peerless, from the hand of the wielder of the thunderbolt— he who, by assailing a demoness such as I, has acted thus.
"Even for you, who have drunk the nectar of immortality, there is liberation [from death].
Hearing Sītā's words, the powerful ten-necked Rāvaṇa struck his hands together and assumed a truly massive form.
Then he spoke these words once more to Maithilī with great intensity:
"I believe that you, who are not mad, have not heard of my heroism and prowess;
for standing in the sky, I could lift up the earth with my two arms."
I could drink up the ocean and, standing in battle, slay Death himself;
I could obstruct the sun with my sharp arrows and cleave the very surface of the earth.
O madwoman, behold me, your husband, who can assume any form at will and grant all desires.
When Rāvaṇa had spoken thus,
his eyes, which were red with rage and bordered by tawny hair, became like the radiance of fire. Immediately abandoning his gentle mendicant form, that Rāvaṇa—
The younger brother of Vaiśravaṇa assumed his own form, which resembled the form of Time (Kāla).
With blood-red eyes, glorious, and wearing earrings of refined gold,
the ten-faced night-stalker became equipped with a bow and arrows.
Casting off that disguise of a wandering mendicant, the great-bodied Rāvaṇa, lord of the rākṣasas, resumed his own form;
with eyes bloodshot from rage, he possessed the splendor of a mass of dark clouds.

Clad in red garments, he stood gazing at Maithilī, that jewel among women. Rāvaṇa spoke to that Maithilī, who possessed dark-tipped hair like the radiance of the sun and was adorned with fine clothes and ornaments.

"If you desire a husband renowned throughout the three worlds, take refuge in me, O lady of beautiful hips; I am a husband worthy of you. Devote yourself to me for a long time; I shall be your praiseworthy beloved."
"O blessed lady, I shall never do anything that is displeasing to you anywhere.
Let this human sentiment be abandoned; let your heart be fixed upon me. [Do not grieve for] Rāma, who has been deprived of his kingdom, whose purpose is unfulfilled, and whose lifespan is limited."

"O foolish woman, you who consider yourself wise, with what virtues are you so enamored? That evil-minded man has abandoned his kingdom and his circle of friends at the word of a woman, and now dwells in this forest haunted by beasts of prey."
Having spoken these words to Sītā, who was worthy of kindness and spoke with such sweetness,
Rāvaṇa seized Sītā— just as Budha seizes Rohiṇī in the sky—
with his left hand grasping the hair of the lotus-eyed woman.
With his right hand, he grasped her by the thighs.
Seeing him— resembling a mountain peak, with sharp fangs and mighty arms,
and appearing like Death itself— the forest deities fled, afflicted by fear.
And that divine, great chariot of Rāvaṇa— illusory in nature, yoked with donkeys, possessing the braying sound of a donkey, and adorned with golden parts— appeared before him.
Then, with a loud voice, he threatened her with harsh words.
Then, taking Vaidehī onto his lap, he placed her upon the chariot. Seized by Rāvaṇa, the illustrious Sītā cried out in great distress, "O Rāma! calling to Rāma, who was far away in the forest.
Though she was unwilling, Rāvaṇa, afflicted by lust, seized her as she writhed like the wife of a lord of serpents and then flew up into the air.
Then, while being carried through the sky by the lord of the rākṣasas, she—
She cried out intensely like one intoxicated, her mind bewildered as if she were afflicted:
"Alas, Lakṣmaṇa, O mighty-armed one, you who gladden the hearts of your elders! You do not know that I am being carried away by a Rākṣasa who can assume any form at will."
"O Rāghava, you do not see me being carried away by unrighteousness, even though you are sacrificing your life, your happiness, and your wealth for the sake of dharma.
Are you not indeed the subduer of the unsubdued, O scorcher of foes?"
"Why indeed do you not punish Rāvaṇa for such a sin?
Surely the fruit of an undisciplined deed is seen immediately;
even time itself serves as a factor here, just as it does for the ripening of crops."
3.047.027a He has committed this deed with his consciousness impaired by fate;
3.047.027c suffer a terrible calamity at the hands of Rāma that shall bring an end to your life. 3.047.028a Alas! Now Kaikeyī, together with her kinsmen, has indeed attained her desire.
"I, the lawful wife of the illustrious Rāma who desires righteousness, am being carried away. I bid farewell to Janasthāna and the flowering Karṇikāra trees;
quickly report to Rāma that Rāvaṇa is carrying Sītā away."
I pay homage to Mount Mālyavat, the peaked mountain, and to Mount Prasravaṇa. Quickly announce to Rāma that Rāvaṇa is carrying away Sītā.
I pay homage to the river Godāvarī, resounding with the cries of swans and cranes.
"Quickly report to Rāma that Rāvaṇa is carrying away Sītā! The deities who dwell in this forest of various trees—unto them I bow; tell my husband that I have been abducted."
"Whatever beings dwell here,
even the multitudes of beasts and birds, I seek refuge in them all. [I seek refuge] in my husband’s beloved, who is dearer to him than his own life, as she is being carried away."
"Proclaim that Sītā has been carried off against her will by Rāvaṇa;
for once he knows my whereabouts, the mighty-armed and exceedingly powerful one will, through his prowess, bring her back even if she has been taken by Vaivasvata himself."
"O Jaṭāyu, you must relate to Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa exactly as it happened— the manner of my abduction— in its entirety and without omission. Then,
while he was fast asleep, Jaṭāyu heard that sound.
He quickly looked about for Rāvaṇa and beheld Vaidehī.
Then that best of birds, resembling a mountain peak with a sharp beak,
majestic and stationed upon a great tree, spoke these auspicious words.
Established in the dharma of the Purāṇas and taking refuge in truth,
I am the mighty king of vultures named Jaṭāyu;
I was once the sovereign of the entire world, equal to Mahendra and Varuṇa.
Rāma, the son of Daśaratha, is devoted to the welfare of the worlds;
this illustrious and noble-limbed woman named Sītā is his lawful wife, whom you desire to abduct from here.
How could a king established in dharma touch another man’s wife? O mighty one, the wives of kings must be protected with special care;
turn your base mind away from violating another’s wife.
3.048.007 A wise man should not practice that which another might censure him for;

as one's own wife is to be protected from suspicion, so too are the wives of others. 3.048.008 Whether it be wealth or pleasure, the learned do not pursue that which has not been prescribed in the scriptures.
O descendant of Purastya, people follow the king in determining what is dharma. The king is both dharma and desire, and he is the supreme treasury of all things;
whether it be auspicious or evil, dharma proceeds with the king as its root.
"O best of Rākṣasas, how have you— fickle and evil by nature—
attained such sovereignty, like a wrongdoer obtaining a celestial chariot? For one whose very nature is desire cannot be cleansed."

"O Noble One, for those of wicked soul do not dwell long in the abode, nor in the realm or the city, of one such as you. Since the righteous and mighty Rāma commits no offense against you, how is it that you commit an offense against him?"
3.048.013a If Khara, who had gone to Janasthāna for the sake of Śūrpaṇakhā,
was previously slain by Rāma of unwearied deeds because he transgressed [the bounds of propriety],
3.048.014a then tell me truly: what was Rāma’s transgression in this matter?
"Having abducted the wife of that Lord of the World,
you shall go [to your doom]. Release Vaidehī quickly, lest he consume you with his terrible eye, which is like fire, as Indra’s thunderbolt consumed Vṛtra."
3.048.016a Having tied a venomous serpent to the hem of your garment, you do not perceive it;
3.048.016c and you do not see the noose of Time fastened around your neck.
3.048.017a That burden, O gentle one, should be borne which does not cause a man to sink.
That food should be consumed which, when digested, causes no ailment.
What action would one perform that results neither in dharma, nor in fame, nor in glory on earth, but only in the exhaustion of the body? One should not do it.
"O Rāvaṇa, sixty thousand years have passed since my birth,
as I have duly governed the kingdom inherited from my father and grandfather.
I am old, while you are young, equipped with a bow, a chariot, armor, and arrows."
"Even so, you shall not depart safely after taking Vaidehī;
you are not capable of seizing Vaidehī by force while I look on,
just as one cannot subvert the eternal Vedic revelation through arguments joined with logic."
"Fight, if you are a hero; stay for a moment, Rāvaṇa!
You shall lie slain upon the ground, just as Khara did before. By him, the Daityas and Dānavas have been repeatedly struck down in battle."
"Before long, Rāma, clad in bark garments, shall slay you in battle.
Now that the two princes have gone far away, what can I possibly do?
You will soon perish, O base one, for you are afraid of them; of this there is no doubt."
"Indeed, as long as I am alive, you shall not carry away this auspicious Sītā, the lotus-petal-eyed beloved queen of Rāma;
for I must certainly do what is pleasing to that great-souled one."
"Even at the cost of my own life for the sake of Rāma and Daśaratha—stay, stay, O ten-necked one! Wait but a moment, O Rāvaṇa;
O night-stalker, I shall offer you the hospitality of battle to the best of my strength."
"I shall strike you down from this best of chariots like a fruit from its stalk"—
when Jaṭāyu spoke these words to Rāvaṇa according to the rules,
all twenty of the enraged demon's eyes blazed like fire.
With eyes bloodshot from rage and wearing earrings of molten gold,
the intolerant lord of the Rākṣasas rushed toward the lord of birds. A tumultuous battle then broke out between the two of them in that great forest.
That battle between the vulture and the rākṣasa was then as wondrous as that between two clouds tossed by the wind in the sky,
like two great winged mountains adorned with garlands.
Then the mighty one showered the king of vultures with *nālīka* and *nārāca* arrows, sharp-pointed *vikarṇi* shafts, and other most terrible weapons.
But that vulture, the lord of winged creatures, [received] those masses of arrows.
In that battle, Jaṭāyu withstood the weapons of Rāvaṇa;
then, with his two feet equipped with sharp claws,
that mighty and best of birds inflicted many wounds upon Rāvaṇa’s body.

Then, out of anger and desiring to crush his enemy, the Ten-necked one took up ten terrible arrows that resembled the staff of Death. With those straight-flying shafts released from a full draw, he of great prowess—
He pierced the vulture with sharp, fierce, and whetted stone-tipped arrows.
Seeing Jānakī with tearful eyes upon the Rākṣasa’s chariot,
he disregarded those shafts and rushed toward the Rākṣasa.
Then the Lord of Birds, possessed of great splendor, crushed with his two feet Rāvaṇa’s bow, which was adorned with pearls and gems and still held an arrow.
And he [crushed] that flaming quiver of Rāvaṇa, which resembled fire.
And with his two wings, the lord of birds, possessed of great splendor, shook the divine,
golden-backed donkeys with their jackal-like faces;
and the powerful one slew them in battle, for they were endowed with great speed.
He shattered that great chariot, which was equipped with three bamboo poles, moved at will, blazed like the flames of fire, and had its body adorned with jewels and gold;
he also broke the parasol, which resembled the full moon, along with the fans.
With his bow broken, deprived of his chariot, his horses slain, and his charioteer killed,
Rāvaṇa fell to the earth, carrying Vaidehī on his lap.
Seeing Rāvaṇa fallen upon the ground, his vehicle destroyed, [the monkeys were filled with joy].
"Excellent! Excellent! the beings cried, honoring the king of vultures.
But seeing that leader of the bird-flocks exhausted by old age, Rāvaṇa, seizing Maithilī, sprang up again with joy.
As he was walking along with the daughter of Janaka, holding her joyfully upon his lap,
Jaṭāyu, the king of vultures, flew up and said this to Rāvaṇa:
"O Rāvaṇa, you are carrying the wife of Rāma, whose arrows have the touch of a thunderbolt!"
O one of little intelligence, you are surely leading her to her destruction for the sake of the Rākṣasas;
together with your friends, kinsmen, ministers, army, and retinue,
you are drinking this poison like a thirsty man drinking water.
Those who lack discernment and do not understand the consequences of their actions perish swiftly, just as you shall perish. Bound by the noose of Time, where can you go to be released from it?
Like a water-dwelling creature that seizes a baited hook for its own destruction,
O Rāvaṇa, you have acted thus; for the two descendants of Kakutstha, the Raghavas, are never to be overcome, and they will not forgive this assault upon their hermitage.
"Since you have performed this deed, censured by the world, out of cowardice—this is the path practiced by thieves, not one frequented by heroes.
Fight, if you are a hero; stay for a moment, O Rāvaṇa!"

"You shall lie slain upon the ground just as your brother Khara did. Whatever action a man undertakes at the time of his departure [from this world], you have undertaken that unrighteous act for your own destruction."

"Indeed, what man— be he a lord of the world or even the self-existent Lord himself— would perform an action that results in such evil consequences? Having spoken these auspicious words to that Rākṣasa, Jaṭāyu—
The valiant one fell heavily upon the back of the ten-necked Rāvaṇa;
seizing him with his sharp claws, he tore at him on all sides,
just as a rider mounted upon a rogue elephant might do.
3.049.030a Piercing his back, he tore at his beak with his claws;
3.049.030c and he whose weapons were his claws, wings, and beak plucked out his feathers.
3.049.031a Thus being tormented again and again by the king of vultures, he—
With his lips quivering in indignation, that Rākṣasa trembled;
embracing Vaidehī with his left arm, Rāvaṇa,
distressed and frantic with rage, struck Jaṭāyu with his palm.
3.049.033 Having bypassed him, Jaṭāyu, the lord of vultures and subduer of enemies, then tore away his ten left arms with his beak.
3.049.034 Thereupon, the powerful ten-necked Rāvaṇa, becoming enraged, released Sītā.
With his two fists and his two feet, he struck down the king of the vultures.
Then, for a moment, a battle took place between those two of incomparable prowess—
the chief of the *rākṣasas* and the foremost of birds.
Then, as he was struggling for the sake of Rāma, Rāvaṇa raised his sword and cut off his wings, feet, and flanks. With his wings severed by that Rākṣasa of fierce deeds, he suddenly—
Slain and with little life remaining, the vulture fell to the earth.
Seeing Jaṭāyu fallen on the ground, drenched in blood,
Vaidehī ran toward him in her grief as if toward her own kinsman.
The lord of Laṅkā beheld him upon the earth, resembling a dark blue cloud, with a brilliantly white chest and noble prowess.
Then Jaṭāyus, crushed by Rāvaṇa’s force, lay fallen upon the earth like a forest fire extinguished.
Again embracing him, Sītā, the daughter of Janaka, whose face has the radiance of the moon, wept then.
The lord of the Rākṣasas [beheld] him, whose life was short, quivering upon the ground.
She saw a vulture fallen near the hermitage of Rāghava. Having beheld that king of vultures slain by Rāvaṇa, she whose face was like the lord of stars (the moon) lamented, deeply distressed.
3.050.003a Omens, the knowledge of bodily marks, and the observation of the cries of birds—
3.050.003c these are inevitably seen by men amidst joys and sorrows.
3.050.004a Surely you do not realize, O Rāma, that your son is in great distress.
"O Kākutstha, surely the beasts and birds are now running for my sake!
Save me today, O Kākutstha, save me, Lakṣmaṇa!"— thus did that beautiful woman,
utterly terrified, cry out as if she were in the presence of those who could hear her.
Rāvaṇa, the lord of the Rākṣasas, rushed toward Vaidehī as she lamented like one who is helpless, her garlands and ornaments soiled;
she was clinging to the great trees as if they were creepers.

Crying out "Release me! Release me! many times, the lord of the rākṣasas—resembling Death himself—seized by the hair Sītā, who was crying "Rāma! Rāma! in the forest, now separated from Rāma, in order to end her life.
When Vaidehī was violated,
the entire world, including all things mobile and immobile, became lawless and enveloped in blinding darkness.
Having seen Sītā seized and distressed with his divine eye, [he perceived this].
"The task is accomplished," the illustrious Grandfather declared. Seeing Sītā seized, all those great ṛṣis dwelling in the Daṇḍaka forest were both overjoyed and distressed.

But Rāvaṇa, the lord of the rākṣasas, taking her as she cried out "Rāma! Rāma! and "Lakṣmaṇa!", departed into the sky—she whose every limb was adorned with ornaments of refined gold and who was clothed in yellow silk.
The princess shone like a flash of lightning from the clouds; and with her yellow garment fluttering upward, Rāvaṇa blazed forth even more intensely,
like a mountain illuminated by fire.
3.050.015 Her lotus petals— most auspicious, copper-hued, and fragrant— were scattered over Rāvaṇa by Vaidehī.
3.050.016 Her silken garment, shining with the luster of gold, fluttered in the air.
She shone like a copper-colored cloud in the sunlight due to the glow of the sun;
yet that stainless face of hers, resting in Rāvaṇa’s lap in the sky,
did not shine without Rāma, like a lotus without its stalk.
He appeared like the moon risen after piercing through a dark blue cloud;

his forehead was beautiful, the hair at his temples well-arranged, and his face, free from blemish, shone with the luster of the interior of a lotus. It was adorned with white, perfectly pure, and radiant teeth.
Wiping away her tears and her weapon, her face— beautiful to behold like the moon,
with its fine nose and lovely copper-hued lips, shining like gold in the sky—
spoke these auspicious words, which were shaken by the lord of the Rākṣasas.
She did not shine without Rāma, like the moon risen during the day.
That golden-complexioned Maithilī shone against the dark-limbed lord of the rākṣasas,
like a golden girdle set upon a blue gem.
3.050.022a That daughter of Janaka, fair as a lotus and radiant as gold, adorned with glowing ornaments, shone as she entered Rāvaṇa like lightning entering a cloud.
3.050.023a By the tinkling sound of Vaidehī’s ornaments, the lord of the Rākṣasas—
It became pure blue and resonant like a rain-cloud. As Sītā was being carried away, a shower of flowers fell from her head in every direction, dropping onto the surface of the earth.
But that shower of flowers, though shaken on all sides by the force of Rāvaṇa,
returned once more toward the Ten-necked one;
it fell back upon the younger brother of Vaiśravaṇa as a torrent of blossoms.
Like the stainless garland of stars upon Mount Meru, the best of mountains,
the anklet adorned with jewels that had fallen from Vaidehī’s foot—
resembling a circle of lightning and emitting a sweet sound— fell down.

Red as the young shoots of a tree, Vaidehī graced the dark-limbed lord of the Rākṣasas, like a golden girth upon an elephant. Blazing with her own splendor like a great meteor in the sky, she shone forth.
Entering the sky, the younger brother of Vaiśravaṇa carried away Sītā.
Her ornaments, glowing like fire, fell upon the earth with a great clamor, like stars falling from the heavens when their merit is exhausted.
3.050.031a The necklace, possessing the luster of the moon, slipped from the space between her breasts;
3.050.031c falling from Vaidehī, it shone like the Gaṅgā descending from the sky.
3.050.032a Struck by the winds of portents, it was filled with various flocks of birds.
"Have no fear!"— thus the trees seemed to speak with their trembling tops;
the lotus ponds, their blossoms crushed and their fish and water-dwellers terrified, appeared as if grieving for Maithilī, who was now devoid of hope, like a friend in distress.
3.050.034a Having rushed together from all sides, lions, tigers, deer, and birds then pursued [him] in their rage, following the shadow of Sītā.
3.050.035a With waterfalls for their blood-stained mouths, they raised their horns like uplifted arms.
As Sītā was being carried away, the mountains seemed to cry out in lamentation.
Seeing Vaidehī being abducted, the glorious sun became dejected;
its splendor vanished, it appeared as a pale orb.
"Where Rāvaṇa carries off Vaidehī, the wife of Rāma, there is no righteousness; how can there be truth, nor uprightness, nor compassion?"—
thus all beings lamented in groups.
Terrified and with dejected faces, the young fawns wailed;
repeatedly gazing upward with eyes clouded by falling tears,
the forest deities stood with their limbs trembling violently.

Seeing Sītā crying out piteously, fallen into such a state of suffering, and looking again and again toward the surface of the earth as she called out "Lakṣmaṇa! Rāma! in a sweet voice, [Rāvaṇa spoke].

3.050.041c He, the ten-necked one, carried away that high-minded woman— her hair disheveled and her forehead-mark rubbed away— for his own destruction. 3.050.042a Then she, with beautiful teeth and a pure smile;
Separated from her kinsmen, Maithilī,
unable to see either Rāghava or Lakṣmaṇa, her face pale and oppressed by a weight of fear, [wandered].
Seeing him springing up into the sky, Maithilī, the daughter of Janaka,
became sorrowful and extremely agitated, dwelling in great fear;
with eyes copper-red from anger and weeping, she [beheld] the lord of the Rākṣasas, who possessed terrifying eyes.

3.051.002c As Sītā was being carried away, she wept piteously and spoke these words: 3.051.003a "O base Rāvaṇa, you feel no shame for this deed! Having known me to be separated from my husband, you steal me away and flee."
"O evil-souled one, surely it was by you, a coward desiring to abduct me,
that my husband was lured away by means of a deceptive deer-form;
for even he who rose up to protect me has now been struck down."

"O lowest of Rākṣasas, your supreme valor is indeed seen; yet, having merely proclaimed your name, you have not actually conquered anyone in battle. Having committed such a contemptible deed, how is it that you do not feel shame?"

In the worlds, men will speak of this contemptible deed— this most cruel and unrighteous act of yours, O you who pride yourself on your heroism: the abduction of another’s wife in secret and in solitude.
"Fie on your heroism and your strength, since you spoke those words at that time! Fie on such conduct of yours, which brings reproach upon your lineage in the world!
For what indeed could be done, even by one who runs with such speed?"

Stay even for a moment; you shall not return alive. For once you have come within the range of vision of those two sons of kings, you will not be able to survive for even a moment, even with your army.

3.051.011a You are not able to endure the touch of their arrows in any way whatsoever, 3.051.011c just as a bird cannot endure the touch of a fire blazing in the forest. 3.051.012a Having done what is beneficial for yourself, do well to release me, Rāvaṇa.
"For my husband, enraged by this assault upon me, will surely bring about your destruction along with his brother if you do not release me—
by whatever resolve you seek to carry me off by force."
"O base one, that resolve of yours will prove to be fruitless;
for, not seeing my husband who is like a god, I,
fallen under the power of the enemy, cannot endure to maintain my life for long."
Surely you do not perceive what is for your own welfare or what is beneficial,
just as a mortal at the time of death indulges in things that are contrary [to his health]. For indeed, among all those about to die, that which is wholesome is not pleasing to them.
For I seem to see you, O Ten-necked One, with the noose of Time already cast around your neck; yet that you do not fear in this place of terror is evident,
for you perceive these trees as being made of gold.
"O Rāvaṇa, you behold the terrible river Vaitaraṇī, which carries a torrent of blood, and the fearsome forest of sword-leaves;
as well as [the trees] with flowers of molten gold and leaves of the finest vaidūrya gem."
"You shall see a sharp *śālmalī* tree covered with iron thorns;
for having committed such an offense against that high-souled one, O pitiless man, you will not be able to endure it for long, just as one who has drunk poison."
"O Rāvaṇa, you are bound by the irresistible noose of Time;
where can you go to find peace from my high-souled husband? In the mere twinkling of an eye, you shall be deprived of your brother in battle."
By whom fourteen thousand *rākṣasas* were slain—
how could that heroic Rāghava, powerful and skilled in all weapons,
not slay you with his sharp arrows for abducting his beloved wife?
3.051.024a And this and other harsh words, Vaidehī, held in Rāvaṇa’s embrace,
3.051.024c overwhelmed by fear and grief, lamented piteously.
3.051.025a Thus she, being deeply afflicted and speaking at great length;
The wicked one first wailed piteously to the beautiful woman, and then carried off the young princess as she writhed,
her limbs trembling with fear.
But Vaidehī, being carried away and seeing no protector whatsoever,
beheld five bull-like monkeys situated upon a mountain peak. In their midst, the large-eyed lady [saw] a silken garment with the luster of gold.
The Maithilī lady,
fearing that they might reveal her identity to Rāma,
cast off her upper garment and her beautiful ornaments, throwing them along with the clothing into the midst of that [fire].
But out of confusion, the ten-necked Rāvaṇa did not perceive that deed, for he lacked wisdom.
Then those bulls among monkeys saw Sītā crying out, her large eyes wide like those of one who does not blink, as she was being gazed upon by those tawny-eyed ones with unblinking stares.
3.052.005a And having passed beyond Pampā, the lord of the Rākṣasas, holding the weeping Maithilī, went toward the city of Laṅkā.
3.052.006a Exceedingly delighted, Rāvaṇa carried her away— his own death.
Like a female serpent with sharp fangs and potent venom cradled in one's lap, he swiftly traversed through forests,
rivers, mountains, and lakes by way of the sky,
like an arrow released from a bow.
Having reached the inexhaustible abode of Varuṇa, the refuge of rivers, which is the dwelling place of whales and crocodiles, he crossed over the ocean; there,
the waves were tossed in agitation, and the fish and great serpents were obstructed.
While Vaidehī was being carried away, the ocean, the abode of Varuṇa, [recoiled],
and then the Cāraṇas dwelling in the sky uttered these words:
"The Ten-necked one is finished!"— thus the Siddhas spoke at that time.

Taking Sītā, who was writhing in his arms, Rāvaṇa entered the city of Laṅkā, which was like death personified for himself. Having reached the city of Laṅkā, with its well-laid-out great highways, he entered.
3.052.012c He entered his own inner apartments, which were filled with well-trained mares.
3.052.013a There Rāvaṇa placed Sītā— her dark-cornered eyes cast down, devoted to grief and delusion— just as Maya placed the Asura illusion.
And the ten-necked one spoke to the Piśācīs of terrible appearance:
"So that no man or woman may see this Sītā without permission,
[provide] pearls, gems, gold, garments, and ornaments."
Whatever she may desire, that very thing should be given to her according to my will.
And as for whoever shall speak any unpleasant word to Vaidehī,
whether out of ignorance or knowledge, life shall not be dear to them.
Having spoken thus to those rākṣasīs, the powerful lord of the rākṣasas emerged from that inner apartment and, reflecting on what ought to be done,
beheld eight exceedingly valiant flesh-eating rākṣasas.
Seeing them, that one of great prowess, deluded by the granting of the boon,
praised them for their strength and heroism and spoke these words:
"Armed with various weapons, go quickly from here with all haste."
Janasthāna, formerly the abode of Khara, has now become a place of slaughter.
Dwell there in Janasthāna, which is now empty and its rākṣasas slain,
relying on your manly strength and casting fear far away.
Indeed, that very great force which I had stationed in Janasthāna has been slain in battle along with Dūṣaṇa and Khara by Rāma’s arrows;
therefore, an unprecedented rage rises within me, surmounting my fortitude.
A very great and most dreadful enmity has arisen toward Rāma;
I wish to exact that vengeance from my enemy,
for I shall not obtain sleep without slaying the foe in battle.
But now, having slain that Rāma who has killed Khara and Dūṣaṇa, I shall obtain peace, just as a pauper obtains wealth. For while you were dwelling in Janasthāna, you took refuge with Rāma.
One must ascertain the truth regarding his movements and what he is doing;
all the night-stalkers must proceed with vigilance and always exert effort toward the slaying of Rāghava.
"For I have known your strength many times on the front lines of battle;
therefore, you have been appointed by me to this Janasthāna. Then the Rākṣasas, having received these pleasing words, [departed].
Having paid homage to the highly significant Rāvaṇa,
they abandoned Laṅkā and set out together toward Janasthāna, remaining invisible to sight.
Then, having found Sītā and seized Maithilī, Rāvaṇa was exceedingly delighted,
having established a supreme enmity with Rāma.
Out of delusion, that Rākṣasa was filled with joy;
having dispatched eight formidable and mighty Rākṣasas, Rāvaṇa,
due to the impairment of his intellect, considered himself to have accomplished his purpose.
3.053.002a Thinking of Vaidehī, pierced by the arrows of desire,
he entered his beautiful palace, hastening to see Sītā. 3.053.003a Having entered that residence, Rāvaṇa, the lord of the rākṣasas—
3.053.003c He saw Sītā in the midst of the rākṣasīs, wholly devoted to her grief; 3.053.004a her face filled with tears, miserable, and oppressed by the weight of sorrow—
3.053.004c like a ship being overwhelmed by the force of the winds and sinking in the ocean.
Like a doe strayed from the herd and surrounded by dogs, with her face cast down in misery, the night-stalker approached her;
and the lord of the rākṣasas beheld her, wretched and helpless, overcome by grief.
By force, he showed him a house resembling a celestial abode,
filled with mansions and palaces, frequented by thousands of women,
graced by flocks of various birds, and endowed with diverse jewels.
With pillars made of gold, refined gold, crystal, and silver, as well as those variegated with diamonds and lapis lazuli— pillars that were enchanting to the sight—
and with archways of molten gold resounding with the sound of divine drums.
He ascended that variegated golden staircase together with her. There, the rows of palaces were beautiful to behold, featuring windows made of ivory and silver, and covered with lattices of gold.
In his own palace, Daśagrīva showed Maithilī all the various grounds adorned everywhere with jewels of refined gold;
he also showed her oblong ponds and lotus pools covered with various kinds of flowers.
3.053.012 Rāvaṇa showed Sītā, who was utterly devoted to her grief.
3.053.013 Having shown Vaidehī that entire, most excellent palace,
the evil-minded Rāvaṇa spoke these words to the daughter of Janaka.
"Furthermore, there are one hundred and twenty-two crores of Rākṣasas,
excluding the aged and the young night-stalkers,
O Sītā; I am the lord of all those who perform terrible deeds."
"One thousand [servants] attend to my every need;
yet this entire administration of my kingdom, O large-eyed one, is established entirely upon you. My very life, O lady of wide eyes, is dearer to me than my own breath."
"Of the many thousands of women who are my dependents, you, Sītā, shall be their sovereign; O beloved, become my wife. Enough! Why do you entertain such other thoughts? Accept my words."
"Be devoted to me, for I am tormented by love; you ought to show me your favor.
This Laṅkā, extending for a hundred yojanas and surrounded by the ocean, cannot be assailed even by the gods and asuras led by Indra."
"Neither among the gods, nor the yakṣas, nor the gandharvas, nor the ṛṣis— indeed,
among all the worlds— I see anyone who could be equal to me in prowess. [Yet here I am], fallen from my kingdom, wretched, a wandering ascetic with my life’s purpose exhausted."
"What will you do with Rāma, a mere human of little splendor?
O Sītā, devote yourself to me alone; I am a husband worthy of you. For youth is transient, O timid one; take your pleasure here with me."
"Do not set your mind on seeing Rāghava, O lovely-faced one. What power does he have to come here, Sītā, even by means of his desires?
The wind of great speed cannot be bound with ropes in the sky."
"O beautiful one, even if one were to attempt to seize the pure flame of a blazing fire,
I do not see anyone in all the three worlds who could carry you away by force while you are protected by my arms."
"Protect this very great kingdom of Laṅkā;
drenched by the waters of consecration and satisfied, take delight with me. Whatever evil deed was committed previously has been expiated by your dwelling in the forest."
"May you now obtain here the fruit of whatever righteous deeds you have performed.
O Maithilī, enjoy here with me all these celestial garlands of divine fragrance and these most excellent ornaments."

"O lady of beautiful hips, there is a delightful celestial chariot named Puṣpaka belonging to my brother Vaiśravaṇa; that chariot moves at the speed of thought. There, O Sītā, sport with me as you please."
Her face, resembling a lotus, was stainless and beautiful to behold;
yet, O lady of noble hips, it did not shine, O fair-faced one, as it was afflicted by grief.
"Enough of this shame, Vaidehī, caused by your violation of dharma."
"This is a divine flow from the Ṛṣis that shall come to you. I have pressed these two feet of yours with my heads;
grant me your favor quickly, for I am your submissive servant."
"3.053.033c These words have not been spoken by me in vain while my throat was parching.
3.053.034a Nor indeed would Rāvaṇa ever bow his head before any woman.
Having spoken thus to Maithilī, the daughter of Janaka, the ten-necked one—
"Having fallen under the power of destiny, he thinks, 'She is mine.
Thus addressed, Vaidehī, though emaciated by grief, remained fearless;
placing a blade of grass between them, she replied to Rāvaṇa.

There was a king named Daśaratha, as immovable as a bridge of dharma; he was known for his truthfulness to his word, and his son is that Rāghava. That righteous-souled one named Rāma is renowned throughout the three worlds.
Long-armed and large-eyed, he is my divine husband; born in the lineage of the Ikṣvākus, with shoulders like a lion and great splendor, he,
together with his brother Lakṣmaṇa, shall take away your life.
"If I had been forcibly violated by you in his very presence,
you would have been slain in battle and lie there like Khara in Janasthāna.
As for these Rākṣasas who have been described— of terrible form and great strength— "
3.054.006c All [the arrows] will become harmless before Rāghava, just as serpents are rendered powerless by Suparṇa.
3.054.007a Released from his bowstring, those arrows adorned with gold 3.054.007c will shatter his body, like waves against the bank of the Gaṅgā.
O Rāvaṇa, even if you are unslayable by either Asuras or Suras,
having provoked such great enmity, you shall not escape him while you still live. That mighty Rāghava will bring an end to your remaining life.
Your life is as difficult to preserve as that of an animal bound to a sacrificial post.
O Rākṣasa, if that Rāma were to behold you with eyes blazing with wrath,
you would be consumed this very day and meet your immediate destruction.
He who could cause the moon to fall from the sky to the earth, or destroy it,
or even dry up the ocean— he alone might release Sītā here.
You, however, have lost your life-span, lost your fortune, lost your vitality, and lost your senses.

"3.054.012c Because of your deed, Laṅkā shall be joined with widowhood. 3.054.013a This sinful act of yours will not result in happiness, 3.054.013c since I was led away by you from the forest, from my husband's side, without his consent."
"For that husband of mine, endowed with divine power and great luster,
dwells fearlessly in the empty Daṇḍaka forest, relying upon his heroism. He shall [destroy] your pride, strength, valor, and such arrogance."
3.054.015c He will take [his life] from his own limbs with a shower of arrows in battle.
3.054.016a When the destruction of beings is seen to be impelled by Time, 3.054.016c then men, having fallen under the sway of Time, become negligent in their duties.
"O lowest of Rākṣasas, this moment has arrived for you to attack me,
leading to the destruction of yourself, your fellow Rākṣasas, and the inner apartments.
It is not possible [to harm] the sacrificial altar situated in the midst of the sacrifice, adorned with ladles and vessels."
"This body, purified by the mantras of the twice-born, must not be defiled by a Caṇḍāla. Bind it or kill it;
O Rākṣasa, neither this body nor my life is to be protected by me."
"For I shall not allow myself to bring reproach upon the earth.
Having spoken these very harsh words out of anger to Rāvaṇa, Vaidehī,
the princess of Mithilā, said nothing more there.
Having heard Sītā’s harsh and hair-raising words, he then replied to her with speech intended to inspire fear:
"Listen to my words, O Maithilī, O beautiful lady; for twelve months," he said.
"If you do not come to me within this time, O lady of lovely smiles,
then the cooks shall cut you into pieces for their morning meal.
Having spoken these harsh words, Rāvaṇa, the one who makes his enemies cry out, [remained there].
Then, filled with rage, he spoke these words to the rākṣasīs:
"O rākṣasīs, deformed and terrible to behold, who feed upon flesh and blood, quickly humble her pride!"
At his mere word, those women of hideous and terrible appearance formed themselves into a circle around the princess of Mithilā with their hands joined in reverence.
Then King Rāvaṇa, of fearsome aspect, spoke to them.
"Stirring up the earth as if tearing it apart with the forceful strides of his feet, he said:
'Let Maithilī be led into the midst of the Aśoka grove;
there she must be guarded by you all, hidden and surrounded.'"
"Therefore, all of you, bring this Maithilī under your control by means of both terrible threats and soothing conciliations, like a wild female elephant. Thus were those Rākṣasīs commanded by Rāvaṇa.
Taking Maithilī with them, they went to the Aśoka grove,
which was filled with trees bearing all kinds of desirable fruits and various flowers and fruits,
and was frequented by birds that were intoxicated at all times.
But Maithilī, the daughter of Janaka, her limbs overwhelmed by grief and fallen under the power of the rākṣasīs like a doe among tigresses,
found no peace there.
Threatened excessively by the Virūpanetrās,
she remembered her husband and her beloved brother-in-law;
afflicted by fear and grief, she lost consciousness.

Having slain the Rākṣasa Mārīca, who was wandering in the form of a deer and could assume any shape at will, Rāma quickly turned back on his path. As he hastened along, eager to see the daughter of Mithilā, he proceeded.
Then a jackal, emitting a cruel sound, howled behind him. Recognizing that harsh and hair-raising cry of the jackal, he became apprehensive and reflected upon it.

"Alas, I consider this inauspicious, for the jackal howls as it does. May it be well with Vaidehī, provided she has not been devoured by the rākṣasas. But Mārīca, having recognized and perceived my voice, [spoke].
If Lakṣmaṇa should hear that cry uttered by the one in the form of a deer,
that son of Sumitrā, having heard the voice and left Maithilī there,
will quickly come here to me, dispatched by her.
Surely the destruction of Sītā was desired by the Rākṣasas acting together; for Mārīca, having become a golden deer, drew me away from the hermitage,
and having led me far off, that Rākṣasa was struck down by my arrow.

"Alas Lakṣmaṇa! I am undone!"—these were the words he uttered. Even if all be well with those two while I am separated from them in the forest, I have indeed incurred the enmity of the Rākṣasas on account of Janasthāna.
"Many terrible omens are seen today," Rāma thought thus as he heard the cry of the jackal and reflected upon his own abduction by the *rākṣasa* in the form of a deer.

3.055.010e Rāghava, filled with apprehension, arrived at Janasthāna. 3.055.011a As he was dejected in mind and distressed, the beasts and birds approached him; keeping the high-souled one to their left, they uttered terrible cries.
Having seen those most terrible omens, Rāghava then beheld Lakṣmaṇa approaching, his radiance departed. Then,
not far away, that Lakṣmaṇa met with Rāma.
Dejected, he who was himself a partaker of sorrow reproached his dejected elder brother, Lakṣmaṇa,
who had returned after abandoning Sītā in the lonely forest frequented by Rākṣasas.
Taking Lakṣmaṇa by his left hand, the joy of the Raghus spoke these harsh words, which were yet sweet in their ultimate effect, like one who is afflicted:
"Alas, Lakṣmaṇa! You have done a despicable thing, in that you have abandoned her."

"O gentle one, having come here for Sītā's sake, I hope that all is well with her. O hero, I have no doubt at all: the daughter of Janaka must have perished or been devoured by the forest-dwelling rākṣasas."
"O Lakṣmaṇa, though these inauspicious omens appear most frequently before me, may we yet attain the reunion with Sītā. For this creature resembles a demon-deer;"
Having enticed me and followed me a great distance,
that Rākṣasa, though slain with immense effort, remained as if dying even as he perished.
"My mind is dejected and lacks joy here, and my left eye throbs;
without a doubt, Lakṣmaṇa, Sītā is no longer alive."

"Has she been carried off, or is she dead, or is she still on the road? Seeing the dejected Lakṣmaṇa in that desolate place, the righteous son of Daśaratha questioned him regarding Vaidehī, who had arrived without her.
"O Lakṣmaṇa, where is that Vaidehī who followed me when I set out for the Daṇḍaka forest? Where is she whom you have left behind to come here?
For one fallen from his kingdom, miserable, and wandering through the Daṇḍakas?"
"Where is that Vaidehī of slender waist, my companion in suffering?
