Without her, O hero, I cannot bear to live even for a moment.
Where is that Sītā, my companion in life, who resembles the daughter of a god?"
O Lakṣmaṇa, neither lordship over the immortals nor even sovereignty over the earth would I desire without that daughter of Janaka, who possesses the luster of refined gold;
does Vaidehī, who is dearer to me than my own life, still live?
"O gentle Saumitri, I hope that my exile will not have been in vain;
for when I am dead and you have departed on account of Sītā,
I hope that Kaikeyī will finally have her desire fulfilled and be happy."

"O gentle one, will Kausalyā— whose purpose was fulfilled by having a kingdom with her son, yet now distressed by her son's death— not wait upon Kaikeyī? If Vaidehī still lives, I shall return again to the hermitage."
"O Lakṣmaṇa, if she of virtuous conduct has been violated, I shall give up my life. O Lakṣmaṇa, if Vaidehī does not speak to me when I have reached the hermitage,
or if Sītā does not smile at me again, I shall perish."
"Tell me, Lakṣmaṇa, whether Vaidehī lives or not; while you were negligent, has that poor woman been devoured by the rākṣasas? She is so delicate, young, and has never before known suffering."
"Separated from me, Vaidehī is clearly grieving, distressed in mind.
In every way, by that crooked and evil-minded Rākṣasa,
even you have been struck with fear as he cried out loudly, 'Lakṣmaṇa!'"
"I suspect that sound was heard by Vaidehī as being similar to my own;
terrified, she sent you, and you have come quickly to see me.
In every respect, a grievous wrong has been committed by abandoning Sītā in the forest."

An opportunity has been given for those cruel Rākṣasas to take revenge. Afflicted by the killing of Khara, those flesh-eating Rākṣasas will undoubtedly have Sītā slain by them— of this there is no doubt.
"Alas! I am utterly submerged in calamity, O destroyer of enemies;
yet what shall I do now? I fear such a fate was destined to befall me.
Thus did Rāghava reflect while gazing upon Sītā of the noble form.
Accompanied by Lakṣmaṇa, he returned to Janasthāna in haste,
reproaching his younger brother who appeared distressed by hunger,
fatigue, and thirst.
Sighing deeply, his mouth parched and despondent, the hero reached his dwelling and, finding it empty,
entered his own hermitage.
Following certain dwelling places,
thinking "this is that very spot" in his place of residence,
he stood with his hair bristling with joy, yet filled with agitation.

Then, as he was returning from the hermitage, Rāma, the joy of the Raghus, afflicted by grief, questioned the son of Sumitrā once more: "Why have you come back, leaving the daughter of Mithilā behind? He said to him: [why have you come, having abandoned Maithilī?]
When she was wandering in the forest with me through her trust in you,
O Lakṣmaṇa, as soon as she saw you approaching and left Maithilī behind,
my mind was truly distressed by the suspicion of some great evil.
"My left eye throbs, as do my arm and my heart,
O Lakṣmaṇa, having seen you from afar on the path, separated from Sītā.
Thus addressed, Lakṣmaṇa, the son of Sumitrā, who possesses auspicious marks, [replied].
Overwhelmed by even greater sorrow, he spoke to the grieving Rāma:
"I did not come here of my own free will, having abandoned her;
urged on by her with harsh words, I have come here into your presence."
The cry of Maithilī, "O noble one! Alas, Sītā! Lakṣmaṇa! Save me!"—that very speech reached his ears. Hearing that piteous sound, Maithilī, out of affection for you, [was overcome].
"Go! Go! she said to me, weeping and overwhelmed by fear.
Though I urged her repeatedly with the words "Go," Maithilī replied with these words, which were full of confidence in you:
"I do not see any such demon who could bring him fear.
Be at ease; this does not exist. How could a noble man speak such a thing, which is both contemptible and base?"
"O Sītā, that cry of 'Save me!'— which could save even the thirty gods—
why has it been uttered by someone else, seizing my brother's voice and making it discordant, saying, 'Lakṣmaṇa, save me'?"

3.057.012e You should not feel distress, which is practiced by base women. 3.057.013a Enough of resorting to despondency; be composed and free from anxiety. 3.057.013c There is no man in the three worlds who can withstand Rāghava in battle.
"Whether already born or yet to be born, he who might defeat me in combat.
Having been addressed thus, Vaidehī, her mind utterly bewildered,
shedding tears, spoke these harsh words to me.
"An exceedingly wicked disposition has been placed by you within me;
even when your brother is destroyed and [Rāma] arrives, you shall not obtain me.
You are following Rāma because of an appointment with Bharata."
For although he is crying out excessively, you do not come to his aid; though you follow me for my sake, you act like a hidden enemy,
seeking a weakness in Rāghava, and thus you do not approach him.
Thus addressed by Vaidehī, his eyes bloodshot with agitation,
he departed from the hermitage with his lips quivering in rage.
To the son of Sumitrā who was speaking thus, Rāma, bewildered by his own anguish, replied:
"O gentle one, you have committed a misdeed in that you have come here without her," he said.
"Even though you know me to be capable of warding off the rākṣasas,
you have departed from Maithilī with these words of anger."
Indeed, I am not at all pleased that you have departed, abandoning Maithilī,
having come here after hearing harsh words from an angry woman;
for in every way, you have acted unworthily by being incited by Sītā.
"Having fallen under the sway of anger, you did not follow my command.
Indeed, that Rākṣasa lies there struck by my arrow—
he who lured me away from the hermitage in the form of a deer."
Having drawn his bow and fixed an arrow, he was struck playfully by me with that shaft; then,
casting off his deer-form, he uttered a piteous cry.
That Rākṣasa, wearing his armlet,
remained there with his voice struck by arrows, yet raising his voice to a pitch that could be heard from afar, he spoke in a pained tone.
Those extremely harsh words were uttered by which you departed, leaving Maithilī behind;
as he was returning in great distress, his downward-looking eyes were filled with tears.
Rāma trembled, faltered, and a shudder arose within him;
repeatedly observing these inauspicious omens,
he indeed exclaimed, "Is Sītā well?"
Then, longing for the sight of Sītā, he went on in haste;
seeing the dwelling empty, his mind became distressed. The joy of the Raghus wandered about as if with great speed, casting his gaze all around.
Having looked all around at the site of the hut in various places,
he then beheld the leaf-hut deserted by Sītā,
stripped of its splendor like a lotus pond withered in the winter.
With its trees appearing as if weeping, its flowers withered and its birds and beasts despondent; bereft of splendor, devastated, and abandoned by the forest deities;
with its deer-skins and *kuśa* grass scattered about, and its cushions and mats strewn hither and thither.
Seeing the site of the empty hut, she lamented again and again:
"She must have been carried off, or dead, or lost, or devoured;
or perhaps the timid one is hiding, or has fled into the forest."
"She has gone to gather flowers or perhaps fruits; or else she has gone to a lotus pond or to the river for water. Though he searched with great effort in the forest, he did not find his beloved.
With eyes reddened by grief, he appeared as if mad with sorrow;
running from tree to tree, from mountain to mountain, and from river to river,
Rāma lamented, submerged in an ocean of mud-like grief.
"O Kadamba, has that beloved who is fond of the kadamba tree been seen by you? If you know, tell me of Sītā, the lady of the beautiful countenance,
who resembles a tender sprout and is clothed in yellow silk."
"O Bilva tree, tell me if you have seen her whose breasts are like bilva fruits; or else,
O Arjuna tree, tell me of that beloved who is dear to Arjuna—
that timid daughter of Janaka, whether she lives or not."
3.058.015a This *kakubha* tree, O lady with thighs like the *kakubha*, clearly knows that Maithilī; 3.058.015c for this lord of the forest shines forth, rich with creepers, sprouts, and flowers.
3.058.016a And it is celebrated by bees, just as this preeminent tree is indeed renowned.
3.058.016c This *tilaka* tree clearly knows the one who is dear to the *tilaka*.
3.058.017a O *aśoka*, dispeller of grief, [know] me whose mind is stricken by sorrow; 3.058.017c Quickly make me one who bears your name by means of the sight of my beloved.
"O Tāla tree, if you have seen her whose breasts are like ripe tāla fruits—
tell me of that woman of noble hips, if you feel any compassion for me.
If you have seen Sītā, who possesses the luster of a rose-apple and gold,"
"If you know my beloved, tell me without hesitation.
Or, O deer, do you know Maithilī, that fawn-eyed one? That lovely woman with the gaze of a deer might perhaps be with the female deer."
"O elephant, if she whose thighs are like an elephant's trunk has been seen by you, I believe she must be known to you; tell me, O noble elephant!
O tiger, if that beloved with a face like the moon has been seen by you—"
"O Maithilī, speak to me with confidence; you have no fear.
Why do you run away, my dear? Surely you have been seen, O lotus-eyed one! Why do you hide yourself behind a tree and not answer me?"
"Stop, stop, O lady of beautiful hips! You have no compassion for me.
You are not by nature excessively prone to laughter; why do you disregard me?
O woman of excellent complexion, you are revealed by your yellow silk garment."
Even as she was running away, I saw her; stay, if you have any affection for me!
Surely that sweet-smiling woman is not there, or perhaps she has been harmed, since she surely would not have neglected me when I had fallen into such distress.
"Clearly that young girl has been devoured by flesh-eating *rākṣasas*; separated from me, her beloved, they must have divided all her limbs.
Surely that face with its beautiful teeth and lips has lost its luster."
For that beautiful neck of my beloved, possessing the hue of a campaka flower and adorned with a necklace,
has been devoured as she lamented;
surely those two arms of hers, tender as young shoots, were also cast aside.
With their trembling fingertips and their armlets and bracelets still upon them,
those two young women were devoured by me while deprived of their protector,
like a caravan abandoned for the ravenous consumption of many kinsmen.
"Alas, Lakṣmaṇa, O mighty-armed one! Do you see my beloved anywhere?
"Alas, my dear one! Where have you gone, O blessed lady? Alas, Sītā! Thus lamenting, Rāma ran from forest to forest.
In some places he wanders about with speed; in others he roams about with force;
in some places, intent on searching for his beloved, he appears like one intoxicated.
He [traversed] forests, rivers, mountains, and mountain cascades.
He wandered through the forests with great speed, unable to find rest;
having thus traversed that vast and immense forest and searched it all over for the sake of Maithilī, he then—
With his hopes unfulfilled, he exerted the greatest effort once more in the search for his beloved;
Rāma, the son of Daśaratha, beheld the hermitage empty.
Seeing the leaf-hut deserted and the seats scattered about, and not finding Vaidehī there despite searching everywhere,
Rāma cried out and, raising his beautiful arms, spoke:
"O Lakṣmaṇa, where indeed is Vaidehī? To what region has she gone from here?
By whom has my beloved been carried off, O son of Sumitrā, or by whom has she been devoured?
If you wish to mock me by hiding behind a tree, Sītā—"
"Enough of your laughter today; come, favor me who am deeply distressed.
O gentle Sītā, those young deer with whom you used to play in confidence—now that they have been deprived of you, my dear, they sit brooding with eyes clouded by tears."
"In the other world, my father, the great king, will surely see me dead from the great grief born of Sītā’s abduction. How could you have urged me on after I had already given you my solemn promise?"
"Having failed to complete that period of time, he has come here into my presence.
In the next world, my father will clearly say to you, 'Fie on you!'— to me, who acted according to desire, who am ignoble, and a speaker of falsehood."

"O lady of beautiful hips, O slender-waisted one, where are you going, having abandoned me here— me who am helpless, consumed by grief, wretched, and with my hopes shattered, like a compassionate man leaving behind a dishonest man for the sake of fame?"
"Separated from you, I shall give up my own life.
Lamenting thus, Rāma, longing for the sight of Sītā and afflicted by extreme sorrow, did not see the daughter of Janaka, O descendant of Raghu.
Seeing that son of Daśaratha unable to find Sītā,
appearing like an elephant sinking into a vast expanse of mud,
Lakṣmaṇa spoke at length to Rāma out of a desire for his welfare.

"Do not despair, O mighty-armed one; exert yourself together with me. For this forest, O hero, is adorned with many caves, and Maithilī delights in wandering through the woods and is infatuated with the forest."
She may have entered the forest, or a lotus pond in full bloom; or she may have reached a river frequented by fish and water-fowl;
or, wishing to terrify [her pursuers], she may be hidden somewhere in the woods.
"O bull among men, Vaidehī is desirous of knowing both you and me;
therefore, O illustrious one, let us exert ourselves immediately in her search. We shall scour the entire forest where that daughter of Janaka may be."
"O Kākutstha, if you think thus, do not set your mind on grief.
Thus addressed by Lakṣmaṇa out of friendship, Rāma, composed in mind,
began to search together with the son of Sumitrā.
3.059.017e Searching everywhere through forests, mountains, rivers, and lakes, those two sons of Daśaratha sought Sītā throughout that mountain— its plateaus, caves, and peaks.
Searching everywhere, they did not find her at all.
Having searched the mountain on all sides, Rāma said to Lakṣmaṇa:
"O Saumitri, I do not see Vaidehī here on this beautiful mountain."
Then, tormented by grief, Lakṣmaṇa spoke these words:
"Wandering through the Daṇḍaka forest, O one of great wisdom, you shall find your brother of radiant splendor and Maithilī, the daughter of Janaka."
"Just as the mighty-armed Viṣṇu bound Bali and [recovered] this earth,"—
having been addressed thus by the heroic Lakṣmaṇa, that descendant of Raghu,
his mind struck by grief, spoke with a piteous voice.
The entire forest has been thoroughly searched, as have the lotus ponds with their blooming lotuses;
and this mountain, O one of great wisdom, with its many caves and waterfalls—
yet I do not see Vaidehī, who is dearer to me than my own life.
Thus lamenting, Rāma, emaciated by the abduction of Sītā,
distressed and overwhelmed by grief, became distraught for a moment. With all his limbs trembling, his intellect departed, and he lost consciousness.
Afflicted by despair and dejected, he sighed a long, cold sigh;
having sighed many times, the lotus-eyed Rāma cried out repeatedly, "O my beloved! with a voice choked with tears.
Then Lakṣmaṇa, his dear kinsman,
who knew the dharma, being humble and with palms joined in reverence, consoled him in many ways;
yet he disregarded those words falling from the lips of Lakṣmaṇa.
Not seeing his beloved Sītā, he cried out again and again.
Distressed, he spoke these words to Lakṣmaṇa in a piteous voice:
"Lakṣmaṇa, go quickly and find out about the Godāvarī river."
"Has Sītā gone to the Godāvarī to fetch lotuses?
Thus addressed by Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa,
moving with swift strides, went once again to the beautiful river Godāvarī.
Having searched that river Tīrthavatī, Lakṣmaṇa said to Rāma:
"I do not see her at the bathing-places; though I call out, she does not hear me. To what region, then, has Vaidehī, the destroyer of my suffering, gone?"
"Indeed, O Rāma, I do not know where that slender-waisted woman is. Having heard Lakṣmaṇa’s words, Rāma, dejected and bewildered by grief,
proceeded himself toward the river Godāvarī.
Approaching her, Rāma asked, "Where is Sītā?
Even though all living beings were being slain by the lord of the rākṣasas, who deserved death, they did not tell Rāma where she was; nor did the river Godāvarī speak of her.
Then, urged by the spirits, they said to him, "Tell us of that beloved one.
But Sītā, though questioned and grieving for Rāma, did not speak of her;
nor did she describe the appearance or the deeds of the evil-minded Rāvaṇa.
Having reflected, that river, out of fear, did not reveal Vaidehī to him. Despairing of seeing Sītā because of that river, Rāma, emaciated by the failure to find her, spoke to the son of Sumitrā.

"O Lakṣmaṇa, what unpleasant words shall I speak when I meet Janaka and Vaidehī’s mother, who are now deprived of her? She who [supported] me when I was stripped of my kingdom, living in the forest on forest fare— "
"Remove all this grief; where indeed has Vaidehī gone? For me, deprived of my kinsmen and not seeing the princess, I think the nights will be long as I remain awake."
"I shall search the Godāvarī, Janasthāna, and this Prasravaṇa mountain;
I will traverse them all if Sītā is indeed to be found.
Thus did those two brothers converse with one another.
3.060.015c They saw a trail of flowers fallen upon the earth. 3.060.016a Seeing that shower of flowers fallen on the ground, the heroic Rāma, distressed, spoke these sorrowful words to Lakṣmaṇa.
"I remember those very flowers here, O Lakṣmaṇa,
which were gathered by me in the forest and given to Vaidehī.
Having spoken thus to Lakṣmaṇa, that bull among men, the mighty-armed one—
Enraged like a lion toward a small animal, he spoke there to the mountain:
"O Mountain, show me Sītā, who is golden-hued and radiant as gold;
otherwise, I shall destroy all your peaks."
"Consumed by the fire of my arrows, you shall be reduced to ashes;
forever unfit for habitation, stripped of grass, trees, and shoots.
Or else, O Lakṣmaṇa, I shall dry up this river today."
"If he does not tell me of Sītā, whose face resembles the moon,
today," Rāma, thus enraged as if wishing to consume him with his very eyes,
beheld upon the ground the great footprint of a *rākṣasa* that had emerged.
3.060.023 Having observed that Sītā had been carried away and that the Rākṣasa was departing,
Rāma, with a bewildered heart, spoke to his beloved brother:
3.060.024 "Behold, Lakṣmaṇa, these scattered fragments of gold from Vaidehī."
O Saumitri, behold the various garlands and ornaments [of the slain],
and the surface of the earth covered on all sides with variegated drops of blood resembling glowing molten sparks.
"Lakṣmaṇa, I think that Vaidehī must have been torn apart again and again by the Rākṣasas who can assume any form at will, or she has been devoured;
it was for her sake that those two were disputing."
"O son of Sumitrā, a terrible battle took place here between these two Rākṣasas.
O gentle one, whose great bow— studded with pearls and gems and adorned with refined gold— has fallen broken upon the earth?"
Whose golden armor is this, resembling the rising sun, studded with beads of lapis lazuli,
shattered and fallen upon the ground? And whose is this parasol with its hundred ribs, adorned with celestial garlands?
"O gentle one, whose broken staff has been cast down upon the ground?
And these donkeys, with faces like Piśācas, golden breastplates,
fearsome forms, and massive bodies— by whom have they been slain in battle?"
Whose war-chariot, brilliant as a blazing fire and bearing a standard in battle, has been cast away and broken? These arrows,
as long as a chariot-axle and adorned with gold, [lie scattered here].
Whose are these arrows, scattered by one of terrible deeds? Behold this hundredfold enmity of mine, which shall bring an end to life,
O gentle one, wrought by Rākṣasas of most cruel heart who can assume any form at will.
"Sītā has indeed been abducted, or killed, or devoured—that poor woman.
Dharma does not protect Sītā as she is being carried away in the great forest. For even if Vaidehī has been devoured or abducted, O Lakṣmaṇa—"

"O gentle one, for who in this world is able to do what is pleasing to me? O Lakṣmaṇa, all beings might, out of ignorance, disregard even the Creator of the worlds, though he be a hero and one who feels compassion."
"Those lords of the thirty gods surely think me to be lacking in vigor— me who am gentle, devoted to the welfare of the world, self-controlled, and compassionate. Behold,
O Lakṣmaṇa, how even my virtue has turned into a fault upon encountering me."
This very day, for the destruction of all beings and the Rākṣasas,
he has risen like a great sun after withdrawing the moonlight;
neither Yakṣas, nor Gandharvas, nor Piśācas, nor Rākṣasas [shall remain].
"Whether they be *kiṃnaras* or humans, O Lakṣmaṇa, they shall find no happiness.
Behold, Lakṣmaṇa, the sky filled with my missiles and arrows;
today I shall make it impassable for those who roam the three worlds."
The multitude of planets was completely obstructed, the moon was eclipsed, the fires,
winds, and the brilliance of the sun were utterly extinguished,
the mountain peaks were crushed, and the reservoirs of water were drying up.
With its trees, creepers, and shrubs destroyed and its oceans utterly ruined,
those lords will not restore Sītā to me in safety;
at this very moment, O son of Sumitrā, they shall witness my prowess.

"O Lakṣmaṇa, no living beings shall fly into the sky, for it will be rendered solid by the nets of arrows released from my bowstring. Afflicted by my iron shafts, the deer and birds will be destroyed and scattered in flight."
"O Lakṣmaṇa, behold today this world agitated and devoid of all restraint;
with arrows drawn back to my ear that are difficult to resist, I shall, for the sake of Maithilī, rid the world of living beings of its Piśācas and Rākṣasas."

"Today the gods shall behold the power of my arrows, released out of indignation and traveling far, as they are impelled by my wrath. Neither the gods, nor the Daityas, nor the Piśācas, nor the Rākṣasas [shall withstand them]."
Through my wrath, when the three worlds have been destroyed,
the worlds of the gods, dānavas, yakṣas,
and even the rākṣasas will fall in many ways, mangled by the floods of my arrows.
"Today, with my arrows, I shall make these worlds devoid of all bounds. Just as old age, death, time, and destiny are never obstructed among all living beings, O Lakṣmaṇa," so shall it be.

3.060.051 Thus, joined with such wrath, I am undoubtedly not to be restrained. 3.060.052 If they do not point out Sītā, the blameless daughter of Mithilā with beautiful teeth, to me today as they did before, [then I shall destroy them all].
I can overturn the entire world— including its gods, gandharvas, humans, and serpents, as well as its mountains.
Likewise, I shall [protect] Rāma, who is thus tormented and emaciated by the abduction of Sītā.
Like the fire of universal destruction at the end of an eon, he was intent on the annihilation of the worlds; beholding his strung bow and sighing again and again,
he appeared like the wrathful Rudra desiring to slay the sacrificial beast at Dakṣa’s sacrifice.
Seeing Rāma enraged as never before, Lakṣmaṇa,
with palms joined in reverence and a parched mouth, spoke these words:
"Formerly you were gentle, self-controlled, and devoted to the welfare of all beings."
3.061.004c You ought not, having fallen under the sway of anger, abandon your true nature.
3.061.005a Splendor is in the moon, radiance in the sun, movement in the wind, and forbearance in the earth; 3.061.005c all these qualities are constant, and in you resides unsurpassed fame.
But I do not know whose broken battle-chariot this is, by whom it was destroyed, for what reason, or why it stands here with its weapons and equipment intact;
yet it is scarred by hooves and wheel-rims, and sprinkled with drops of blood.
"O prince, this region, where the battle has ceased, is most terrible. O best of speakers, this is the carnage wrought by one alone, not by two;
for I do not see the tracks of a great army."
"You ought not to destroy the worlds for the sake of a single individual;
for lords of the earth are gentle and peaceful when their punishment is just.
You are always the refuge and the supreme goal for all living beings."
"O Raghava, who indeed would consider the loss of your wife to be right?
Neither the rivers, the oceans, the mountains, nor the gods, gandharvas,
and dānavas are capable of doing you harm, just as virtuous men do not act against one who is consecrated for a sacrifice."
"O King, you ought to search for him by whom Sītā was abducted—
searching with me as your second, bow in hand, and accompanied by these supreme ṛṣis. We shall scour the ocean, the mountains, and the forests."
We shall search the various and formidable caves, the lotus ponds, and the mountain ranges;
with concentrated minds, we shall explore the realms of the gods and the Gandharvas until we find the one who has carried away your wife.

"O Lord of Kosala, if the lords of the thirty gods do not give you your wife through conciliation, then you shall later perform what the time demands. [Win] Sītā through your character, conciliation, and humility."
O lord of men, if you do not obtain it by this means,
then destroy them with volleys of gold-tufted arrows resembling the thunderbolt of great Indra.

To him who was thus tormented by grief, lamenting like one without a protector, overcome by great delusion, utterly dejected, and unconscious— then Lakṣmaṇa, the son of Sumitrā, after consoling him for a moment as it were, [spoke].
Pressing his feet, he addressed Rāma:
"O Rāma, by means of great austerity and great deeds,
King Daśaratha obtained you, just as the immortals obtained the nectar of immortality."

"Bound by your very virtues, the lord of the earth has attained divinity because of his separation from you, just as was heard regarding King Bharata. O descendant of Kakutstha, if you cannot endure this sorrow that has been met,"
3.062.005c And who else— being ordinary and of little strength— will endure this? 3.062.006a For if you, being thus distressed, should consume the worlds with your splendor,
3.062.006c O tiger among men, where indeed will the afflicted creatures find relief?

3.062.007a This is indeed the very nature of the world: Yayāti, the son of Nahuṣa, 3.062.007c attained the same world as Śakra, yet misfortune touched him. 3.062.008a As for the great seer Vasiṣṭha, who was our father’s domestic priest—

In a single day, he begot a hundred sons, and likewise they were slain again. O you who are true to your word, this very Earth, the mother of the world and the goddess honored by all the worlds, is seen to tremble.
3.062.010a And these two eyes of the worlds, upon whom everything is established—
3.062.010c the sun and the moon, those of great power— have come under eclipse.
3.062.011a Even the greatest beings and the gods, O bull among men, [are affected].
3.062.011c No embodied beings can escape the power of destiny.
3.062.012a Even among the gods, beginning with Śakra, both right conduct and misconduct are heard of; O tiger among men, you ought not to be distressed.
"O sinless one, O hero, even though Vaidehī has been lost or even abducted, you ought not to grieve like an ordinary man. For those such as you, who constantly perceive the truth, do not grieve."
Even in the midst of great hardships, Rāma’s vision remains undaunted.
O best of men, reflect upon this with your intellect according to the truth;
for those endowed with wisdom and great insight discern the auspicious and the inauspicious through their intellect.
For actions whose merits and defects are unseen and which remain unperformed,
their desired fruit does not come to pass without the execution of those acts. Indeed,
O hero, in the past you yourself have instructed me many times on this very point.
"Who indeed could instruct you, even Bṛhaspati himself in person? Your intellect, O man of great wisdom, is difficult to follow even for the gods.
I am awakening your knowledge, which has been lulled to sleep by grief."

"O bull among the Ikṣvākus, having considered your divine, human, and personal prowess, strive for the destruction of your enemies. O bull among men, what is the use to you of this total annihilation?"
"But you ought to recognize that very same wicked enemy and uproot him. As soon as these well-spoken words were uttered by Lakṣmaṇa,
Rāghava, who grasps the essential meaning, accepted that most profound truth.
Restraining his own surging anger, the mighty-armed Rāma took up his wonderful bow and said to Lakṣmaṇa:
"What shall we do, my child? Or where shall we go, Lakṣmaṇa?"
"By what means might I see Sītā? Reflect upon this.
To Rāma, who was thus afflicted by intense grief, Lakṣmaṇa said:
"It is right for you to search this very Janasthāna."
It is strewn with many rākṣasas and filled with various trees and creepers. Here there are mountain fastnesses, waterfalls, and caves;
and there are various terrible caverns teeming with herds of diverse wild animals.

"The abodes of the kinnaras and the palaces of the gandharvas— you ought to search for them together with me, being diligent. For those like you, O bull among men, who are endowed with wisdom and possessed of great soul."
"In times of calamity they do not tremble, like mountains before the force of the wind.
Having been told this, Rāma, together with Lakṣmaṇa, roamed through that entire forest;
enraged, he fixed a terrible, razor-sharp arrow upon his bow.
Then he beheld the highly fortunate Jaṭāyus, the best of the twice-born, resembling a mountain peak, fallen upon the ground and drenched in blood; seeing him,
who looked like a mountain summit, Rāma spoke to Lakṣmaṇa.
"By him Vaidehī Sītā has been devoured; there is no doubt of this.
Clearly, this demon is wandering the forest in the form of a vulture;
having eaten the large-eyed Sītā, he now sits at his ease."

"I shall slay him with these terrible, straight-flying arrows with blazing tips," having said this, Rāma, enraged as if shaking the earth bounded by the oceans, fixed a razor-sharp arrow upon his bow and rushed toward the vulture.
Vomiting blood mixed with foam,
the bird addressed Rāma, the son of Daśaratha, in a most piteous voice:
"O long-lived one, that medicinal herb which you seek in the great forest— "
3.063.014c That queen was my very life, and both have been taken away by Rāvaṇa.
3.063.015a Deprived of you and Lakṣmaṇa, O Rāghava,
the queen was seen by me being carried off by the powerful Rāvaṇa.
"I did not abandon Sītā; rather, Rāvaṇa was struck down upon the surface of the earth by me in battle, his chariot and parasol shattered.
This is his broken bow, and this is his quiver."
"O Rāma, this is his war-chariot, shattered in battle.
Having severed my wings with his sword while I was exhausted, Rāvaṇa took Vaidehī Sītā and leapt into the sky."
"You were killed by a *rākṣasa* previously; you ought not to kill me.
But Rāma, having learned from him that dear story concerning his attachment to Sītā, embraced the king of vultures and wept along with Lakṣmaṇa.
Seeing him somehow sighing alone on that difficult, narrow path, the sorrowful Rāma spoke these words to the son of Sumitrā:
"The fall from the kingdom, the dwelling in the forest, Sītā lost, and the twice-born slain."
Such is this misfortune of mine that it could even consume fire;
even if I were today to cross the great ocean in its full extent,
that lord of rivers would surely dry up because of my ill fortune.
"In this world of mobile and immobile beings, there is no one more unfortunate than I,
by whom this great snare of calamity has been encountered.
This king of vultures, advanced in years, is a friend of my father."
"Slain, he lies upon the ground due to the reversal of my fortune.
Having spoken thus many times, Rāghava, together with Lakṣmaṇa,
touched Jaṭāyu, demonstrating his paternal affection.
Embracing that king of vultures, whose wings were severed and who was drenched in blood, Rāma cried out,
"O Maithilī, my life’s equal, where are you?"
Having released his speech, he fell to the ground.
But Rāma, seeing that vulture struck down upon the earth by the fierce [hawk],
spoke these words to Saumitri, who was endowed with every virtue:
"Surely this bird, while striving for my sake,
has been slain by a Rākṣasa in battle and is now giving up his life, which is so difficult to relinquish. O Lakṣmaṇa, the vital breath still remains within this body of his."
"Thus, deprived of his voice, Jaṭāyu looks on in distress. If you are able to speak again,
tell me of Sītā— blessings upon you— and tell me of your own death."
For what reason did Rāvaṇa carry off Sītā, and what offense against him was committed by me, seeing which my beloved was abducted by Rāvaṇa?
And how was that captivating face, resembling the moon, [formerly]?
O best of the twice-born, what did Sītā say at that time?
What is the prowess, what is the appearance, and what is the nature of that Rākṣasa?
And where, O father, is his abode? Tell me as I ask you.
Then, looking up at Rāma who was immediately thereafter lamenting, Jaṭāyu, his soul distressed, spoke these words to him with a very feeble voice:
"She has been carried away through the sky by Rāvaṇa, the lord of the rākṣasas."
Resorting to a vast illusion filled with wind and storm clouds, O dear one,
that night-stalker cut off my wings while I was exhausted and departed toward the south, taking Sītā, the princess of Videha, with him.
"O Rāghava, my life-breaths are failing and my vision is spinning;
I see golden trees with hair made of *uśīra* grass,
[trees] by which Rāvaṇa travels in an instant taking Sītā with him."
Lost wealth is quickly recovered by its owner. This moment is named Vinda; however, O descendant of Kakutstha, he did not perceive it.
Like a fish that has swallowed a hook, he will soon perish.
"You must not feel any distress regarding the daughter of Janaka;
having slain that Rākṣasa in battle, you will soon take your pleasure with Vaidehī.
Thus spoke the undeluded vulture, addressing Rāma.
From the mouth of the one dying prematurely, blood mixed with flesh flowed out.
Having spoken thus— "I am the son of Viśravas and the very brother of Vaiśravaṇa"—
the Lord of Birds gave up his life, which is so difficult to attain.
As Rāma, with palms joined in reverence, cried out, "Speak!
Speak!", the life-breaths of the vulture abandoned its body and ascended into the sky.
Then, casting its head upon the ground and stretching out its feet, it lay there.
Having cast aside his own body, he fell upon the surface of the earth.
Beholding that vulture, copper-eyed and lifeless like a mountain,
Rāma, dejected by his many sorrows, spoke to the son of Sumitrā.
Having lived happily for many years in the dwelling of the rākṣasas,
this bird has wandered here in the Daṇḍaka forest;
he is one who has been present for many years and has remained there for a long time.
"Here he lies slain today; for time is indeed difficult to overcome. Look, Lakṣmaṇa, this vulture who was my benefactor has been killed;
he indeed rescued Sītā from the powerful Rāvaṇa."
Having renounced his great ancestral kingdom of the vultures, this lord of birds has given up his life for my sake. Indeed,
virtuous practitioners of dharma are seen everywhere.

"O son of Sumitrā, you heroes who provide refuge even to those born as animals— O gentle one, O scorcher of foes, the grief I feel from the abduction of Sītā does not weigh upon me so heavily as this destruction of the vulture on my account."
"Just as the illustrious King Daśaratha was worthy of worship and honor by me, so too is this lord of birds. O Saumitri, fetch some wood; I shall kindle a fire by friction."

"I wish to cremate the king of vultures, who has met his death on my account; I shall place upon the funeral pyre the protector of the world of birds. O Saumitri, I will burn this one who was slain by the fierce Rākṣasa."
3.064.029a That destination which belongs to those devoted to sacrifice, and that destination of those who maintain the sacred fires;
3.064.029c and that which belongs to those who never retreat, and that which belongs to those who bestow land— 3.064.030a permitted by me, go you to those unsurpassed worlds.
"O great-souled king of vultures, you have been consecrated by me;
now depart. Having spoken thus, the righteous Rāma, filled with grief like one mourning his own kinsman, placed the lord of birds upon the blazing pyre and cremated him.

Then the valiant Rāma, accompanied by the son of Sumitrā, having gone into the forest and killed large deer, spread them out before that twice-born man. Having extracted the venison and cut it into pieces, the highly illustrious one—
On a delightful patch of green grass, Rāma gave [the bones] to a bird;
then Rāma quickly recited that prayer which the twice-born say leads a mortal who has passed away to heaven.
Then, having gone to the river Godāvarī, both those sons of the best of men offered water for that king of vultures. That king of vultures had performed a deed that brought him glory.
Having performed most difficult deeds and being struck down in battle,
he was then consecrated by one equal to a great seer and went to his own auspicious and meritorious destination.
Having thus offered water to him, the two descendants of Raghu then set forth;
searching for Sītā in the forest, they proceeded toward the western direction.
Having gone toward that southern quarter, bearing their arrows, bows, and swords, they continued on.
The two descendants of Ikṣvāku entered upon a path that had never been trodden before;
it was entwined with many shrubs, trees, and creepers,
obstructed on all sides, difficult to traverse, dense, and terrible to behold.
Having proceeded with speed toward the southern direction,
those two of great strength passed through that most formidable great forest.
Then, having traveled three *krośas* beyond Janasthāna, the two Rāghavas—
Those two of great luster entered the dense Krauñca forest,
which resembled a mass of various thick clouds and seemed joyful on all sides,
filled with beautiful flowers of many colors and with flocks of beasts and birds.
Desiring to see Vaidehī, the two of them searched through that forest,
stopping here and there, emaciated by the abduction of Sītā.
Then Lakṣmaṇa, possessed of great splendor, courage, good character, and purity—
With palms joined in reverence, he spoke these words to his brother of blazing splendor:
"My arm throbs violently and my mind is as if agitated;
moreover, I perceive for the most part that the omens are unfavorable."
"Therefore, noble one, prepare yourself and carry out this beneficial advice.
For these omens of mine immediately portend a great upheaval.
This bird named Vañculaka is most formidable."
"3.065.011c Roaring as if to proclaim our victory in battle,
[the lion roars]. 3.065.012a While the two of them were thus searching that entire forest with vigor, 3.065.012c a great sound arose, as if shattering that forest."
As if intensely enveloped by the wind,
the sound of that forest arose, as though filling the very heavens. Anticipating that sound, Rāma, together with his younger brother, remained in the thicket.

He beheld a Rākṣasa of immense body and broad chest. Then those two approached him as he stood before them— a headless trunk with no neck, its mouth situated in its belly, and grown to a massive size.
Covered with sharp bristles, it rose high like a great mountain;
fierce and resembling a dark blue cloud, it roared with the sound of thundering clouds.
With its large, tawny, broad, and long eyelashes, it stood there.
With one terrible eye upon his chest that saw with lightning speed,
he possessed great fangs and a massive mouth which he was licking;
he was devouring most horrific bears, lions, deer, and elephants.
He was terrifying, distorting both his arms which were each a yojana in length;
with his two hands, he seized various bears, flocks of birds, and deer,
dragging them in and pulling away many leaders of deer herds.

Blocking the path of those two brothers who had approached it, he stood there. Then, having passed him by at a distance of one *krośa*, they beheld a massive, cruel, and terrifying headless trunk (*kabandha*) with arms outstretched.
That mighty-armed one, stretching out his two vast arms to the utmost,
seized both Raghavas together, pressing them with force—
those two who possessed swords, firm bows, fierce energy, and long arms.
3.065.023c The two brothers, though possessed of great strength, were rendered helpless as they were being dragged away.
3.065.024a To them spoke the mighty-armed Kabandha, the best of the Dānavas: 3.065.024c "Who are you two, with shoulders like those of bulls, wielding great swords and bows?"

"Having reached this terrible region, you have presented yourselves as my prey. Tell me, what is your business here, and for what purpose have you both come to this place? You stand here before me, afflicted by hunger."
"Equipped with arrows, bows, and swords, like two bulls with sharp horns, they have come before my mouth; their life shall be difficult to regain.
Having heard those words of the evil-minded Kabandha, [Rāma spoke].
3.065.027c Rāma, with a parched face, spoke to Lakṣmaṇa:
3.065.028a "O you whose valor is truth, having passed from hardship to even greater hardship,
3.065.028c a terrible calamity leading to the end of life has been reached, yet that beloved one has not been found."
"O Lakṣmaṇa, the power of Time over all beings is exceedingly great;
behold, O tiger among men, how both you and I have been deluded by calamities. There is no burden too heavy for destiny to impose upon all living creatures, O Lakṣmaṇa."
"Even those who are brave, powerful, and skilled in weapons on the field of battle perish when overtaken by Time, like bridges made of sand. Speaking thus was he of firm truth and prowess;
The highly illustrious and powerful son of Daśaratha,
having observed the son of Sumitrā whose valor was exalted,
then reaffirmed his own firm resolve within himself.

Seeing those two brothers, Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, standing there with their arms encircled as a noose, Kabandha spoke these words: "O bulls among Kṣatriyas, why do you stand still upon seeing me, who am tormented by hunger?"
"Commanded by fate for the sake of food, they have lost their senses.
Having heard those words, which were timely and beneficial, Lakṣmaṇa—
though overcome with distress— spoke, having resolved upon a course of valorous action.
"Before that lowest of Rākṣasas can quickly seize both you and me,
let us therefore swiftly cut off his two heavy arms with our swords.
Then those two Rāghavas, who were aware of the proper place and time, [acted] with their very swords.
Highly delighted, they both lopped off his two arms at the shoulders. Then Rāma swiftly severed the right arm with his sword without hesitation, while the hero Lakṣmaṇa cut off the left.
With his arms severed, that mighty-armed one fell with a great roar,
making the sky, the earth, and the very quarters of space resound like a thundercloud.
Seeing his two arms lopped off, he was drenched in a torrent of blood.
Dejected, the Dānava asked those two heroes, "Who are you?
To him who was speaking thus, the mighty Lakṣmaṇa, endowed with auspicious marks,
described Kākutstha to Kabandha.
3.066.010a This heir of Ikṣvāku is known by people by the name of Rāma;
3.066.010c know me to be his younger brother, Lakṣmaṇa. 3.066.011a While he, who possesses the power of a god, dwells in this lonely forest...
"Our wife was carried off by a *rākṣasa*, and desiring her, we have come here.
But who are you, and for what purpose are you in this forest, looking like a headless trunk (*kabandha*),
struggling with your thighs broken and your blazing mouth in your chest?"
Thus addressed by Lakṣmaṇa, Kabandha, remembering those words of Indra, spoke this reply with great joy:
"Welcome to you both, O tigers among men! By good fortune do I behold you."

"By good fortune, O tigers among men, these two arm-bonds have been severed by you both. Now hear from me, as I tell it to you in truth, O tiger among men, how this deformed appearance was acquired by me through my own lack of discipline."
"O Rāma, O mighty-armed one of great strength and prowess, formerly my form was inconceivable and renowned throughout the three worlds,
like the bodies of Soma, Śakra, and Sūrya."
"O Rāma, having assumed this great form that terrifies the world, I then and there terrified the sages dwelling in the forest. Thereupon,
the great seer named Sthūlaśiras was provoked to anger by me."
"3.067.003c While gathering various forest fruits, I was overcome by this form of yours. 3.067.004a Upon seeing me thus, he spoke these words, pronouncing a terrible curse:
'Let this very form of yours remain cruel and contemptible.'"
When I asked him, "How might there be an end to this curse? he, being enraged, spoke these words regarding the curse he had pronounced:
"When Rāma, having severed your two arms, shall burn you in a lonely forest..."
"Then you shall regain your own vast and auspicious form,
O son of Danu, resplendent with glory; know this, Lakṣmaṇa,
that you have obtained this appearance on the field of battle due to the wrath of Indra."
"For by means of fierce asceticism, I indeed gratified the Grandfather;
he granted me long life, and then delusion touched me:
'I have obtained long life; what can Śakra do to me?'"
Having thus resolved my mind, I assailed Śakra in battle.
By the hundred-knotted thunderbolt released from his arm,
both his thighs and his head were driven back into his body.
Though entreated by me, he sent him to the abode of Yama;
he said to me, "Let the word of the Grandfather be true.
How can one who is without food, with his thighs, head, and face shattered, be capable [of anything]?
"Struck by the thunderbolt, one cannot live even for a very long time.
When I had spoken thus, Śakra gave me two arms a yojana in length,
and he fashioned a mouth with sharp fangs within my belly.
3.067.014a Drawing in the forest-dwellers with my two long arms, 3.067.014c I devour lions, elephants, deer, and tigers on all sides.
3.067.015a But Indra said to me: "When Rāma, along with Lakṣmaṇa..."
"When your arms are severed in battle, then you shall go to heaven.
You are that Rāma—blessings be upon you; O Rāghava, I cannot be slain by anyone else. Thus was it spoken by the great seer according to the truth.
"O bull among men, I shall indeed provide counsel with my intellect,
and once consecrated by you both through the fire, I shall also designate a friend for you.
Having been addressed thus by that Dānava, the righteous Rāghava—
While Lakṣmaṇa listened, he spoke these words:
"My illustrious wife Sītā was carried off by Rāvaṇa while I had gone out from Janasthāna with my brother at our ease."
"I know only the name of that Rākṣasa, but not his form;
nor do we know his dwelling place or his power, as we wander thus about, afflicted by grief and without a protector."
"Let him act with compassion and remain intent on doing us a favor.
Having gathered dry logs broken by elephants at the proper time,
O hero, we shall eat you once a great pit has been prepared."
"Therefore, tell us of Sītā—by whom she was taken or where;
perform this great service for us, if you know the truth.
Thus addressed by Rāma, Danu spoke these unsurpassed words.
Skilled in speech, he addressed Rāghava, who was himself a master of eloquence:
"I possess no divine knowledge, nor do I know Maithilī.
Once I have been consumed by fire and have resumed my own form, I shall tell you of him who will know her."
"O Lord, as long as I am not consumed by fire, I have no power to discern that immensely powerful Rākṣasa by whom your Sītā was abducted,
O Rāghava; for my great knowledge has been lost through the fault of a curse."
"By my own actions, I have obtained this form, which is despised by the world. However,
O Rāma, as long as the sun has not set with its weary horses, throw me into a pit and burn me according to the prescribed rites."
"O descendant of Raghu, I have been burned by you in the pit according to justice.
O hero, Raghava, I shall tell you of that one who will recognize that Rakshasa; he must form a friendship with him, acting in a righteous manner."
"Delighted, he of swift prowess will provide you assistance;
for there is nothing in the three worlds unknown to him, O Rāghava,
as he has previously traversed all the worlds for other purposes."
When those two heroes had been thus addressed by Kabandha, O lord of men,
they reached a mountain cleft and discharged fire.
Lakṣmaṇa, moreover, [threw] great flaming meteors on all sides.
She set the pyre ablaze, and it flared up on all sides. That great body of Kabandha, resembling a mass of clarified butter,
burned slowly as it was being cooked by its own fat.
Having quickly shaken off the funeral pyre, he rose up like a smokeless fire; the one of great strength, wearing two stainless garments and a celestial garland,
then emerged from the pyre with speed, radiant and clad in spotless raiment.
3.068.005c He leapt up quickly, filled with joy, adorned with ornaments on every limb;
3.068.006a standing in a radiant, glory-bestowing celestial chariot drawn by swans,
3.068.006c that one of great splendor illuminated the ten directions with his brilliance.
Moving through the air, Kabandha spoke these words to Rāma:
"Listen, O Rāghava, to the truth of how you shall reach the boundary. Rāma, there are six expedients in this world by which everything is deliberated."
Polished by the edge of the blade, it is used for a tenth part of its length;
O Rāma, you have become diminished, along with Lakṣmaṇa, having fallen to that tenth part,
on account of which you have suffered this calamity— the assault upon your wife.
"Therefore, O best of friends, you must certainly act as a friend toward him;
for I see no success for you, even upon reflection, if you do not do so.
Listen, Rāma, I shall tell you: there is a monkey named Sugrīva."
Banished by his angry brother Vālin, the son of Śakra,
that self-controlled hero dwells on Ṛṣyamūka, the best of mountains, adorned by the shores of Lake Pampā, together with four other monkeys.
"O Rāghava, go from here this very day and quickly make him your friend;
having met him before the blazing fire, do so without malice.
And you must not hold that Sugrīva, the lord of monkeys, in contempt."
He is grateful, able to assume any form at will, a seeker of allies, and full of vigor.
For today you two are capable of accomplishing the task he desires to perform;
whether his purpose has already been achieved or not, he will carry out your business.
The son of Ṛkṣarajas,
the legitimate son of Bhāskara who has incurred the enmity of Vālin, wanders apprehensively around Lake Pampā;
having quickly laid aside his weapons, that monkey dwells at Ṛṣyamūka.

"O Raghava, by means of truth, make your forest-dwelling friend [your own]. For that elephant among monkeys, through his skill, thoroughly knows all the haunts in this world of those who eat human flesh."
"O Raghava, subduer of enemies, there is indeed nothing in this world that is unknown to him,
as long as the thousand-rayed sun shines.
He [traversed] the vast rivers, mountains, mountain fastnesses, and caves."
Having searched together with the monkeys, he will find your wife;
and Rāghava will dispatch monkeys of massive form to scour the quarters for that Sītā who grieves because of her separation from you.
That foremost of monkeys, having searched for your blameless beloved whether she was situated on the peak of Mount Meru or even dwelling in the depths of Pātāla, [did not find her].
Having slain the *rākṣasas* and having shown Rāma the way to recover Sītā,
Kabandha, who understood the true meaning of things, spoke these meaningful words once again.
"O Rāma, this is the auspicious path where these flowering trees,
taking recourse in the western direction, shine forth, enchanting to the mind—
jambū, priyāla, and panasa trees, as well as plakṣa, nyagrodha, and tinduka."
There are *aśvattha* trees, *karṇikāra* trees, mangoes, and other trees as well;
having climbed them or having forcibly brought them down to the ground,
you two shall go along eating their fruits which are like nectar.
Wandering through excellent regions from mountain to mountain and forest to forest,
you two heroes will then reach a lotus pond named Pampā,
which is free of gravel, without steep descents, with level landing-stairs, and devoid of moss.
O Rāma, [there is a lake] filled with sand and adorned with lotuses and water-lilies.
There, O descendant of Raghu, swans, ducks, cranes,
and ospreys, dwelling in the waters of Pampā, warble with beautiful voices.
"Those auspicious creatures do not tremble upon seeing men, for they are unacquainted with slaughter.
You shall devour those large birds, which resemble lumps of ghee.
And there are the rohita fish, the vakratuṇḍas, and the nalamīnas, O Rāghava."

O Rāma, at Pampā, Lakṣmaṇa— filled with devotion to you— will present to you choice fish that have been killed there with arrows; they shall be stripped of skin and fins, roasted over glowing iron, plump, and possessed of but a single bone.
3.069.011 While you were eating fish in abundance amidst the heaps of flowers at Pampā,
the water was auspicious, fragrant as a lotus, pleasantly cool, and free from impurity. 3.069.012 Having drawn up that untroubled water, which resembled silver and crystal—
Then Lakṣmaṇa will cause [the deer] to drink from a lotus leaf— those large, forest-dwelling boars who lie in mountain caves and have returned [to the water] out of a longing for it,
bellowing like bulls.
"O best of men, O Rāma, wandering at evening, you will see those endowed with beauty upon the Pampā, trees bearing garlands;
and having seen the cool waters of the Pampā, you shall cast off your grief."
There, O Rāghava, are *tilaka* and *naktamāla* trees covered with *sumana* flowers, as well as blooming blue lotuses and red lotuses;
yet no man there has ever placed these as garlands.

3.069.016 There were the disciples of Mataṅga, sages who were deeply concentrated in meditation. 3.069.017 As they, oppressed by the weight of their burden, were gathering forest produce for their teacher, drops of sweat fell rapidly from their bodies onto the earth.
Those garlands, produced at that time by the ascetic power of the sages,
arose from drops of sweat and do not perish, O Rāghava.
Even today, their attendant woman is seen right there.

"O descendant of Kakutstha, there is a long-lived female ascetic named Śabarī. Having seen you, O Rāma— who are like a god, eternally established in righteousness, and honored by all beings— she shall go to the heavenly world."
Then, O Rāma, having reached the western shore of the Pampā,
you shall behold, O descendant of Kakutstha, that incomparable and secret hermitage site;
there, the elephants are not able to invade that hermitage.
By the decree of that seer Mataṅga, that forest was established;
in that grove, which resembles Nandana and is like the celestial groves of the gods, filled with various birds, you shall take delight, O Rāma, in perfect peace.
To the east of Pampā stands Mount Ṛṣyamūka, with its trees in full bloom;
it is known as Suduḥkhārohaṇa (Difficult to Ascend) and is guarded by young elephants.
It is magnificent and was fashioned in ancient times by Brahmā himself.
"O Rāma, whatever wealth a man lying on the summit of that mountain obtains in a dream, he acquires upon waking. However, one of wicked conduct or evil deeds cannot ascend it."
Right there, the rākṣasas seize him while he is asleep and strike him;
even from that place, O Rāma, the great roar of young elephants dwelling in the Mataṅga forest as they play in the Pampā lake is heard.
Drenched by streams of blood, those supreme elephants,
swift as clouds and scattered about, move separately in groups;
having drunk there the pure, cool, and inexhaustible water.
3.069.029c The forest-dwellers, having turned back, enter the forests in agitation.
3.069.030a O Rāma, on that mountain there is a great cave that shines brightly;
3.069.030c it has a stone covering, O Kākutstha, and entry into it is difficult.
At the eastern gate of that cave there is a great lake of cool water,
delightful with its many roots and fruits and surrounded by various trees.
Sugrīva dwells there together with four monkeys.
3.069.032c At times he would remain upon the peak of that mountain.
3.069.033a But Kabandha, having thus instructed both Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa,
3.069.033c garlanded and radiant as the sun, shone forth in the sky, O valiant one.
Then Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, as they were setting out, spoke these words from nearby to the illustrious Kabandha who was stationed in the sky:
"Go! You must go for the sake of accomplishing our purpose. And he replied to them both, "Let it be so; you may go."
Having taken leave of those two who were well-pleased, Kabandha then departed. Having resumed that form,
Kabandha was enveloped in splendor, his body resembling the sun.
Pointing this out while standing in the sky, he looked at Rāma and then said, "Form a friendship [with him].
Those two [brothers] followed the path to Pampā shown by Kabandha in the forest.
Taking their stand facing the western direction, the two sons of the best of men proceeded;
observing many honey-like fruit-bearing trees growing on the mountains,
Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa went on to see Sugrīva.

Having made their dwelling upon the mountain ridge, those two descendants of Raghu approached the western shore of Lake Pampā. Having reached the western bank of the lotus pond Pampā, the two Rāghavas took their stand there.

Then, as they looked about, they saw there the beautiful hermitage of Śabarī. Having reached that hermitage, which was surrounded by many trees and exceedingly lovely, they gazed upon it and approached Śabarī.

Seeing them then, the perfected one (siddhā) rose with palms joined in reverence and grasped the feet of Rāma and the wise Lakṣmaṇa. Then Rāma spoke to that female ascetic (śramaṇī) who was firm in her vows.

"Are your obstacles conquered? Does your asceticism increase? O you whose wealth is penance, is your anger restrained and is your diet regulated? Have your observances been fulfilled? Is there peace in your mind?"
"O lady of lovely speech, has your service to your gurus been fruitful? Thus questioned by Rāma, the aged Śabarī— a perfected ascetic honored by the Siddhas— responded to him as she stood before him.

"When you arrived at Citrakūṭa, those whom I used to attend upon ascended from here to heaven in celestial chariots of incomparable splendor. And I was addressed by those illustrious great seers, who are knowers of dharma:"
Rāma will come to this most meritorious hermitage of yours;
he, together with the son of Sumitrā, must be received by you as a guest.
And having seen him, you shall go to the excellent, imperishable worlds.
"O bull among men, O tiger among men, I have gathered various forest provisions for your sake, grown on the banks of the Pampā.
Thus addressed by Śabarī, that righteous-souled one spoke this to Śabarī:
Rāghava spoke to her, who was ever excluded from such knowledge:
"I have heard the truth regarding the power of that high-souled one from Danu; now, if you agree, I wish to see it for myself."
Having heard these words issuing from the mouth of Rāma,
Śabarī showed that great forest to them both:
"Behold this vast forest, resembling a dense mass of clouds and teeming with beasts and birds."
"O descendant of Raghu, this place is renowned as Mataṅgavana.
Here, my gurus of purified souls, O one of great luster,
performed oblations at this sacred ford (tīrtha) with mantras, honoring it with sacred incantations."
"This is the sacrificial altar on this western ground where they, having honored me well,
present offerings of flowers with hands trembling from exhaustion.
O best of the Raghus, behold even now the power of their asceticism."

Illuminating all directions with their splendor, these altars of incomparable radiance shine forth. Behold the seven oceans gathered together here, arrived as soon as they were thought of by those who, weary from the fatigue of fasting, were unable to proceed further.
"O descendant of Raghu, the bark garments cast by them here after their consecration have not dried even to this day in this place.
This entire forest has been seen by you, and what was to be heard has been heard."
Therefore, being permitted by you, I wish to cast off this body;
I desire to go into the presence of those sages of purified souls, whose hermitage I shall serve as an attendant.
Having heard those most righteous words, Rāghava, together with Lakṣmaṇa, spoke with a joyful countenance: "I give you leave;
go. Having been permitted by Rāma, she offered herself as an oblation into the sacrificial fire.
Resembling a blazing fire, she went straight to heaven,
where those great seers of virtuous soul dwell;
by means of her own meditative concentration, she reached that holy abode of Śabarī.
When that Śabarī had departed for heaven by her own karma,
Rāghava, together with his brother Lakṣmaṇa, began to reflect. Having reflected upon that power of the high-souled ones, the righteous-souled one [continued his journey].
3.071.002c Rāghava spoke to Lakṣmaṇa, who was acting for his benefit and was single-mindedly focused:

3.071.003a "O gentle one, this hermitage of those who have perfected themselves has been seen; it is full of many wonders, 3.071.003c where deer and tigers dwell in confidence, and which is frequented by various birds."
O Lakṣmaṇa, having performed ablutions according to the rules at these sacred fords of the seven oceans and having offered libations to the ancestors,
whatever inauspiciousness there was has been destroyed, and prosperity has arrived.
"Because of that, O Lakṣmaṇa, my mind is now filled with joy;
for, O tiger among men, auspiciousness shall manifest within my heart. Therefore, come, let us go to that lovely Pampā lake."
3.071.007a There, not far away, the mountain Ṛśyamūka is visible;
3.071.007c upon it dwells the righteous Sugrīva, the son of Aṃśumat,
3.071.007e who, constantly terrified by the fear of Vālin, lives there with four other monkeys.
"I am in haste to see Sugrīva, that bull among monkeys;
for, O gentle one, the search for Sītā depends entirely upon him.
To Rāma, who was speaking thus, the son of Sumitrā replied as follows:
"Let us go there quickly; my mind also hastens there. Then, having departed from that hermitage, the lord of the people, the subduer of foes, went to Lake Pampā together with Lakṣmaṇa.
Beholding that great forest on all sides,
rich with flowers and vast trees, it resounded with the cries of koyaṣṭis, arjunakas, śatapatras, and kīcakas, as well as various other birds.

3.071.012a That Rāma, though observing the trees and various lakes according to the prescribed manner, 3.071.012c being tormented by desire, proceeded toward a great lake. 3.071.013a Having reached it from afar, Rāma beheld that river flowing with water.
He plunged into the lake named Mataṅgasarasa; Rāma, the son of Daśaratha, overcome with grief,
entered the Pampā lotus pond, which was covered with lotuses.
[It was] filled with *tilaka*, *aśoka*, *puṃnāga*, *bakula*, and *uddālaka* trees, crowded with delightful groves, its waters thick with lotuses,
rich in water as clear as crystal, and strewn with smooth sands.
Crowded with fish and turtles, adorned with trees standing upon its banks,
entwined by creepers as if by companions,
and frequented by kinnaras, uragas, gandharvas, yakṣas, and rākṣasas.
It was filled with various trees and creepers, a beautiful reservoir of cool water; it appeared copper-colored with *saugandhika* lotuses, white with clusters of night-lilies (*kumuda*),
and blue with the abundance of water-lilies (*kuvalaya*), like a multi-colored rug.
3.071.019a Abounding with *aravinda* and *utpala* lotuses, filled with fragrant *padma* flowers, 3.071.019c And endowed with groves of blossoming mango trees, resounding with the cries of peacocks—
3.071.020a Having seen that Pampā lake, Rāma, together with the son of Sumitrā, [was filled with joy].
And the glorious son of Daśaratha lamented out of love:
"With *tilaka* trees, *bījapūra*, *vaṭa*, and white trees,
as well as with blossoming *karavīra* and beautifully flowering *puṃnāga* trees."
It was graced like a young woman by clusters of *mālatī* and *kundaka*, as well as by *bhaṇḍīra*, *nicula*,
*aśoka*, *saptaparṇa*, *ketaka*, and *atimuktaka* trees,
and by various other kinds of trees.
On its bank stands the mountain previously mentioned, adorned with minerals,
renowned as Ṛśyamūka, with its forests variegated by blossoming flowers.
The son of that high-souled one, named Ṛkṣarajas, is a monkey.
"The one of great heroism known as Sugrīva occupies that place.
O bull among men, go to Sugrīva, the lord of monkeys.
Thus he spoke again to Lakṣmaṇa, whose valor is truth.
Then, having traveled by degrees along that great path which extended for a long distance, and gazing upon the forest,
he beheld the Pampā lake, beautiful to behold and surrounded by woods.
crowded with many various kinds of birds.
